<term>Manichaeism</term>: A major religious movement that saw the universe as a struggle between a good world of light and an evil world of darkness.
<term>Alticozzi</term>: An 18th-century Jesuit author who wrote "The History of Manichaeism."
<term>Hermetic Philosophy</term>: A philosophical and esoteric tradition based on writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.
<term>Pelican in its piety</term>: A Christian and alchemical symbol of sacrifice and rebirth.
<term>Roses</term>: Often used in esoteric traditions (like Rosicrucianism) to represent the unfolding of the soul or the heart.

# A HISTORICAL-CRITICAL
## DISSERTATION
### CONCERNING THE ANCIENT AND NEW MANICHAEANS.

<note>Manichaeism was a major dualistic religion that taught a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness. St. Augustine was famously a member before converting to Christianity and later became its most famous critic.</note>

# PREFACE
## TO THE READER.

The reason that drove me to write this Historical-Critical Dissertation on the ancient and new Manichaeans <note>Manichaeism was a major dualistic religion founded in the 3rd century AD by the prophet Mani, teaching a struggle between a good world of light and an evil world of darkness</note>, Dear Reader, was this: when I prefixed three Prefaces to the last three books of my Augustinian *Summa* <term>Summa: a comprehensive compendium or "summary" of a body of knowledge, common in theological writing</term>, the first of which embraced the Pelagian <note>the followers of Pelagius, who emphasized human free will over divine grace</note>, the second the Semi-Pelagian, and the third the Predestinarian history, these did not seem entirely useless or ill-timed for our present age to those into whose hands they came. Therefore, those who hold great influence over me through their authority, kindness, and favor, strongly encouraged me to devote my labor to writing dissertations of this kind—especially since the most excellent records of these matters are found in the works of Saint Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a primary source for early Christian history and a fierce opponent of Manichaeism</note>, of whom they knew I was a devoted student. Yielding, therefore, to their enthusiasm, I took up the history of the Manichaeans. To prepare this work, I did not follow small streams, but went to the sources themselves, so that I might draw the purer truth from their crystal-clear waters. For besides secular writers, and besides the historians of Church affairs—Eusebius, Socrates, Theodoret, Peter of Sicily, Photius, Baronius, Noël Alexandre, and Tillemont <note>original: "Tillemontium"; the author refers here to a list of significant Greek and Roman historians and contemporary ecclesiastical scholars</note>—

<summary>The author explains his motivation for writing this historical-critical study of Manichaeism, citing the success of his previous works on Augustine and his commitment to using primary sources.</summary>
<keywords>Manichaeism, Saint Augustine, Church History, Pelagianism, Historiography, Primary Sources, Ecclesiastical Writers</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the list of authorities and sources from the previous page, completing the name of Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont ("Tillemontium"). It transitions from citing historical witnesses to defining the author's argument regarding the "perpetuity" of heresy.</meta>

tmont, to whom add Possidius of Calama <note>Possidius (370–437 AD) was a close friend of St. Augustine and wrote his first biography</note>, and Bossuet <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704), a celebrated French bishop and theologian known for his oratory</note> of more illustrious memory. I have used as most certain witnesses Archelaus, Athanasius, Titus of Bostra, Epiphanius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Augustine, Leo the Great, John of Damascus, and others like them. 

Since I have decided to deal not only with the old Manichaeans <note>followers of a dualistic religion that saw the world as a struggle between light and dark</note>, but also with the *new* Manichaeans—or rather the successors of the Manichaeans—such as the Predestinarian Cathars <note>The Cathars were a medieval sect in Europe who held dualistic beliefs similar to Manichaeism</note>, or Albigensians, and those whom I judge to be Lutherans, Calvinists, and Jansenists <note>Jansenism was a Catholic theological movement, later condemned, that emphasized original sin and divine grace in a way the author finds similar to older heresies</note>; regarding the Albigensians, I consulted the work of Moneta <note>Moneta of Cremona (c. 1180–1240), a Dominican inquisitor who wrote a famous refutation of heretics</note>, published from the shadows into the light by the Reverend Father V. C. Richinius, Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace <note>Thomas Augustinus Ricchini (1695–1779), who edited Moneta’s historical manuscripts</note>, and illustrated with most excellent annotations. Regarding the Lutherans, I consulted Martin Luther himself and Wolf; for the Calvinists, John Calvin; and for the Jansenists, I turned to Cornelius Jansen himself. By employing their own testimonies, I might demonstrate what I had proposed for myself: namely, to show not only the antiquity but also the *perpetuity* <term>perpetuity: the idea of an unbroken, continuous existence through time</term> of the Manichaean heresy. 

Perhaps someone here might say that, by this path and reasoning, nearly the whole of Church tradition is being attributed to the Manichaean heresy—which is a monstrous thing to say <note>original: "nefas dictu"</note> and tears up the very foundations of religion. To these concerns I respond: if antiquity and perpetuity alone were sufficient to define tradition, then one would have to say that all errors and all vices—which have invaded the whole human race from the beginning of the world, after the Fall of Adam, even to our own times—belong to the tradition of the Church. Therefore, besides antiquity and per-

He defends his method by clarifying that "tradition" requires more than just long-standing existence, otherwise sin and error themselves would be considered Church tradition.</summary>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous page's mention of "Cornelius Jansenius" and concludes the word "perpetuity" (per-petuitatem) which began on the previous leaf. The author is transitioning from a list of sources to defining the theological requirements of "tradition."</meta>

perpetuity <note>original: "perpetuitatem"</note>, several things are required for the nature of tradition: first, the truth and holiness of the doctrine handed down; likewise, the authority of God who speaks; and again, the authority of men—both those to whom such doctrine was divinely delivered, such as the Apostles, and those who succeeded them, such as the bishops, who have continually propagated it by the living voice <note>viva voce</note>, and delivered the doctrine and discipline to their posterity as if received hand to hand. Furthermore, for the nature of tradition, no discrepancy is allowed; indeed, the highest conformity with the written word of God and good morals is necessary; finally, the authority of the universal Church in accepting, guarding, and defending the doctrine handed down. Augustine provides the notion of Ecclesiastical tradition in these words in Book 2 of *On Baptism, against the Donatists* <note>The Donatists were a North African sect who argued that the validity of sacraments depended on the moral purity of the priest; Augustine argued against them, stating sacraments belong to Christ, not the minister</note>, chapter 7, number 12, volume 9:

> *There are many things which are not found in the writings of the Apostles, nor in the Councils of their successors; and yet, because they are kept by the whole Church, they are believed to have been handed down and commended by none other than the Apostles themselves.*

And again in Book 4 of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 24, number 31, volume 9:

> *That which the universal Church holds, and which was not instituted by Councils but has always been retained, is most rightly believed to have been delivered by nothing less than Apostolic authority.*

Furthermore, concerning that ancient custom of receiving baptized heretics who return to the Church by the Christian rite without a repetition of baptism <note>The early Church debated whether people baptized by heretical groups needed to be "re-baptized" upon joining the mainstream Church; Augustine held that the original baptism was valid because of the Holy Spirit, not the person performing it</note>—just as he does regarding many other things—the Holy Doctor <note>A title for St. Augustine</note> writes these things in Book 5 of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 23, number 31, volume 9:

> *That custom, which was opposed to Cy-*

livered from Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage, a 3rd-century bishop and martyr</note>, must be believed to have taken its origin from the tradition of the *Apostles*; just as there are many things which the universal Church holds, and for this reason are rightly believed to have been commanded by the *Apostles*, although they are not found in writing. Now truly, neither the ancient pagans <note>original: "gentiles"</note>, nor their philosophers, nor the more ancient heretics, nor Scythianus, nor Terebinthus <note>In early Christian polemics, Scythianus and Terebinthus were described as the predecessors of Mani, the founder of Manichaeism</note>—who were the precursors of the Manichaeans—nor Manichaeus himself, nor the Paulicians, nor the Albigensians <note>Medieval dualist sects often accused by the Catholic Church of being modern-day Manichaeans</note>, nor the Lutherans, nor the Calvinists, nor the Jansenists <note>The followers of Cornelius Jansen; the author is grouping contemporary Protestant and Catholic dissenters with ancient heresies</note> (the successors of the Manichaeans), possess any authority at all in the Church of God. For the doctrine of these men is false, impious, nefarious, and pestiferous, and utterly contrary to good morals and the written word of God; which the Church of Christ has not only never accepted, nor guarded, nor defended, but has even always detested with universal, solemn, and public execrations <note>formal condemnations or curses</note>. Therefore, this execrable doctrine neither has, nor can have, God and Christ the Lord as its author, nor the Apostles as its first teachers, nor the successors of the Apostles, the bishops, as its propagators. Thus, so far is it from the case that the Manichaean heresy—although it be long-lasting and persistent—pertains to the Tradition of the Church, that it rather stands at the furthest distance from Catholic Tradition and is most exceedingly abhorrent to it. These are the things about which I wished you to be forewarned. *Friend Reader, Farewell.*

# LORENZO RICCI
## Superior General of the Society of Jesus.

SINCE several theologians of our same Society have reviewed the book written by Father Lorenzo Alticozzi <note>Lorenzo Alticozzi (1711–1777) was a Jesuit scholar specializing in church history and the refutation of heresies</note>, a Priest of our Society, titled *A Historical-Critical Dissertation on the Ancient and New Manichaeans* <note>original: "Dissertatio Historico-Critica de antiquis, novisque Manichæis". The work seeks to link ancient dualist heresies to contemporary 18th-century theological movements</note>, and have approved that it may be published, we grant the faculty <note>official permission or license, often called an "Imprimatur"</note> for it to be sent to the press, if it so seems fit to those to whom it pertains. In witness of this, we have issued these letters, signed by our hand and secured with our seal. Rome, February 20, 1763.

# A P P R O V A L S .

Having read attentively and with the necessary diligence the *Historical-Critical Dissertation on the Ancient and New Manichaeans* <note>original: "Dissertationem Historico-Criticam de antiquis novisque Manichæis"</note> by Lorenzo Alticozzi of Cortona, a member of the Society of Jesus—a man distinguished not only by the gravity of his character and his profession of the Religious Institute, but also by the books he has more than once published for the public utility and benefit—and having done so at the command of the Most Reverend Father Thomas Augustine Ricchini, Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, I confess that I have found nothing in it that is repugnant to the sincere Religion of Christ our Lord or to the correct rules of morality. And if perhaps it might seem that the boundaries of Manichaeism <note>A dualist heresy originating in the 3rd century; here, the author is likely applying the label to modern theological opponents to suggest they share the same errors.</note> are stretched wider than is strictly proper by a somewhat loose use of the name, the studious Author nevertheless works toward that end led by his own reasons. For which reason, we are of the opinion that this same Dissertation may safely be published to the public through the art of the printers.

Given at Rome in the house of Saint Sylvester on the Quirinal Hill, on the 8th day before the Ides of February <note>February 6, 1763.</note> in the Year of Restored Salvation <note>original: "A. R. S." or "Anno Reparatae Salutis," a common liturgical way to denote the year of the Lord.</note> 1763.

*Antonio Francesco Vezzosi, Cleric Regular.* <note>Vezzosi (1708–1783) was a member of the Theatine Order (Clerics Regular) and a noted scholar and biographer in Rome.</note>

I have read with an attentive mind the *Historical-Critical Dissertation on the Ancient and New Manichaeans* <note>original: "Dissertationem Historico-Criticam de antiquis novisque Manichæis"</note>, written by the Very Reverend Father Lorenzo Alticozzi of Cortona, of the Society of Jesus <note>original: "S. J." (Societatis Jesu). Alticozzi (1711–1777) was a prominent Jesuit polemicist.</note>, at the command of the Most Reverend Father Master of the Sacred Palace. In the explanation of the ancient false doctrine, in the discovery of its primary authors and the uncovering of its new supporters, and in the recitation of the Ecclesiastical and Imperial laws <note>original: "Cæsareisque." This refers to the legal codes of the Roman Emperors (the Caesars), who heavily persecuted the Manichaeans in late antiquity.</note> passed against those same dogmatists, the most diligent Author presents almost nothing that he has not drawn from the very sources themselves. For this reason, he has provided not only for the pleasure but especially for the benefit of those whose interest it is to know the history of the Church. Therefore, I judge that dissertation—which is in no way contrary to the Orthodox Faith or to good morals—to be worthy of the public light, provided that the permission for its publication is granted by those to whom it pertains.

At Rome, in the Monastery of the Twelve Holy Apostles, on the Ides of December, 1762 <note>December 13, 1762.</note>.

# BY LORENZO ALTICOZZI
### OF CORTONA
### PRIEST OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS <note>The Society of Jesus, or the Jesuits, is a Catholic religious order founded by Ignatius of Loyola. Alticozzi was an 18th-century Jesuit scholar.</note>
## DISSERTATION
## HISTORICAL-CRITICAL
### On the Ancient and New Manichaeans. <note>Manichaeism was a major dualistic religion founded by the Iranian prophet Mani in the 3rd century AD, teaching a struggle between a good world of light and an evil world of darkness.</note>

---

# CHAPTER I.
### *Concerning the ancient Pagans who were the precursors of the Manichaeans.*

<margin>The error of the ancient Pagans concerning an eternal evil nature as the cause of all evils.</margin>
I. <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C featuring a classical landscape with buildings and foliage.</image-desc>WHEN the ancient Pagans <note>original: "Gentiles." This refers to non-Christian, polytheistic peoples of antiquity.</note> perceived themselves oppressed and almost overwhelmed by infinite calamities and the heaviest evils, they sought the cause from which so many and such great evils flowed into the entire human race. Since, however, they thought it wicked and impious to say that God—who is supremely good, and whom they were not ignorant of as nature pointed the way—was the author of all the evils by which we are afflicted, they fell by an easy slip into that error in which they believed that a certain eternal evil nature exists, from which all evils flow and emanate to us. # DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS

<margin>Jupiter and Vejovis: the good God and the evil God among the ancient Pagans.</margin>
...produces evil works. But others say that the one who is better is *God*, and the one who is worse is a *Demon*. This is the origin, according to Gellius (1), of those names and the divine worship of Jupiter <note>original: "Jovis." Jupiter was the king of the gods in Roman mythology.</note> and Vejovis <note>An early Roman deity often associated with the underworld or a "negative" Jupiter; the name implies a god who lacks the power to help.</note>, of whom the former was named by the ancient Pagans for helping, and the latter for not helping—or rather, for doing harm. *When they had named Jupiter from helping,* he [Gellius] says, *they also called his opposite "Vejovis"—that god who had not the power of helping but the force of harming—by removing and taking away the capacity for helping. For they celebrated certain Gods so that they might be beneficial, and they appeased others so they would not be harmful. Therefore, the statue of the God Vejovis, which is in the temple between the Citadel and the Capitol, holds arrows, which are ready to do harm.* Arnobius (2) bears witness that this false opinion prevailed among the Pagans right up until Christian times; addressing them, he says: *We have received it from your own words that some of the Gods are good, while others are evil and more prone to the lust for harming; and that solemn sacred rites are performed for the former so they might help, and for the latter so they do not harm.* Nor was that discordant opinion—concerning good and evil Gods, with the former being the authors of good and the latter the authors of evil—entirely erased from the minds of those Pagans who still lived among Christians in the age of Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Christian theologians.</note>. *Some think,* says the Holy Doctor (3), *that evil Gods must be appeased with sacrifices so they do not harm, while the good are to be invoked so they might help.*

### AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS

<note>This header refers to the Manichaeans, a religious group that believed the universe was a struggle between a good realm of light and an evil realm of darkness. The "New Manichaeans" likely refers to later groups the author considers heirs to this dualistic philosophy.</note>

...how brilliantly Chrysostom (1) speaks: "For what reason," he says, "do many know that man Zoroaster, and likewise Zamolxis <note>A legendary social and religious reformer of the Getae people in Thrace, often compared to Pythagoras.</note>, by name, yet in truth almost no one—or only a very few—actually knows them? Is it not because everything circulated about them was a fabrication?"

<margin>Zoroaster, a Persian-Mede and philosopher of the Persians in the time of Darius Hystaspes <note>Darius I, King of Persia (r. 522–486 BCE).</note>, taught there were two Gods: a good one, whom he called Oromazas <note>original: "Oromazam," referring to Ahura Mazda, the supreme creator god in Zoroastrianism.</note>, and an evil one, whom he called Arimanius <note>original: "Arimanium," referring to Angra Mainyu or Ahriman, the destructive spirit.</note>; and between these he placed Mithra, namely the Sun.</margin>

Yet it seems certain and well-investigated, as many writers record, that a certain man existed who was celebrated by the name of Zoroaster. Jacobus Burckhard <note>original: "Burkerius." Likely refers to Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), a pioneering historian of philosophy.</note> thinks it not improbable, nor to be rashly rejected (2), that this man was a Persian-Mede who flourished in the times of Darius Hystaspes. To him are usually attributed the introduction of Magic among the Persians and the restoration of the religion of the Magi, as well as the writings praised under Zoroaster’s name. Indeed, Clement of Alexandria (3) identifies Zoroaster as a Mede-Persian. Laertius (4) writes: *It is recorded that the Magi were the authors of philosophy among the Persians, and that their leader was Zoroaster the Persian.* Plutarch (5) follows Zoroaster’s opinion and his teachings regarding two principles—one the author of all good things, the other the author of all evil—with these words:

*Some believe there are two Gods, as if devoted to contrary arts, such that one effects good works and the other evil. Others call the better one "God" and the worse one a "Demon." This was the opinion of Zoroaster the Magus, who they say existed five hundred years before the Trojan War. This Zoroaster, then, gave the name Oromazas to the better one and Arimanius to the worse. The former he considered most like light, and the latter like darkness and ignorance. Between these is Mithra (the Sun). This is why the Persians call Mithra "Mesites" <note>original: "Meſiten," a Greek term for "Mediator."</note>, that is, the Mediator or intermediary. And he taught that votive offerings and victims offered for the sake of giving thanks should be sacrificed to him...*

III. Now I turn my attention to the Persian Magi, whose name among their own people was a mark of virtue and praise; it signified the same thing as "Philosopher" does among the Greeks and "Wise Man" among the Latins. These men taught that there are two principles: a good one, from which all good things proceed, and an evil one, from which all evil things originate. They called the good principle the "Good Spirit," as well as "Jupiter" and "Horosmadis"; conversely, they called the evil principle the "Evil Spirit," "Pluto," and "Arimanius." So says (1) Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius (3rd century CE), a biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note>, having produced the most reliable witnesses such as Aristotle, Hermippus, Eudoxus, and Theopompus. *Aristotle is the authority in his first book "On Philosophy,"* he says, *that the Magi are more ancient than the Egyptians, and that according to them there are two principles: a good spirit and an evil spirit. <margin>The religion, customs, and discipline of the Persian Magi.</margin>

*He says the Magi devote themselves to the worship of the Gods, and offer prayers, vows, and sacrifices to them, as if they alone are truly heard by the deities. They discuss the substance and generation of the Gods, whom they also consider to be earth, water, and fire. They condemn the use of statues and images, and especially disapprove of the errors of those who claim that the Gods are male and female. They speak of Justice and consider it a great wrong to bury the dead by fire <note>original: "igni sepelire," referring to the Zoroastrian prohibition against cremation, as fire was considered a sacred, pure element that should not be defiled by dead flesh.</note>.*

For they worshipped fire as a great God. <note>The author refers here to the Persian Magi, who viewed fire as a physical manifestation of the divine.</note> They considered it lawful for a son to be joined to his mother or a father to his daughter. However, what Plutarch says—that Horomasdes was born from the purest light and Arimanius, conversely, from gloom—must not be understood as if one was the literal son of light and the other the son of gloom. This is because these two contrary deities were, among the Persians, eternal, unbegotten, and uncreated principles. Therefore, Horomasdes is said to be "born" from the purest light because he consisted of the purest light; Arimanius, truly, was "born" from gloom because he consisted of gloom and darkness. Nor indeed does that testimony of Theodore of Mopsuestia <note>A 4th-century Christian theologian and influential biblical interpreter.</note> stand in the way, which is found in (2) Photius regarding Persian history...

> *At that time,* he says, *a certain Manichaeus attempted to secretly introduce the dogma of the pagan philosopher Empedocles <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 490–430 BCE) who theorized that the universe was composed of four elements acted upon by two opposing forces: Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion).</note> into the Christian Religion. For in this way it will be understood who Manichaeus was and from where he came to break forth into such audacity. Scythianus introduced the opinion of Empedocles and Pythagoras into the Christian Religion. For he asserted that there are two natures, one good and the other evil, just as Empedocles did, who called the evil nature "Discord" and the good nature "Friendship."*

Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 CE), the scholar and Bible translator.</note> (3) is the authority for the claim that the Stoic philosophers first, and then the Manichaeans, taught that the souls of individual men are particles of the divine nature; he wrote these things to those consulting him about the origin of the soul:

> *Regarding the state of the soul, I remember your question: Whether it fell from heaven, as the philosopher Pythagoras, all the Platonists, and Origen think; or whether it is from God’s own substance, as the Stoics, Manichaeus, and the Spanish heresy of Priscillian <note>Priscillian of Avila, a 4th-century bishop executed for heresy whose teachings were often linked by his enemies to Manichaeism.</note> suspect.*

Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman orator and philosopher.</note> (4), the most keen observer of all the Stoics, affirms and proves that Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans held this same opinion which Manichaeus seized upon:

> *I used to hear,* he says, *that Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans—almost our own neighbors, who were once called the "Italian philosophers"—never doubted that we possessed souls plucked from the universal divine mind.*

Furthermore, that Mani taught the transmigration of souls—which is called <term>Metempsychosis</term> <note>From the Greek meaning "the passage of the soul from one body to another."</note> by the Greeks—from one body into another, and that he took this from the ancient philosophers...

### Concerning Scythianus, the Precursor of the Manichaeans.

<margin>Scythianus the Saracen <note>In this context, "Saracen" refers generally to Arab peoples of the desert.</note>, a Pagan, an Arab by nation, an Egyptian by residence, and a precursor of the Manichaeans.</margin>
VIII. **I** draw the history of Scythianus from St. Cyril of Jerusalem, St. Epiphanius of Salamis, St. Archelaus the bishop of Mesopotamia, Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380–439 AD), a Greek Christian church historian.</note>, Photius <note>Photius the Great (c. 810–893 AD), Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar.</note>, and Tillemont <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French ecclesiastical historian known for his meticulous accuracy.</note>. Regarding the fact that he was named Scythianus, was a Saracen by race, and a Pagan <note>original: "Gentilis"</note> by superstition, almost all agree to a man. As for what pertains to Scythianus's homeland, (2) Epiphanius records that he was born on the borders of Palestine and educated in Arabia. Tillemont (3), who has served the polished history of the Church extremely well, differs little from Epiphanius, stating that Scythianus emerged from the part of Arabia closest to Palestine. It must be said, therefore, that Scythianus was born in Arabia, which the Saracens inhabited at that time. But indeed, we have received from Archelaus (4) that Scythianus was from Scythia...

However, it is well established that in that age the *Saracens* were inhabitants of *Arabia*, not *Scythia*. Photius (2), perhaps because of *Scythianus's* long residence in *Egypt*, records that *Scythianus* was an *Egyptian* by homeland.

<margin>
*Scythianus was born at the end of the 1st Century and came to Jerusalem in the middle of the 2nd Century.*
</margin>
The question of establishing the age of *Scythianus* is more serious. Archelaus (3) writes that he existed in the time of the Apostles; Epiphanius (4) says he arrived in *Jerusalem* during the time of the Apostles; Tillemont (5) writes that *Scythianus* lived in the year of Christ 150. These dates, however, seem to conflict with the established age of *Mani*, which must be dealt with in its proper place. But if we say that *Scythianus* was born at the end of the first century, when *John*—the last of the Apostles—passed away, and that he arrived in *Jerusalem* in the middle of the second century when many disciples of the Apostles were still surviving (such as *Simeon*, the successor of *James* and bishop of *Jerusalem*, who died at the age of 120), and if those times were commonly referred to as the "Apostolic age," then all these accounts are easily reconciled with one another.

<margin>
*Scythianus, abounding in wealth, came to Egypt, where he married a slave and prostitute. He was trained in Greek, Egyptian, and Christian literature, and the magic of the Indians. He published four books: the Gospel, the Chapters, the Mysteries, and the Treasure.*
</margin>

# DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS

...-laus and Epiphanius, he fell in love with a certain young woman who was remarkably beautiful but of low status—a slave and a common prostitute. He later married her and eventually granted her freedom. At her persuasion—as recorded by Archelaus (1) and Socrates—he left the desert regions of the Thebaid and arrived in Alexandria, the primary city of Egypt. There, according to Cyril (2), Socrates, and Photius, he established a permanent home. Archelaus (3) describes him as a man of outstanding talent, and Photius (4) testifies that he was skilled in the Greek language through a long habit of reading Aristotle, whose works he misused <note>original: "abusus est"</note> to bolster his own errors. Tillemont (5) records that he learned the sciences of the Egyptians, the magical arts of the Indians, and the religions, rites, and customs of the Jews and Christians, as well as the Scythians. Epiphanius (6) further notes that he was devoted to magical illusions <note>original: "Magicis etiam præstigiis"</note> drawn from Indian, Egyptian, and pagan <note>original: "Gentiliumque"</note> superstition.

Cyril (7), Epiphanius, Photius, and Archelaus record that he produced four books addressed to his disciple, Terebinthus. He titled the first the ***Gospel***, the second the ***Chapters***, the third the ***Mysteries***, and the fourth the ***Treasure***. These four mentioned books contain the entirety of the Scythian heresy. According to Archelaus (8), Epiphanius, and Tillemont, he cobbled this heresy together <note>original: "confarcinavit," literally "stuffed together" or "crammed."</note> not only from the secular teachings of Aristotle, Pythagoras, and Empedocles, but also from the divine oracles of the Jews and Christians, which he maliciously corrupted and craftily interpreted. The most fundamental and most destructive error of Scythianus...

## AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS

...from which, as if from a most filthy spring <note>original: "tanquam ex sordidissimo fonte," a common polemical metaphor used by Church historians to describe the origin of heresies.</note>, his other absurdities flowed. It was rooted in the fact that he established two eternal principles fighting against each other, which were likewise unbegotten: one good, from which all good things flow; the other evil, from which all evil things necessarily flow forth: as is found in Archelaus (1), Epiphanius, and Tillemont.

<margin>Scythianus teaches two eternal, contrary principles. He travels from Alexandria to Jerusalem, where he is refuted by the Christian Elders <note>original: "Presbyteris"</note>, disciples of the Apostles. Indulging in magical illusions, he is cast down by a demon and dies.</margin>

X. It is fitting here to present the very words of Scythianus, as we have them in Epiphanius (2), which are as follows: *“For what reason is it,” he said, “that the things contained in this whole universe are unequal—such as white and black, yellow and green, moist and dry, heaven and earth, night and day, soul and body, good and evil, just and unjust—unless it be that these have arisen from two principles?”* By these words, Scythianus contended that from the contrary things which we perceive in this universe, two eternal and unbegotten contrary principles are demonstrated, which serve as the opposing causes of opposing things. Since such a most deadly <note>original: "capitalissimus," literally "head-offense" or "most fatal."</note> error is the foundation of the entire Manichaean heresy, it is with the best of right that not Mani, but Scythianus, is called the author and prince of this sect by Archelaus (3). 

Infected with this plague of doctrine, and accompanied by his disciple Terebinthus, Scythianus departed from Alexandria and traveled to Jerusalem—the primary city of Judea and Palestine—so that he might debate with the more learned elders <term>presbyters: early Christian leaders or priests</term> there and, if possible, persuade them of his errors. But it happened with a completely contrary outcome: he was refuted by the Jerusalem elders, nor was he able to corrupt anyone among the people with his heresy, as recorded by Cyril (4), Photius, Archelaus, and Tillemont. <margin>With Terebinthus dead, the old widow took possession of his riches and the books of Scythianus.</margin>
She, however, felt no distress at the death of Terebinthus, but rather rejoiced greatly. This was partly because she was freed from the terror that had often made her shudder when Terebinthus devoted himself to horrid sorceries, foul mysteries, and the summoning of the Manes <note>original: "Manibus". In Roman and late antique belief, the Manes were the spirits of the dead; here, it refers to the practice of necromancy or spirit-summoning</note>, and partly because she had come into a most wealthy inheritance of gold, silver, and precious goods. These were the riches that Scythianus had brought from Egypt into Palestine, which Terebinthus—as the heir of Scythianus—had then carried into Persia and brought into the widow's house.

Furthermore, she obtained the four books of Scythianus mentioned above, which Terebinthus had claimed as his own. Enriched by these goods, the old widow spent many years living a pleasant and luxurious life. During this time, I believe that a certain Zaranes <note>Zaranes is cited by Byzantine historians as a pivotal "middle link" in the development of Manichaean thought between the earlier Scythianus and the later Manes</note> existed—a defender of this same heresy before the fable was concocted and promulgated by Manes.

Regarding Zaranes, I have only two witnesses; though they are few in number, they are of the greatest weight: Photius <note>Photius (c. 810–893 AD) was the Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar who documented many heretical groups</note> and Peter of Sicily <note>Peter of Sicily was a 9th-century Byzantine diplomat and historian who wrote an influential treatise against the Paulicians and Manichaeans</note>.

And indeed, Peter of Sicily (1), in his work *On the Vain and Foolish Manichaean Heresy*—as it is titled by him—says this of Zaranes: *But before this man (Manes) there was another author of this impiety, Zaranes, who was not unlike him in character.*

<margin>Zaranes, the most recent precursor to the Manichaean.</margin>
Photius (2), in his *History of the Manichaeans*, recorded these things for the memory of posterity: *Furthermore, another man slightly older in time than this one (Manes), equal in impiety and named Zaranes, brought no small amount of harm to the human race through his wicked deeds.*

Therefore, three singular men are remembered as the predecessors of Manes, who sowed the seeds of almost all the same impieties later held by Manes: Scythianus, Terebinthus, and Zaranes.

# CHAPTER V.

## *Concerning Manes, who was first called Curbicus, and afterwards Manichaean.*

<margin>
Manes, a Persian by nation, a slave by condition, a Pagan by religion, a Persian Magus, and priest of Mithras; while in slavery he was called Curbicus, but having become free, he was named Manes—which means "wise" in Persian—and finally he was called Manichaeus and Mannichaeus by his Greek disciples.
</margin>

XIV. Manes, a Persian by nation (1), was from his earliest origin (2) a slave, and by religion (3) a pagan, just as his predecessors Scythianus, Terebinthus, and Zaranes had been. As long as he remained in servitude (4), he was called Curbicus; though perhaps through a slight slip of the scribes, or some other accident, he is referred to as Corbicius in the works of (5) Archelaus, while in Augustine he is called Urbicus. When he was granted his freedom (6), he exchanged the obscure name of Curbicus for the more illustrious name of Manes, which among the Persians signifies a "dialectician" <note>A person skilled in logical disputation and reasoning</note>, but among the Chaldeans <note>The language of ancient Mesopotamia, often associated with astrology and magic in the late antique period</note> signifies a "Vessel fashioned for honor" <note>original: "Vas ad honorem factum". This is a biblical allusion to Romans 9:21, suggesting a vessel chosen for a special, divine purpose</note>. However, since among the Greeks (7) the name "Manes" sounds exactly like "insane" or "raving" <note>The author is highlighting a linguistic pun: the name Manes sounded like the Greek word "mania," meaning madness</note>, the disciples of Manes—in order to more smoothly influence the ears of the Greeks whom they were striving to corrupt with their heresy—called their master "Manichaeus," as if to suggest "flowing Manna" <note>original: "fluens Manna". Manna was the miraculous food provided to the Israelites in the desert; the disciples used this name to make his teachings seem like divine, life-giving bread</note>. But this was surely a foolish plan, because among the Greeks "Manichaeus" signifies...

...ichaean and pouring out madness <note>original: "maniam fundens"</note>, that is, fury and insanity. For this reason, some of the more clever and sharp-witted Manichaeans, by doubling the letter 'n', used to call him not "Manichaean" but "Mannichaean," as if their master were pouring out not insanity, but Manna <note>The miraculous "bread from heaven" provided to the Israelites in the Bible; the followers used this wordplay to distance their leader from the Greek word for madness</note>. XV. Regarding the era of Manes, this must be traced from his arrival in the Roman Empire, when he escaped from a Persian prison and sought refuge as a fugitive in Mesopotamia, which marked the eastern boundary of the Roman Empire. This incursion of Manes into Mesopotamia occurred in the second year of the Emperor Probus, during the consulship of Probus and Paulinus—that is, in the year of Christ 277. In establishing this as the starting point <note>original: "epocha"</note>, almost all reputable writers agree: Archelaus (2), who was a contemporary of Manes, Cyril of Jerusalem, Epiphanius, Leo the Great, Jerome, Freculphus, and others who came after them. Nor do the other indications about Manes' era provided by these and other writers contradict this; but if they do differ, either a probable interpretation or a proper correction must be applied to them. And indeed, Archelaus (3) clearly taught that Manes became known under the Roman Emperor Probus; yet, in the heat of his debate with Manes—who claimed to be the Holy Spirit...

# DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS #

<page-num>20</page-num>

<header>DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS</header>

...was most impiously preaching that he was the Paraclete <note>original: "Paraclitum"; the Holy Spirit or "Comforter" promised by Jesus in the New Testament</note> promised by Christ. Archelaus, mocking him, said: *"Jesus, who had said that he would send the Paraclete not long after, is found to have sent Manes after three hundred and more years."* Yet this age does not align with the time of Emperor Probus <note>Reigned 276–282 AD</note>. One must say, therefore, that this occurred either through a mistake of the scribes, or of the Greek or Latin translator, since Archelaus wrote in Syriac (or Syro-Chaldean). If this explanation is not satisfactory, I would say that Archelaus—either using the license permitted to an orator, or in the very heat and fervor of the debate which he held with Manes in the year 277—shouted out those "full three hundred and more years" for greater rhetorical effect. However, Leo (1) the Great, indicating that time when the cursed name of Manes became known throughout the Roman Empire, records the following: *"Manes, the minister of diabolical falsehood and founder of a filthy superstition, became known and was to be condemned at that time when the two hundred and sixtieth year after the Lord’s resurrection was completed, during the reign of Emperor Probus and the consulship of Paulinus, while the eighth persecution was already raging against the Christians."*

XVI. You will say that the chronology wavers in this passage, or rather falls flat, and Leo seems to contradict himself. For if, as he himself teaches, Manes first became known in the Roman Empire during the reign of Emperor Probus and the consulship of Paulinus—that is, in the year of Christ 277—it is impossible for him to have first become known in the Roman Empire in the two hundred and sixtieth year after the resurrection of Christ. For if you add the thirty-three years of Christ's life to the two hundred and sixty years after the Lord's resurrection (according to the common opinion), you will arrive not at the year of Christ 277, but at the year 293 for the time of Emperor Probus and Consul Paulinus. The eminent Petavius <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a famous Jesuit scholar and chronologist</note>, in his notes on the 66th heresy of Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop who wrote the 'Panarion' against heresies</note>, believes that an error was made here by Leo’s scribe, who misplaced the Roman numeral 'X', and instead of writing 240 years after the Lord's resurrection, wrote 260 years. # AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS #

Indeed, the distinguished <term>V. C.</term> <note>abbreviation for *Vir Clarissimus*, a title of honor for a high-ranking man, meaning "most distinguished"</note> Cacciarius, in his published annotations on Saint Leo, judges that the "two hundred and sixty years" after the Lord’s resurrection should be entirely retained. He bases this on the fact that all the codices of Leo he consulted have the years expressed not in Roman numerals, but in common letters as *two hundred and sixty*. The distinguished Ballerini brothers, in their edition of Saint Leo—to whom you may add Quesnel in his own edition—believe that in place of the 260 years after the Lord's resurrection, one should read 250 years. <margin>The words of St. Leo regarding the arrival of Manes in Mesopotamia are explained.</margin> To explain this difficulty, I believe it must be said that Saint Leo, in that passage of his sermon to the people, was not overly concerned with counting the exact years from the resurrection of the Lord to the arrival of Manes in Mesopotamia (the furthest eastern province of the Roman Empire). For in that passage, Saint Leo had proposed to demonstrate that Manes had sold himself <note>i.e., promoted himself or "sold" the idea</note> as the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Spiritum-Sanctum"</note> promised by Christ the Lord with an utterly unbelievable lie. Indeed, Christ the Lord, after he rose and before he ascended into heaven, promised that he would send the Holy Spirit after only a few days; therefore, He did not mean after the very many years that passed from the resurrection of Christ until the arrival of Manes in Mesopotamia. In order to demonstrate this, Leo—speaking according to the occasion and the circumstances, and using the "oratorical license" common to speakers—pronounced a certain and definite number of years (namely 260) to represent a generally large number. This number does not stray too far from the 244 years that had actually elapsed from the resurrection of Christ the Lord until the arrival of Manes in Mesopotamia. If these explanations are not pleasing, it remains to be said that the earlier scribes of this sermon—from whom others subsequently copied—made a slip of the pen, writing "sixty" instead of the full number "forty," a mistake easily made and worthy of forgiveness. As for what pertains to the eighth persecution, this is the persecution of Valerian, which the ninth persecution, under Emperor Probus and the Consul Paulinus, had not yet followed.

XVII. I come now to Cyril of Jerusalem,

For it could happen that elderly men of eighty, ninety, or a hundred years were still living then, who—according to the rule of a good reasoner—might have seen Manes in Mesopotamia in the year 277 during their ninth year of childhood, their fifteenth year of adolescence, or their twenty-fifth year of youth. Nor do these words of Cyril differ from those in which he mocks Manes, who impiously and impudently preached that he was the Holy Spirit promised to the Apostles. *“What then?”* he says mockingly (2), *“Were the Apostles, who had been dead for two hundred years, waiting for Mani so that they might finally put on the power (of the Holy Spirit)?”*

And may the <term>right hand of light</term><note>A technical term in Manichaean theology; Mani often used Christian-sounding language to mask his dualistic concepts of Light and Dark.</note> preserve you from this present evil age, and from its ruin, and from the snares of the wicked one.* The main point of the letter was this: that he had been sent for the correction of the human race. He claimed that Marcellus and the rest of the Christians were involved in that error which the "teachers of the emperors" <note>A likely reference to the mainstream or orthodox church leaders of the Roman Empire.</note> teach: that good and evil, and all other opposites, arise from one and the same principle. Likewise, he claimed that Christ the Lord was the son of a certain woman named Mary, generated from blood and flesh and the rest of the filth of women. Thus far speak the (1) most abundant witnesses, who are worthy of the strongest faith.

<margin>Marcellus, a foremost Christian nobleman, writes back to Mani; Mani receives the letter from Callistus, a servant of Marcellus.</margin>
XXI. Having received the letter from Mani through <term>Turbo</term><note>Mani’s disciple who, according to tradition, eventually became disillusioned with Mani's teachings and provided Archelaus with information to refute them.</note> his disciple—whom Marcellus had welcomed with very kind hospitality—Marcellus read it aloud in the presence of Archelaus, the distinguished bishop of the people of Caschara. Then, without any delay, he wrote back to Mani. The version of the letter from Marcellus to Mani, as found in Archelaus, was of this sort: *Marcellus, a man known to Mani, who indicated himself to him by a letter, greetings. I have indeed received the letter written by you, and I have welcomed Turbo with my usual hospitality. However, I have by no means understood the sense of your letters, unless perhaps you, being present, might explain it to us word by word, just as you promised. Farewell.* Having sealed the letter, he gave it to be carried by Turbo—who had already been called back from the errors of Mani by the efforts of Marcellus and Archelaus—

<margin>Turbo stays with Marcellus and Archelaus, the Bishop of Caschara, to whom he recounts the entire heresy of Mani; through their efforts, he rejects Mani's errors.</margin>
Meanwhile, questioned by Archelaus and Marcellus, Turbo explained the entire myth of Mani to both in a very detailed account, as read in the works of Archelaus. This account was reduced to a shorter summary by <term>Epiphanius</term><note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a bishop known for his massive compendium of heresies titled the *Panarion*.</note> as follows: *Mani established two principles, which both lacked a beginning and would never end, and were contrary to one another. One he called light and good; the other darkness and evil, so that they are the same as God and the devil. Indeed, he sometimes called them both "Gods"—specifically, a good God and an evil God. From these two principles, all things arose and were established; from one all good things proceed, and from the other all evil things, which find their existence in this world through both principles. Furthermore, he claimed the body was created by one of them, and the soul by the other. This soul is present not only in humans but also in other animals—even in birds, serpents, and beasts—and indeed, even in plants.*

<margin>Mani arrives at Caschara accompanied by twelve chosen youths; he searches for Turbo in vain and enters to see Marcellus.</margin>
On that very same day, Mani arrived at Caschara bringing twelve chosen young men with him. First, he searched for Turbo at Marcellus's door but did not find him, because Turbo, having already rejected the errors of that <term>old trickster</term><note>Latin: "veteratoris." A derogatory term used by the author to describe Mani's perceived deceitfulness.</note>, had hidden himself to avoid the sight of his detestable master. And so Mani entered to see Marcellus, presenting an elderly and solemn appearance; yet his body was dressed like a vainglorious soldier, in a manner quite unusual and ridiculous. 

<margin>Archelaus, the Bishop of Caschara, debates Mani in a public and solemn trial; he refutes him excellently, and the judges award the victory to Archelaus.</margin>

Four judges were chosen: Manippus, Aegialus, Claudius, and Cleobulus—men outstanding in literature and learning, but <term>pagans</term><note>Latin: "gentiles." The author notes they were chosen specifically because they were not Christians, ensuring they would appear impartial to Mani.</note> by religion, so that, if they were Christians, they might not be suspected by Mani of being disciples of Archelaus. It was agreed. The selected Judges sat in their designated place, and Mani began with these opening words:

> *I, my brothers, am indeed a disciple of Christ, and an Apostle of Jesus. I am indeed the <term>Paraclete</term><note>From the Greek *paraklētos*, meaning "Advocate" or "Comforter." The summary of Mani’s argument was this: that there are two contrary principles, both eternal and uncreated, neither of which depends on the other. One is good, from which all good things come; the other is evil, from which all evil things proceed. Each of these occupies a nearly infinite space, separated from the other by a vast distance. He claimed the Old Testament was the work of the evil principle. Everything we see in this earthly world, including humans themselves, arose from a mixture of the good nature with the evil nature. Mani’s concluding speech was immediately followed by the refutation of Archelaus (1). This response was so vigorous, strong, and invincible—and supported by so many clear reasons and firm arguments—that the judges easily awarded the victory to Archelaus.

<margin>Archelaus and Marcellus calm the mob’s attack against Mani.</margin>
But indeed, the people were so violently moved by Mani’s exceedingly absurd, jarring, and impious opinions that they first began to riot, and then attempted to stone the charlatan and impious man. They would have succeeded, had Marcellus and Archelaus not used the great authority and dignity they held among the people to calm the rioting multitude.

<margin>Mani flees Caschara for Diodoris on the borders of Mesopotamia by the banks of the Stranga river.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the organizational structure and leadership of the Manichaean sect following the death of its founder. It focuses on the primary disciples of Mani and the discrepancies between historical accounts regarding their number and names.</meta>

->### AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS.<-

Eusebius (1), Theodoret, Peter the Sicilian, Photius, and the most distinguished of them all, Augustine (2), whose words these are:

> *Mani had twelve disciples after the pattern of the apostolic number, a number which the Manichaeans preserve even today. For from among their "elect" they have twelve whom they call masters, and a thirteenth who is their leader.*

Peter the Sicilian, mentioned above, with whom Photius agrees, provides the names of each one in these words:

> *The disciples of Mani the Antichrist were twelve: Siginius, who succeeded Mani; Thomas, who composed a new Gospel for the Manichaeans; Buddas, and Hermas; Adantus, and Adimantus, whom he sent out to various parts of the world as a herald. The interpreters and explainers of Mani were Hierax, Heraclides, and Aphtonius. Joined to these were three other followers of this sect: Agapius, who devised the Heptalogum <note>original: "Heptalogum," likely a reference to a lost work of "Seven Treatises."</note>, Zarvus, and Gabriabius.*

Adimantus, of whom Photius and Peter the Sicilian speak, seems to be the one against whom Augustine wrote, and who in that place (3) is described as:

> *One of the disciples of Mani, whom they record as having been a great teacher of that sect.*

And in another place (4):

> *If you review what I have written against Adimantus, who is boasted to have been a follower of Mani while he was still alive.*

But Epiphanius (5) disagrees with the witnesses mentioned above, asserting that Mani appointed twenty-two disciples for himself. Archelaus, in a similar matter, contradicts himself, or so the words suggest. For Archelaus (6), according to Zacagnius, who published the Cassinese manuscript, relates that Mani came into Mesopotamia surrounded by a crowd of twenty-two "elect" young men.

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the discrepancy between various historical accounts of Mani's life. Specifically, it resolves a contradiction between the number of disciples (12 vs. 22) reported in the writings of Archelaus—a 4th-century Christian bishop known for his "Acts of the Disputation with Mani"—and other sources.</meta>

->### DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS ###<-

<meta>The word "rat" completes the word "publicaverat" (had published) from the previous page.</meta>

...had published. But this same <term>Archelaus</term><note>A bishop of Caschar who wrote a famous, though partially legendary, account of a debate with Mani.</note>, according to Valesius—who placed the incomplete <term>Bobbio manuscript</term><note>A famous Latin manuscript from the Bobbio Abbey, now held in the Ambrosian Library in Milan.</note> at the end of his notes on Socrates and Sozomen, having received it from the distinguished Emericus Bigotius—testifies that <term>Mani</term><note>The Persian founder of Manichaeism (216–274 AD).</note> slipped into Mesopotamia with a company of only twelve chosen young men. However, both contradictions are easily resolved if we say, as is most probable, that this happened through a simple slip of the pen—a pardonable error by either a Latin or Greek translator or scribe. They may have used the Greek numerical mark **KB** (which signifies twenty-two in Greek) instead of the Greek numerical mark **IB** (which signifies twelve). Therefore, the number of twelve disciples for Mani ought to be retained. Regarding the mission of the three specially selected disciples of Mani, <term>Turbo</term><note>In the "Acts of Archelaus," Turbo is a disciple of Mani's student Addas who eventually defects and reveals the sect's secrets.</note> in both versions of the Archelaus manuscript records the following:

<margin>Mani delegates his three primary disciples, Addas, Thomas, and Hermas, to spread the heresy in the primary parts of the world.</margin>

> *This is the entire doctrine that Mani delivered to his three disciples, and he commanded them to set out for the three regions of the world. Of these, Addas was assigned the regions of the East, while Thomas took up the lands of the Syrians, and Hermas set out for Egypt; and they remain there to this day for the sake of preaching this dogma.*

Yet, writers do not entirely agree on this journey; nor does the Cassino manuscript of Archelaus even agree with itself. The matter itself does not seem to be of great weight. <term>Epiphanius</term><note>Bishop of Salamis and a fierce opponent of heresies.</note> also records that Hermas set out for Egypt; he testifies that he received the history of Mani from those who had actually heard Hermas himself in Egypt, which is certainly of the greatest importance for placing trust in Epiphanius.

XXIV. <meta>This page transitions from the historical origins of Mani’s disciples discussed on the previous page to a detailed description of the Manichaean social hierarchy, specifically focusing on the "Hearers" (Auditores) and their relationship to the "Elect" (Electi).</meta>

->### AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS ###<-

<margin>The Hearers of the Manichaeans: who they were, of what sort, what laws they were bound by, and what duties and services they were assigned.</margin>
The **Elect** (1) <note>The elite ascetic class of the Manichaean religion, who lived lives of strict poverty and celibacy.</note> were accustomed to call their **Hearers** <term>catechumens</term><note>In mainstream Christianity, a 'catechumen' is a student preparing for baptism. The Manichaeans adopted the term but changed its meaning.</note> as well. This was not because these Hearers were eventually to be initiated through the baptism of Christians—for the Manichaeans rejected baptism—but rather because the Hearers were considered to be of a much lower grade, rank, and holiness than the Manichaean Elect. The common duty of the Hearers (2) was to serve the needs of the Elect along with their wives, children, households, servants, and lands. Furthermore, (3) they were to cultivate the earth, dig the fields, plow the lands, pluck fruit from trees, harvest vegetables, and cut melons and gourds, bringing these to the Elect to sustain them. It was permitted for the Hearers, however, (4) to take wives and to consume meat and wine. Yet they were forbidden (5) to kill animals with their own hands; and—what is most detestable and contrary to the law of nature—they were strictly warned to avoid procreating children while living with their wives <note>The Manichaeans believed that trapping a soul in a physical body through birth was a great evil.</note>.

<margin>The Elect shared their entire doctrine and discipline with their Hearers.</margin>
The ritual of the Hearers (6) was to throw themselves at the feet of the Elect and place their necks under the Elect’s hands to be pressed down. As for what they held in common with the Elect, <term>Augustine</term><note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD) was famously a 'Hearer' in the Manichaean sect for nine years before his conversion to Christianity.</note>, formerly a Hearer himself, describes it in these words:
> They worship the Sun and Moon along with the Elect; they fast on the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note> with the Elect; and they believe all the same blasphemies with them, for which the Manichaean heresy is to be detested. <note>original: "Solem, & Lunam cum Electis adorant; die Dominico cum Electis jejunant: & omnes blasphemias cum illis credunt, quibus Manichæorum hæresis detestanda est."</note>

<margin>The Hearers were excluded only from the wicked mysteries of the Elect.</margin>
Thus, the Elect passed down the entire Manichaean mythology to their Hearers; the Hearers were excluded only from those impious and wicked mysteries to which the Elect devoted themselves in great secrecy, which we shall discuss in the proper place. The reward (7), indeed, which they promised to their Hearers in exchange for their heavy and long-lasting servitude...

<margin>The Elect of the Manichaeans: who they were, of what sort, what laws they were bound by, and to what duty they were destined.</margin>
XXV. Those among the Manichaeans were called **Elect** (1) who professed to hold the highest degree of sanctity, righteousness, severity, and self-restraint. These (2) abstained entirely from wine and meat, because they claimed that particles of the divine nature had flown away from dead bodies; moreover, they taught that wine was the "gall of the prince of darkness" <note>original: *fel esse principis tenebrarum*</note>. They were nourished, therefore, by fruits, herbs, vegetables, melons, and gourds, which they believed were still alive even after being plucked, pulled, or cut. They believed these contained the good nature of God mixed with the evil nature of the demon, which they boasted they could separate from the evil nature in their own stomachs through the processes of digestion, belching, and excretion. Augustine, mocking them (3), said:
> *O blessed vegetables*, he says, *to which it is granted—even when plucked by hand, cut with iron, and tortured by fire—to reach the altars of your intestines alive. And O miserable cattle, which, since they leave their own bodies more quickly, cannot enter into yours.* (4)

Furthermore, they considered it a wicked crime to cultivate fields, to take a wife, or to devote effort to procreating children. Indeed, (5) they even judged it a monstrous and impious act to pull up grass, pluck leaves, cut vegetables, or pick fruit, because they preached that these things lived a divine life.

<margin>The Elect of the Manichaeans, segregated from the Hearers, performed their secret and accursed mysteries alone.</margin>
However, the life, morals, customs, and sacred rites performed by the Elect were entirely hidden from the Manichaean **Hearers** <term>Auditores</term> <note>The 'Hearers' were the lay followers who supported the 'Elect' but did not follow the same strict rules.</note> because of their detestable foulness. Augustine, who was a primary Hearer of the Manichaeans, is a witness to this...

Those who presided over and ministered the sacred rites of the Manichaeans were chosen from the assembly of the Elect. The Bishops also have Deacons. They claim that baptism in water brings no salvation to anyone, nor do they think that any of those whom they deceive should be baptized.*

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the dualistic core of Manichaean belief, citing historical testimonies from Turbo and Epiphanius, and detailing the debate between St. Augustine and the Manichaean Bishop Faustus regarding whether "Matter" functions as a second deity.</meta>

# AND ON THE NEW MANICHAEANS.

[Turbo, the student] <note>Turbo was a disciple of Mani's followers, often cited in the 'Acts of Archelaus' as a source for their secret doctrines.</note> witnesses before Marcellus and Archelaus that his Master established two Gods: one good, the other evil. Epiphanius (1) brings forward this same Turbo as a witness—just as he had found him described by Archelaus—stating that Mani *established two principles, which both lacked a beginning and would never end, and were contrary to each other: one of which he called light and good; the other darkness and evil, such that they were the same as God and the devil: both of whom he would sometimes name as Gods—namely, a good God and an evil God.* 

But indeed (2), Augustine, having reproached Faustus, the Manichaean Bishop, for the Manichaeans establishing two Gods, heard Faustus arguing back in these words: *The name of "two Gods" has never been heard in our assertions... It is true that we confess two principles; but one of these we call God, and the other <term>Hyle</term> <note>original: "Hylen," from the Greek word for "matter." In Manichaean thought, matter is not just physical stuff, but an active, evil force.</note>; or as I might say in common and everyday language, a demon. I teach two principles, God and Hyle; therefore, I should not seem to you to be showing two Gods.* 

To this, Augustine—a frequent and diligent witness who, along with other <term>Auditors</term> <note>The "Auditors" (Hearers) were the lower rank of Manichaean followers; Augustine himself was an Auditor for nine years before converting to Christianity.</note>, had heard this Manichaean impiety regarding a double God—replied: *We are indeed accustomed to hearing "two Gods" in your disputations.* Soon, setting aside the hollow question of terminology, he attacks the core of the matter more forcefully with these words: *Faustus seems to have defended himself quickly when he says, "We do not say two Gods, but God and Hyle." However, when you ask what he calls Hyle, you will hear him clearly describe another God.* And indeed, since they affirmed that Hyle was the procreator of all bodies, and that she was eternal, unbegotten, dependent on no beginning and no cause—attributes which can only be assigned to a divine nature—the Manichaeans were forced, even if unwillingly and reluctantly, to concede that Hyle was a God.

### DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS

<margin>The Manichaeans taught that the light visible to our eyes is the good God, and the contrary darkness is the evil God.</margin>
...the Manichaeans taught that [the nature of God] is the light which is perceived by the eyes of all living creatures. Regarding physical light, <note>original: "Lucem corpoream"</note> Augustine reports: *Physical light, which lies before the eyes of mortal creatures—not only in those ships (the Sun and the Moon) <note>Manichaeans believed the Sun and Moon were celestial "ships" or "vessels" used to transport purified light-souls back to the Kingdom of Light.</note> where they believe it exists in its purest form, but also in all other bright things, where they claim it is held in a mixed state and must be purified—this, they say, is the nature of God.* Conversely, they said the evil God was darkness, which they considered to be something self-existing, eternal, and unbegotten. (2) *They are fond of asking,* Augustine says of the Manichaeans, *from where did the darkness over the abyss come before God made light? Who had made or begotten it? Or if no one had made or begotten it, then darkness was eternal.* Augustine responds: *This is as if darkness were actually something; but, as has been said, this name is simply given to the absence of light. But because they were deceived by their own fables, they believed there was a <term>Nation of Darkness</term> <note>original: "gentem tenebrarum"</note>, in which they imagined there were bodies, forms, and souls within those bodies. Thus they think darkness is a thing, and they do not understand that darkness is only felt when we do not see, just as silence is only felt when we do not hear. Just as silence is nothing, so too darkness is nothing. Yet, just as these people claim a "Nation of Darkness" fought against the light of God, another person, equally foolish, could claim a <term>Nation of Silences</term> fought against the voice of God.*

The reason that drove the Manichaeans into this absurdity—believing in an eternal, unbegotten evil nature from which all evils flow—was that they observed the many evils that strike everyone's eyes from every side. Judging it entirely impious to attribute these to a good God, they established an eternal, unbegotten evil principle as the cause of all evils. From this came that most frequent question with which they deceived the unwary: FROM WHERE [DOES EVIL COME?] <note>The Latin text ends with "UNDE," and the catchword "MA-" indicates the next page begins with "MALUM" (Evil). This refers to the classic theological problem: "Unde Malum?" or "From whence comes evil?"</note>

### AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS

<margin>The very famous Manichaean question: "Where does evil come from?"</margin>
EVIL? Often (1) and indeed always, says Augustine when addressing the Manichaeans, you ask those whom you strive to persuade of your heresy, *Where does evil come from?* <note>original: "Unde sit malum"</note> In this, the Manichaeans used to boast that they had triumphed. By this question (2), Augustine says, the Manichaeans think they reign supreme—as if, indeed, to ask were the same as to know. For they did not understand that since there are two kinds of evil—namely, the **evil of fault** <note>original: "malum culpæ"; refers to sin or moral wrongdoing</note> and the **evil of punishment** <note>original: "malum pœnæ"; refers to suffering or the consequences of sin</note>—the latter belongs most justly to God, who is the most righteous avenger of crimes, while the former belongs to the will, which is good by nature but free in its choice, whether of an Angel or a human. For those searching for the origin of evil must arrive at this point, and one must not progress any further.

<margin>The Manichaean fable about the battle of the Nation of Darkness against the God of Light.</margin>
XXVIII. Titus of Bostra (3) follows the narration of the Manichaean myth, just as he testifies he received it from the books of the Manichaeans themselves, which is as follows: That eternal and "unbegotten" <note>Self-existent; not created by anything else.</note> matter was carried along without any order; it generated and it grew. When, however, it had been increased by an innumerable multitude of offspring, the greatest discords and seditions arose among that most wicked brood. A bitter and fierce battle followed the insane enmity of the brothers. However, when the victors were pursuing those who had turned to flight, it happened that they reached the borders of the <term>Kingdom of Light</term>. Captivated by its beauty and having entered into a pact with one another, they invaded the Kingdom of Light by common counsel. Then the God of Light, since he could not sustain the attack of the <term>Nation of Darkness</term> <note>original: "gentis tenebrarum"</note> and feared the imminent devastation of his kingdom, took measures for himself and his affairs. He threw against the enemies some power and virtue—certainly a most radiant part of himself—so that he might recall them from hatred to love, once they were captured by these enticements. At the presence of the most beautiful light, the darkness blazed with a vehement desire; mixed with this light, the darkness absorbed it and bound it deep within itself with the tightest bond. <margin>The Manichaeans said all living creatures were the aborted offspring of the women of the nation of darkness, because they suffered a violent dizziness during the first rotation of the heavens.</margin>
XXVIII. Regarding the formation of the world, which followed that great battle between the nation of darkness and the God of light, the Manichaean myth is such that—much like the ravings of the sick—it is inconsistent and constantly contradicts itself. As <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who was a Manichaean for nine years before converting to Christianity and becoming their most famous critic.</note> testifies, the Manichaeans recorded the origin of all living creatures in their writings as follows (1): When the male and female princes of darkness were captured and the world was being constructed from them, many were bound within the celestial structures. Among them were several pregnant females. When the heavens began to rotate, these females could not endure the dizzying motion and cast out their offspring in miscarriages. These aborted fetuses, both male and female, fell from the sky to the earth, where they lived, grew, mated, and gave birth. From this, they claim, is the origin of all flesh that moves on the earth, in the water, and in the air. All other things—not just living creatures, but both those that stand still and those that move—they contended were composed and grew together from a dual nature and a dual soul: a bad soul, which was part of the evil God, and a good soul, which was a part of the good God. These became mixed and glued together following that ridiculous battle.

<margin>The Manichaeans said all bodies are animated because they consist of a good soul, which is part of [the good] God, and a bad soul, which is part of the evil God.</margin>
Consequently, they believed that everything in the world—elements, stones, metals, trees, fruits, and vegetables—was animated, possessing a soul endowed with sensation, cognition, and reason. We have a rich witness in Augustine, who recounts these things about the Manichaeans (2):

> Those members of God, they say, which were captured in that battle, are mixed throughout the entire world, and are present in trees, in herbs, in fruits, and in crops.

Likewise (3):

> They say the good and true God fought with the nation of darkness, and mixed his own part with the princes of darkness; they assert that this part is defiled and bound throughout the whole world.

*You say (4),* he writes, *that some other nation of darkness rebelled against the kingdom of God. In Manichaean theology, this refers to the "Primal Man" or the soul, a divine spark sent to confront the darkness.</note>, from whose mixture with evil and the nation of darkness the world was fashioned. Likewise (5): That at a certain time, the nation of darkness rebelled against God. But because God, while occupied with other things, did not have [another way], and could not find how else he might resist the enemy, being pressed by necessity, he sent here a good soul, a certain particle of his own substance. They dream that by the mixing and mingling of this particle, the enemy was overcome and the world was fashioned. Furthermore (6): The Manichaeans say that before the foundation of the world, there was a nation of darkness which rebelled against God. In this war, those wretched people believe that Almighty God could not have helped himself in any other way than by sending a part of himself against it. The princes of this nation, as they say, devoured that part of God and were calmed <note>original: "temperati," suggesting they were "tempered" or diluted, losing their pure destructive fury.</note>, so that the world could be fashioned from them. They say these members of God are mixed within the dark intestines of those princes, so that he might temper them and restrain them from their fury.*

# AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS.

XXVIII. Concerning the constitution of the world, which followed that battle of the nation of darkness with the God of light, the <term>Manichaean</term> <note>Followers of Mani, who believed the physical world was an accidental or forced mixture of pure spirit and evil matter.</note> myth is such that, like the delusions of the sick, it is inconsistent and frequently contradicts itself. The Manichaeans recorded in writing that the origin of all living creatures was as follows, according to the testimony of <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who was a Manichaean for nine years before converting to Christianity and becoming their most famous critic.</note> (1):

<margin>
The Manichaeans said that all living creatures were the aborted fetuses of the women of the nation of darkness, because they suffered violent dizziness during the first turning of the heavens.
</margin>

> Once the princes of darkness of both sexes were captured, when the world was being constructed from them, many of them were bound within the celestial structures. Among them were also some pregnant females who, when the heavens began to rotate, were unable to bear that dizziness and cast out their offspring by miscarriage. These same aborted fetuses, both male and female, fell from heaven to earth, lived, grew, mated, and gave birth. They say the origin of all flesh that moves on the earth, in the water, and in the air comes from this.

All other things—no differently than living creatures—both those that remain unmoving and those that move, they contended were composed and fused from a double nature and a double soul: an evil one and a good one. The evil soul was a part of the evil God; the good soul was a part of the good God. After that ridiculous battle, they were mixed and stuck together. Hence they believed that everything in the world—elements, stones, metals, trees, fruit, vegetables, and crops—were <term>animate</term> <note>original: "animata." Having a soul or life-force.</note>, and indeed endowed with a soul possessing sensation, knowledge, and reason.

<margin>
The Manichaeans said that all bodies were animate because they consisted of a good soul, which is part of the good God, and an evil soul, which is part of the evil God.
</margin>

The reliable witness Augustine is at hand, who relates these things about the Manichaeans (2): 

> "Those members of God," they say, "which were captured in that battle, are mixed into the entire world, and are in trees, in plants, in fruits, and in crops." 

Likewise (3): 

> "They say that the good and true God fought with the nation of darkness, and mixed his own part with the princes of darkness; they assert that this part is defiled and bound throughout the whole world." 

Again (4): 

> "Plants and trees in this way..."

They believe that they live, so that they believe life is within them, and that they feel and suffer pain when they are harmed; and that no one can pluck or pick anything without causing them torture. XXIX. Regarding the nature of man, however, the error of the Manichaeans was far more destructive. For they taught that there are two souls in every single human: one evil, which was a part of the <term>nation of darkness</term> <note>In Manichaean myth, the eternal realm of evil matter that attacked the realm of light.</note> and of the same nature as that nation; and from it, all the evils of man—both those pertaining to nature and those pertaining to morals—necessarily arise. The other soul is good, a part of the good God and of the same nature as the good God; and from it, all the goods of man—both those of nature and those of virtue—necessarily flow (7). Augustine is a witness to this in many places.

...stine <note>original: "nus"; the conclusion of "Augustinus" from the previous page.</note> (1). Furthermore, according to these authors, in that conflict, if the evil soul prevails over the strength of the good soul, it subjects the good soul to itself, drags it along by its own weight, twists it from virtue to vice, and thrusts it into every kind of outrage and crime (4). The *Manichaeans* extend their excuse into an accusation of God; they are miserable by divine judgment, but blasphemous in their own fury, and they say they only sin when the nature of evil prevails over the nature of God. This is the most filthy insanity of the Manichaeans.

Thus says Augustine.
