And we souls, they say, are from the very members of God; but here we are weighed down by the entrails of the race of darkness, and whatever we are said to sin, that race sins. ... Do you wish, O wicked, false Elect one, to defend your sin so that when you have done something evil, you do not seem to have done it? You seek someone upon whom to pour back your sin, and you pour it back upon the race of darkness. But look toward God, and see if you do not actually pour it back upon Him. For if that race of darkness which you imagine could speak, it would say to you: "Why do you accuse me?" ... When therefore you wish to defend yourself for your sin, you cannot praise God... Turn instead to your own blame, and then you will praise God... Say: "I have said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you." <note>A quotation from Psalm 41:4.</note> "I have said," "I have sinned"—not fortune, not fate, not the race of darkness.*

Nevertheless, this opinion pleased Augustine once when he was a young man, back when he was involved in the Manichaean heresy. It was, after all, quite convenient and opportune for removing the mark and ignominy of fault from himself, and for dulling the stings and sharp pricks of conscience. ### AND CONCERNING THE NEW MANICHAEANS.

<margin>The Manichaeans, because of their belief in two souls—one a necessary cause of all good and the other of all evil—rejected the free will of man.</margin>

> *They say,* he says, *that the Powers of Light are transformed into beautiful males and set against the females of the race of darkness; and these same Powers of Light are transformed back into beautiful females and set against the males of the race of darkness; so that by their beauty they may inflame the most filthy lust of the Princes of Darkness, and in this way the vital substance—that is, the nature of God, which they say is held bound in their bodies—is released from their limbs as they are relaxed through that same concupiscence <note>The "Seduction of the Archons": a Manichaean myth where divine beings trick the demonic rulers into releasing the "Light" (divine substance) they had swallowed by provoking them to sexual arousal.</note>, and being loosened, it escapes, and being received or purified, it is set free.*

# A DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS

<margin>The Manichaeans excused their sins by claiming it was not they who sinned, but an evil soul within them that acted whenever it prevailed over the good soul.</margin>
So says Augustine. And again in another place (1): *The Manichaeans*, *he says*, *contend that from the substance of evil—to which they attribute its own principle and leaders—the very substance of the good God, in that part where it was captured, has been corrupted*, *oppressed*, *and led to the necessity of sinning.* Augustine’s dialogue regarding this impious and insane Manichaean excuse is truly elegant. Let it be heard (2). *Who are these Elect? <note>The "Elect" were the inner circle of the Manichaean sect, who lived under strict ascetic rules and were considered holy.</note> To whom if you say*, *"You have sinned,"* *they immediately bring forward that impious defense, worse than the others and more sacrilegious: "It was not I who sinned*, *but the race of darkness." <note>The "race of darkness" refers to the Manichaean concept of the kingdom of evil that invaded the kingdom of light.</note> What is this race of darkness? That which waged war with God. And does it sin when you sin? "It does,"* *he says*, *"because I am mingled with it"*...... *And we souls*, *they say*, *are of the very members of God; but we are pressed down here by the entrails of the race of darkness*, *and whatever we are said to sin*, *it is that race that sins*..... *Do you wish*, *O wicked*, *false "Elect,"* *to defend your sin*, *so that when you have done something evil*, *you do not seem to have done it? You seek someone upon whom to cast your sin*, *and you cast it upon the race of darkness.* *But attend to God*, *lest you cast it upon Him. For if that race of darkness*, *which you invent*, *could speak*, *it would say to you*, *"Why do you accuse me?"*..... *Therefore, when you wish to defend yourself regarding your sin*, *you cannot praise God*... *Turn instead to blaming yourself*, *and you will praise God*... *Say*, *"I said*, *Lord have mercy on me*, *heal my soul*, *for I have sinned against you."* *I said it*, *I have sinned;* *not fortune*, *not fate*, *not the race of darkness.* Yet this opinion pleased Augustine once when he was a young man, while he was involved in the Manichaean heresy, as it was quite convenient and opportune for removing the mark and shame of guilt from himself, and for dulling the stings and bites of conscience—something he himself frankly confesses and deplores in these words (3). *For it still to me* <note>original: "Adhuc enim mihi." This sentence continues on the next page with the word "seemed" [videbatur].</note>

# AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS.

<margin>The Manichaeans rejected human free will because they believed in two souls—one good and one evil—which were the unavoidable causes of all actions.</margin>

"...it seemed that it was not we who sin, but some unknown other nature within us that sinned; and it pleased my pride to be free from blame. When I had done something evil, I would not confess that I had done it, so that You might heal my soul because it had sinned against You; instead, I loved to excuse myself and accuse some other thing that was with me, but was not I." <note>original: "videbatur non esse nos qui peccamus... et ego non essem." This is a famous passage from Augustine's *Confessions* (Book 5, Ch. 10), reflecting on his own nine-year stint as a Manichaean auditor.</note> From all of this, it is evident that the Manichaeans exerted all their efforts, much like the heretics of our own age, toward the total destruction of the free choice of the human will. Augustine testifies to this fact repeatedly and in numerous places (1).

XXX. But indeed, God was moved by the calamity of His own **members** <note>The Manichaeans believed that human souls were literally fragments or "members" of the divine substance trapped in matter during a primordial war.</note>. According to the teachings of Manichaeus—as recorded by Titus of Bostra (2)—God planned to separate these divine parts from that wretched mixture with the **race of darkness** <note>The "race of darkness" is the Manichaean term for the realm of matter and evil.</note> and to reunite them with Himself, so that a portion of His own nature would not remain in eternal misery. The Manichaean explanation for how this separation occurs is multifaceted. Regarding the heavenly elements stuck fast to the race of darkness, the method of "tearing away" described by Manichaeus is so impious, foul, and obscene that I do not dare to relate it in my own words. I will rely solely on the words of Augustine, who quotes the passage from Manichaeus himself (3):

<margin>The Manichaeans claimed that the separation of the good nature from the evil nature in heaven was achieved through the power of intense lust, by the design of the good God.</margin>

In this way, the **vital substance**—that is, the nature of God—which they claim is held bound in their bodies, might be loosened and escape from their limbs when they are relaxed by that very desire; once released, it is gathered up or purified and thus set free. ...eternally. **They say** this, they hear this; it is placed thus in the seventh book of their *Thesaurus* <note>The *Thesaurus* (or "Treasure of Life") was one of the seven canonical works written by Mani, the founder of Manichaeism. > *Whatever is purified from all sides is returned to the Kingdom of God as its proper home through certain **Ships**, which they claim are the Moon and the Sun. They likewise assert that these ships were fashioned from the pure substance of God. They say that within these ships are holy powers, which transform themselves into males to entice the females of the hostile race; and again into females, to entice the males of the same hostile race. Through this allure, their lust is stirred, and the light that they held mixed within their limbs flees from them; it is then received by the Angels of Light for purification, and once purified, it is placed upon those ships to be carried back to their own kingdoms.* <note>original: "Quidquid undique purgatur... ad regna propria deportandum." This describes the "Seduction of the Archons," a myth explaining how divine "light" is extracted from the "darkness" of physical bodies through celestial attraction.</note>

From this, another most ridiculous new fable of the Manichaeans was born, concerning the waxing and waning of the Moon, which I set forth in Augustine's own words (2).

<margin>The Manichaean fables regarding the waxing and waning of the Moon.</margin>

> *Those who have scrutinized these matters more subtly have inferred the lunar waxing and waning from the rotation of its globe; not that any substance is either added to it when it increases, or departs from it when it diminishes. But the Manichaeans, thinking with delirious ignorance, said that it is filled—just as a ship is filled—from the fugitive part of God. They do not hesitate to believe and speak with a sacrilegious heart and mouth that this part was committed to the princes of darkness and defiled by their filth. Hence they say the Moon is filled when that same part of God, purified with great labor from its defilement and fleeing from the whole world and all its sewers, is returned to God while He grieves until it returns. They claim it is filled throughout half the month, and in the other half, it is poured back into the Sun, as if into another ship.*

Oh, what illustrious Manichaean astronomers! But I return to the separation of the divine nature from the nature of the race of darkness. As far as it pertains to terrestrial bodies—

# AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS.

The Manichaeans taught that the particles of the divine nature are released from their painful bonds with the race of darkness in many different ways, constantly and assiduously, so that they may finally fly back to the kingdoms of light. Augustine (1) describes these multiple and various modes of the aforementioned liberation in these words:

<margin>Among the Manichaeans, there is a manifold reason for the separation of the good nature from the evil nature which occurs in terrestrial bodies.</margin>

> *Something of that divine part escapes, as you claim, when crops and fruits are gathered; it escapes when they are bruised by rubbing, or by grinding, or by cooking, or even by biting and chewing. It also escapes in all movements of animals, whether they are playing, or exercising, or working, or performing any task at all. It even escapes during our very rest, while that process called digestion is carried out within the body by internal heat. And so, with the divine nature escaping on so many occasions, something most filthy remains, from which flesh is formed through sexual intercourse—though still with a soul of a good kind; for although a great deal escapes, not all of the good flies away during those mentioned movements.* <note>original: "Fugit aliquid partis illius divinæ..." Augustine here mocks the Manichaean belief that every physical action, even eating or walking, causes the "trapped" divine light within matter to be shaken loose and set free.</note>

<margin>A more efficient separation of the good nature from the evil nature was performed in the stomachs of the Elect.</margin>

But besides these other methods, there was a shortcut and most efficient system for separating the good nature of God from the evil nature of darkness, found only among the **Elect** <note>The Manichaean community was divided into two ranks: the "Elect" (ascetics who followed strict rules) and the "Hearers" (laypeople who supported the Elect). Only the Elect were believed to have the spiritual "purity" to release light through their digestion.</note> of the Manichaeans. They preached that by chewing, cooking, digesting, and belching <note>original: "ructando." This was a point of intense ridicule for Christian critics like Augustine: the idea that the "Elect" were literally walking refineries who liberated God from food through their digestive tracts.</note> from the foods they were accustomed to eating, they dissolved the particles of the divine nature from the dregs of the dark race, through a unique gift granted by **Mani** <note>original: "Manetis." Mani (c. 216–274 AD) was the Persian prophet and founder of Manichaeism.</note>. Augustine says (2):

> *If some "Saint" ate a fig—picked, to be sure, by someone else’s sin and not his own—he would mix it with his internal organs and breathe out Angels from it; or rather, by groaning in prayer and by belching, he would release particles of God. These particles of the highest and true God would have remained bound in that fruit, had they not been loosened by the teeth and belly of the Holy Elect.*

And again in another place (3):

> *They say that the good and true God fought with the race of darkness, and mixed a part of himself with the princes of darkness, and [defiled] it throughout the whole world...*

They affirm that there will always be joined and attached to this globe, like a cover or a coating, those souls which are good by nature, but which nevertheless could not be freed from the contagion of the evil nature.*

### AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS

<margin>The Manichaeans taught the transmigration of souls into all sorts of foreign bodies.</margin>
**Augustine** (1) testifies that the Manichaeans taught that once the separation of the good nature from the entire evil nature was achieved: *The souls of the dead that are evil, or less purified, either enter into cycles <note>original: "revolutiones," referring to the cycles of rebirth or reincarnation.</note>, or into certain more severe punishments; whereas the good souls are placed upon ships <note>In Manichaean myth, the Sun and Moon were seen as celestial vessels that ferried purified light/souls back to the divine realm.</note>, and sailing through the heavens, they cross from here into that phantom land of light, for the sake of which they perished in battle.* This cycle of souls, of which **Augustine** speaks, is that most famous "metempsychosis" <term>Metempsychosis: The Greek philosophical term for the migration of a soul into a new body after death.</term> of **Pythagoras** and other ancient philosophers—the transmigration of human souls into foreign bodies. The Manichaeans, according to the testimony of **Socrates** (2) and **Theodoret**, revived this idea, though they made it far more absurd and much more foul than the reincarnation taught by the ancient philosophers. For they taught that human souls departed not only into the animal bodies of birds, swimming creatures, field animals, serpents, wild beasts, and livestock; but even into bushes, vegetables, fruit, gourds, melons, onions, and garlic.

Indeed, even **Pythagoras** did not rave to such an extent. *They think,* says **Augustine** (3), *that souls return both into cattle and into all things which are fixed by roots and nourished in the earth.*

<margin>The Manichaeans taught that the souls of their Hearers pass either into the bodies of the Elect, or into the foods which the Elect eat.</margin>
But by a singular gift of the Manichaeans, and by a law established by them, the souls of their **Hearers** <note>original: "Auditores," the rank of believers who were not yet "Elect" and who performed manual labor to support the leaders.</note> were the most fortunate of all. They believed that once these souls were liberated from the body, they either immediately entered the bodies of the **Elect**, or they passed into gourds, melons, grains, vegetables, and fruit—the future nourishment of the Elect. By eating, cooking, belching <note>The Manichaeans believed the "Elect" had special digestive powers; as they digested food, they physically liberated the "divine light" trapped within it, which was then released through breath and prayer.</note>, and praying, the Elect would transmit the souls of their Hearers (who had once provided faithful service to the Elect) to the kingdom of light by the nearest and, as it were, shortcut path. *They believe,* says **Augustine** (4), *that the souls of their Hearers are returned into the Elect, or by a happier shortcut, into the food...*

# DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS
**Page 50**

[The souls] of their Elect, so that once purified they might never again return into any bodies. **Augustine**, however, ridicules this Manichaean fable with a truly witty and very playful interrogation. He asks **Adimantus** <note>Adimantus was a disciple of Mani whose writings Augustine sought to refute.</note> what he thinks he should do if he were riding a donkey that was either too slow or too spirited. Should he strike and torment the fast one with a bit to restrain it, or beat and urge the struggling slow one with a club? Yet it is possible that his own father's soul is enclosed and contained within that donkey's body. If that were the case, what a wicked and impious crime **Adimantus** would have entangled himself in! Nay, it could even easily happen that among fleas and lice, he might crush and burst his own parents with his fingernail. Would he then abstain from the slaughter of lice for fear of parricide <term>Parricide: The murder of a parent or close relative.</term>, and endure their most annoying stings with a calm mind? But **Augustine** himself must be heard, for we should see with what wit and playfulness he attacks this little story (1).

> What will **Adimantus** himself do according to his own opinion, by which he believed that rational souls—that is, the souls of humans—can be drawn into the bodies of beasts? What then will he do regarding such a great crime, if he ever tires out a slow beast of burden with blows, or a spirited one with a bit, in which perhaps his father's soul resided? This is to say nothing of the fact that he could also kill his parents among lice and fleas, from whose slaughter these people do not refrain. For what does it profit them that they sometimes deny human souls can be cycled back <note>original: "revolvi," referring to the cycles of reincarnation or metempsychosis.</note> into these most minute animals? They deny this only so they are not held guilty for so many killings, or forced to spare lice, fleas, and bedbugs, and thus endure such great annoyances from them without any permission to kill them.

<margin>The Manichaeans taught that the body of Christ the Lord was not true and solid, but a shadow and a phantom of a body.</margin>
[They] taught that the Son of God was neither joined to a true human body, nor born as a true man from Mary, nor truly suffered, died, or was buried; nor did a true, living man rise from the tomb. Instead, they claimed he exhibited only a false image and a fictional phantom of a man to mortal eyes. To prove this, I bring forward the most wealthy witnesses, worthy of the highest faith: **Socrates** (1) <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380 – after 439), a Greek Christian church historian.</note>, **Theodoret**, **Fulgentius**, **Leo the Great**, and in many places, **Augustine**.

But no witness is more certain than the Manichaean himself, who recommended these views against the Catholics in his own execrable writings (2): *I wish they did not say that Christ the Lord, the Only-begotten Son of God, who descended from the Father’s bosom, was the son of some "paltry woman" <note>original: "mulierculæ"</note> named Mary, and that he came forth from blood and flesh, and indeed the remaining foulness of women.*

<margin>The Manichaeans rejected the entire Old Testament as if it were the work of the prince of darkness, but they "circumcised" <note>In this context, meaning they cut out or edited parts.</note> the New Testament according to their own judgment.</margin>
Indeed, regarding what the Manichaeans either borrowed from their master or devised on their own concerning Christ the Lord, it is helpful to learn from **Augustine** how nefarious, impious, and absurd these ideas are (3). *They affirm,* he says, *that Christ was the one whom our Scripture calls the serpent; they assert that Adam and Eve were enlightened by him so that they might open the eyes of knowledge and distinguish good from evil. They claim this Christ came in the most recent times to liberate souls, not bodies. Nor was he in true flesh, but offered a simulated appearance of flesh to mock human senses, where he would lie not only about his death, but also about his resurrection.* It will perhaps seem strange that the Manichaeans, who rejected the Old Testament entirely, interpreted a passage from the book of **Genesis**, however absurdly; but this wonder will cease if we remember the [habit] of heretics...

XXXIII. Concerning the nature of things, Manichaeus and his disciples taught such fables as are usually told by certain good old women sitting by the fireside: these I shall touch upon briefly and summarily, having brought forward most excellent witnesses (2). They used to say there were five elements enclosed in as many dark caverns: smoke, darkness, fire, water, and wind, which belonged to the nation of darkness like limbs severed from it. ...with your most filthy rags <note>The author is likely quoting Augustine, who uses the metaphor of "filthy rags" to describe the Manichaean doctrines being "sewn" onto the pure Christian concept of the Trinity.</note> you attempt to stitch together the ineffable *Trinity, saying that the Father dwells in a certain secret light; that the power of the Son resides in the Sun, and His Wisdom in the Moon; while the Holy Spirit resides in the air.* With these words, the Holy Doctor <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a former Manichaean who became their most formidable theological opponent.</note> quite clearly indicates that, according to the Manichaean authors, the Father is a kind of most secret light; the light of the Sun is the power of the Son; the light of the Moon is the wisdom of the same; and the Holy Spirit is the light of the air. <margin>The Manichaeans worshipped the Moon along with the Sun.</margin>

*The Hearers, along with them—that is, with the Elect—worship and pray to the Sun and Moon.* The rite of worshipping these two noble planets is described by Augustine as follows (4). *They offer prayers to the Sun throughout the day, following it wherever it circles, and to the Moon by night if it appears; if it does not appear, they stand praying toward the North, the direction through which the Sun returns to the East after it has set.* And again, in another place, censuring the Manichaeans, he says (5): *Thus it happens that you bow your back and neck to this Sun—not indeed to the one visible in such bright roundness, but to I know not what ship you imagine, shining and glowing through a triangular opening.* <note>The Manichaeans believed the Sun and Moon were "ships" or celestial vessels used to transport purified "light-particles" (souls) back to the divine realm.</note>

<margin>The Manichaeans worshiped all physical bodies as demigods, because they were partially formed from the nature of God.</margin>
The Manichaeans did not truly limit themselves only to worshiping the Sun and the Moon; rather, they venerated as many gods as possible (1). *In their sect*, says Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, a former Manichaean turned critic.</note> concerning the Manichaeans, *they mention and recommend a most numerous family of gods, whom they venerate and adore in the place of the light of truth.* Titus of Bostra <note>A 4th-century bishop known for his refutation of Manichaeism.</note> testifies to these same things regarding the Manichaeans (2): *They venerate everything and know nothing other than to adore everything: they always prostrate themselves on the ground, yet they have a haughty mind: they err and wander in their mental senses: they have turned everything into gods according to their own whim: they have surpassed the pagans in both number and vanity.* Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century Christian historian.</note> agrees with the above, having left this record for posterity in his *Ecclesiastical History* (3): *Manichaeus impiously commands that many gods must be worshiped; he also teaches that the Sun must be adored.* Nor should this seem a wonder to anyone. For since the Manichaeans established that all bodies consist of the nature of the Good God mixed with the nature of the Evil God, they were compelled to venerate men, cattle, shrubs, and stones along with all other things as if they were demigods.

<margin>The sacred mysteries of the Elect, forbidden to the Hearers, were especially impious and accursed.</margin>
XXXVIII. Regarding the sacred—or rather, accursed—mysteries of the Elect <note>The "Elect" were the inner circle of the Manichaeans who practiced strict asceticism, while the "Hearers" were the lay followers.</note>, these were so foul, impious, obscene, and wicked that they seem shameful not only to speak of or hear, but even to know. Therefore, because of the impiety and filth of such intolerable mysteries, the Elect removed them from the eyes of their "Hearers" and performed them in secret. Augustine indicates this with these words (4): *Because such seeds of living beings <note>original: "animalium semina." This refers to the polemical accusation that the Elect consumed human semen during rituals to "release" divine light.</note> cannot be brought to you by your Hearers to be purified, who would not suspect that a secret purification of this kind is carried out among yourselves by eating, and is therefore hidden from them, lest they desert you?* But that impious and filthy custom of the Elect was exposed by the most well-tested evidence in...

<margin>The particularly foul, impious, and sacrilegious Eucharist of the Elect, to be cursed by all things dire.</margin>
*On which occasion,* he says, *or rather by a certain necessity of an abominable superstition, their Elect are compelled to consume a sort of Eucharist sprinkled with human seed, so that from this, just as from the other foods they receive, that divine substance may be purged.* <note>The Manichaeans believed that "Light" or "Divine Substance" was trapped in matter and could be released through digestion by their holy "Elect."</note> Since, however, the Elect of the Manichaeans persistently and stubbornly denied such a wicked crime—as it was celebrated by them in extreme secrecy—Augustine demonstrates it by producing the legitimate legal records (3).

<margin>Public, solemn, and most certain records regarding the admission of the wicked Eucharist of the Elect.</margin>
*But this,* he says, *they deny they do, and they claim others—I know not who—do it under the name of Manichaeans. <margin>
Those who abstain from using the chalice, contrary to common custom, reveal themselves as Manichaeans by such abstinence.
</margin>

Pope Leo [the Great] <note>Saint Leo I (c. 400–461 AD), known for his efforts to maintain Church unity and his opposition to various heresies.</note> attacks them with these words (1): *“While they dare to participate in our mysteries to hide their infidelity, they conduct themselves in the <term>Communion of the Sacraments</term> <note>The ritual of the Eucharist or Lord's Supper.</note> in such a way that sometimes—lest they fail to remain completely hidden—they receive the Body of Christ with an unworthy mouth, but they utterly refuse to drink the Blood of our Redemption. We make this known to your Holiness so that such men may be identified by these signs, and so that those whose sacrilegious deception has been uncovered may be driven from the fellowship of the Saints by priestly authority.”*

Since in that era the Christian people had the freedom to receive <term>Communion</term> either under the single <term>species</term> <note>original: "specie." In theology, this refers to the outward appearance of the bread or wine.</note> of bread or under both species of bread and wine, Saint Leo commanded that the Christian people should henceforth receive it under both species. This was done to expose the sacrilegious Manichaeans: if they saw anyone abstaining from the use of the chalice, they would know him to be a Manichaean and report the man as such. In addition to their other more notable and impious customs was their practice of fasting on Sunday and Monday in honor of both planets, which they especially worshiped as gods. Regarding this, Leo the Great says (2):

<margin>
The Manichaeans fasted on the Lord's Day [Sunday] in honor of the Sun, and on the second day [Monday] in honor of the Moon.
</margin>

*“Let no contagion of their error touch us,”* he says, *“for they are polluted by their own observances, serving the creature rather than the Creator. They devote a foolish abstinence to the lights of heaven; there can be no doubt that those caught fasting on the Lord’s Day and the second day of the week in honor of the Sun and Moon are Manichaeans. By a single act of perversity they are twice impious and twice profane, for they intend their fast both as a worship of the stars and as a show of contempt for the resurrection of Christ. Indeed, they shrink from the <term>Sacrament of human salvation</term> and do not believe that Christ our Lord was truly born in the real flesh of our nature, truly suffered, was truly buried, and was truly raised. For this reason, they condemn the day of our salvation and joy with the gloom of their fasting.”*

# DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENT [MANICHAEANS] 68

Augustine also expresses his detestation of the Manichaean rite in these words (1):
> To fast on the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note> is a scandal; it is especially a great one now that the detestable heresy of the Manichaeans has become known—a heresy most clearly contrary to the Catholic faith and the Divine Scriptures. They established this day as a legitimate time for fasting for their **Hearers** <note>The *Auditores* (Hearers) were the lower rank of Manichaean followers, who served the higher-ranking 'Elect'.</note>, as a result of which fasting on the Lord’s Day came to be held as more horrible.

<margin>The Manichaeans did not offer bread to the poor for a clearly ridiculous reason.</margin>
Finally, lest I go through every detail, they used to deny bread to the poor, even if they were dying of hunger, for a clearly ridiculous reason which nevertheless followed from their "old wives' tale" <note>original: *anili... fabula*; a reference to the complex and bizarre Manichaean mythology involving fragments of the divine trapped in matter.</note> (2).
> [The Manichaean] does not offer bread to a beggar, says Augustine. See if there can be a greater iniquity than this "justice." He does not offer bread to a beggar. Ask him: Why? Lest the life which is in the bread—which they call a limb of God, a **Divine substance**—be received by that beggar and bound within his flesh. <note>Manichaeans believed that "sparks of light" or divine life were trapped in plants and food; they believed only their high-ranking 'Elect' could release this light through digestion, whereas a common beggar would only further imprison the light in their own body.</note>

## CHAPTER IX.

### Concerning the laws passed under Imperial law against the Manichaeans.

XLI. Nine years after the most bitter execution <note>Mani was executed in Persia in the 270s AD.</note> of Mani, the Manichaeans had already burst into Africa. For, as we touched upon above, the death of Mani fell in the year of Christ 278, at the end of the month of March. For in that year, the Feast of Easter fell on the 31st of March. Moreover, the Manichaeans celebrated the day of their master Mani's death in the month of March, which they called the festival of the **Bema** <note>original: *Bematis festum*. The *Bema* (Greek for 'platform' or 'step') was the most important Manichaean holiday, commemorating the martyrdom of Mani.</note> from the steps of the magnificent altar. Indeed, the decree of Diocletian and Maximian against the Manichaeans staying in Africa—which is the first of all the Imperial laws against the Manichaeans—dates to the year of Christ 287.

<margin>
The decree of Diocletian and Maximian against the Manichaeans residing in Africa, given to Julian, the Proconsul of Africa, in the year 287 AD.
</margin>
The decree was given to Julian, the Proconsul of Africa. We now present it (1). *Diocletian and Maximian, the most noble Augusti <note>A title for the senior Roman Emperors during the Tetrarchy</note>, to Julian, Proconsul of Africa: We have heard that the Manichaeans have very recently progressed or emerged into this world like new and unexpected portents <note>original: "prodigia"; in this context, it refers to something unnatural, monstrous, or an ill omen</note> from the Persian nation, which is hostile to us; and that they commit many crimes there. We command that the authors and leaders, together with their abominable writings, be subjected to a more severe punishment, so that they may be consumed by flaming fires. However, we order that their followers, and those who are particularly stubborn, be punished by the head <note>meaning execution, likely by the sword</note>, and we decree that their goods be claimed by our treasury <note>original: "fisco"; the private funds of the Emperor</note>. If any have transferred themselves to this unheard-of, shameful, and entirely infamous sect or doctrine of the Persians, you shall cause their patrimonies to be joined to our treasury.* It will perhaps seem strange to anyone that Diocletian and Maximian—impious and wicked men, excelling in no virtue—passed a most severe law against the Manichaeans. But the wonder will cease if we consider that the Manichaeans were always held to be common and especially deadly enemies of the entire human race. Since they refrained from no lust, even if it were most ruinous and contrary to all nature, they cursed the procreation of children—without which the human race cannot endure—with every dire oath. They deterred even spouses from procreating children as if from an inexpiable crime; nothing is more hostile to the human race than this. <note>Manichaeans believed that trapped "light" was further imprisoned in the material world through birth; thus, they viewed procreation as a spiritual evil.</note>

<margin>
The decree of Valentinian I against the Manichaeans, given on the 6th day before the Nones of March <note>March 2nd</note>, during the consulship of Modestus and Arintheus; that is, on March 2nd in the year 372 AD at Trier.
</margin>
Furthermore, very grave laws by the Christian Emperors followed against the Manichaeans. By Valentinian I, on the 2nd of March in the year of Christ 372, this law was enacted (2): *Wherever a gathering of Manichaeans or a crowd of this sort is found, the teachers having been punished with a heavy penalty, the houses and dwellings in which they teach their profane institution shall be claimed for the rights of the treasury without doubt.* Given on the 6th day before the Nones of March at Trier <note>original: "Trever."; modern-day Trier, Germany, then a major imperial residence</note>, during the consulship of Modestus and Arintheus.

<margin>
The decree of Theodosius the Elder against the Manichaeans, given on the 15th day before the Kalends of June <note>Traditionally May 18th</note> at Rome, during the consulship of Primasius and Promotus; that is, on June 17th in the year 389 AD.
</margin>

-># DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS<-

In the year 389, Theodosius <note>Theodosius I, also known as the Great, who made Nicene Christianity the official state religion of the Roman Empire</note> restrained the impious Manichaean sect with this enacted law (1): *Whoever disturbs the world under the name of Manichaeans shall be expelled from the entire world, but most especially from this city <note>original: "ab hac urbe"; referring to Rome, where the decree was issued</note>, under the threat of judicial sentence. Their wills, or rather their very assets, are to be made public property; they shall not have the power to make wills, nor is it lawful for anything to be left to them or by them. In short, let them have nothing in common with the world.* Given on the 15th day before the Kalends of July <note>June 17</note> at Rome, in the consulship of Timasius and Promotus. Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, the influential Bishop of Milan</note> seems to indicate this law of Theodosius, having committed these words to writing in that very same year (2): *A Manichaean is one who denies the truth, who denies the flesh of Christ. And therefore, for him there is no remission of sins, but rather the impiety of the Manichaeans, which even the Most Clement Emperor has cursed.*

### XLII.
<margin>The decree of Valentinian III against the Manichaeans, given on the 13th day before the Kalends of July <note>June 19</note> at Rome, in the fourth consulship of Valentinian Augustus and the consulship of Nomus—that is, June 19, 445 AD.</margin>
To the previous laws established by Caesar's right against the Manichaeans is added the *Novella* <term>Novella: A "New Law" issued after the publication of the official Theodosian Code</term> of Valentinian III, given on June 19, 445 AD. This occurred during the papacy of Saint Leo the Great, and is as follows (3): *The Emperors Theodosius and Valentinian to Albinus, Praetorian Prefect and Patrician: The superstition of the Pagans, also condemned in the times of [Diocletian and Maximian], being an enemy to public discipline and a foe to the Christian faith, has not without merit provoked our Clemency to its destruction. We speak of the Manichaeans, whom the statutes of all former Princes have judged execrable and to be expelled from the whole world. Nor do their recently detected crimes allow for any indifference. For what obscenities, both in the telling and the hearing, were laid open by their own clear confession in the judgment of the most blessed Pope Leo, before the most distinguished Senate? This went so far that he who was called their Bishop betrayed them with his own voice and wrote out all the secrets of their crimes, a matter which could not remain hidden from our knowledge—for it is not safe for us to neglect such detestable divinity—*

Discern what it means to suffer persecution for justice; look again and again in your own books to see for which of these causes you are suffering.”*

The Emperors, following the division of both the Eastern and Western Empires, determined that because the headlong frenzy of the Manichaeans could not be restrained by lighter laws, this entire pestilential and impious race had to be removed from human society by the ultimate punishment <note>Original Latin: *supplicio ultimo*, referring to the death penalty</note>. <margin>Decree of Basil the Macedonian and his sons regarding the Paulicians and Manichaeans, who were to be subjected to the death penalty and their books burned.</margin> The most reliable witnesses to this are Photius and Peter of Sicily, writers of the 9th century. <margin>Decree of Basil the Macedonian and his sons concerning the <term>Paulicians</term> <note>A dualist Christian sect influential in the Byzantine Empire, often identified by contemporaries as "New Manichaeans."</note>, who are also Manichaeans, regarding their being subjected to the ultimate punishment and the burning of their books.</margin>
The most abundant witnesses are Photius and Peter of Sicily, writers of the 9th century. Indeed, Peter of Sicily, who was sent by Basil the Macedonian to Armenia as an envoy to settle the disturbances caused by the Manichaeans, left these records for posterity (1): *To their other distinguished deeds, the divine and orthodox Emperors added this: they commanded that the Manichaeans and <term>Montanists</term> <note>Followers of an early Christian movement characterized by prophetic claims and rigorous ethics.</note> be sentenced to death, and that their books, wherever they might be found, be committed to the flames. Furthermore, if anyone were discovered to have hidden these books, he too would be sentenced to the penalty of death, and his goods would be confiscated to the <term>fisc</term> <note>The state treasury.</note>.* The specific Emperors of the East who brought capital laws against the Manichaeans are commemorated by Peter of Sicily and Photius as Justinian II, Michael Curopalates, and Leo the Armenian. Concerning Justinian, Peter of Sicily has this to say (2):

<margin>Justinian II's decree regarding the burning of the stubborn Paulicians, or Manichaeans.</margin>
*Justinian Augustus, who governed the scepters of the Empire after Heraclius (and Constantine Pogonatus), ordered all the Manichaeans to be gathered together immediately, interrogated individually, and delivered to the flames—as many as were stubborn in their error. Thus, a huge pyre having been built in a heap, they were all set on fire and burned.* Photius agrees with Peter of Sicily, having committed these things to writing regarding the same Justinian (3): *The Emperor then was Justinian, who had succeeded after Heraclius (and Constantine Pogonatus, his partner in the Empire), and who commanded that these matters (concerning the Manichaeans) be subjected to investigation and just judgment; so that those who refused to return to their senses, or who had once promised repentance but nonetheless persisted in their <term>apostasy</term> <note>The total desertion or departure from one's religion.</note>, should undergo the punishment of fire.* Concerning Michael Curopalates, who took up the monastic habit, and Leo—

<margin>Decree of Michael <term>Curopalates</term> <note>A high Byzantine court title; here referring to Emperor Michael I Rangabe (reigned 811–813).</note> and Leo the Armenian regarding the execution of Paulicians or Manichaeans everywhere.</margin>
Regarding the decrees issued against the Manichaeans by Leo the Armenian—who succeeded Michael when the latter departed to become a monk—Peter of Sicily records these details (1):

> The Emperor Michael, a most religious monk, and Leo, who ruled after him, seeing that Christians were being harassed in various and shameful ways by this Manichaean heresy, sent letters throughout all the Roman <note>original: *ditionis Romanæ*; referring to the Byzantine or Eastern Roman Empire.</note> territories and ordered all participants of this wicked sect to be put to death. Therefore, when the royal edict reached Armenia—specifically to Thomas, the Bishop of Neocaesarea, and to Paracordaces the Prefect—all those found to be leaders of this deadly ruin who were worthy of death were executed by royal command.

Photius recounts the same events as Peter of Sicily in these words (2):

> Michael, who had exchanged his imperial robes for those of a monk, and his successor Leo, took great care to conduct an investigation into this apostasy. With the necessary diligence, they sent men of high rank throughout all the borders of the Roman Empire. Since those heretics had frequently been warned by bishops and priests but had neither obeyed nor repented, the officials were to strike them with the sword as a common plague and a destruction to the human race, if they found any guilty of such impiety who refused to return to a better way of life.

### CHAPTER X.

#### Concerning the laws enacted under Papal Law against the Manichaeans.

XLIV. <term>Papal Law</term> <note>Latin: *Jus Pontificium*; the body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority (the Church).</note> differs greatly from <term>Imperial Law</term> <note>Latin: *Jus Cæsareum*; the civil law of the Emperors.</note>, and Papal laws disagree with Imperial ones in many respects. For the former are carried out by the **authority of the keys**, by which the power of binding and loosing is given; the latter, however, are carried out by the **authority of the sword**, by which the power to kill the impious is granted. In short, the former pertain to the correction of the wicked, while the latter pertain to their destruction. <margin>Siricius excludes the Manichaeans from Christian rites; he ensures that those who are stubborn are expelled from the city, while those who repent are assigned to perpetual penance in monasteries, where the last communion <term>Viaticum</term> <note>Literally "provision for a journey," this is the final reception of the Eucharist given to those near death.</note> is granted to them only when in danger of death.</margin>

From this, two things follow: that monasteries existed before Siricius, and that perpetual penance was imposed for the more serious crimes—yet with this moderation, that the <term>Viaticum</term> would be granted to those at their end.*

# AND THE NEW MANICHÆANS.

...who by his own time had already grown into a much larger number. Following the Vandal persecution and the devastation of Africa under Genseric <note>Genseric, also known as Gaiseric, was the Vandal king who conquered North Africa and sacked Rome in 455 AD.</note>, King of the Vandals, the Manichaeans—who lived in that Province in great numbers—fled Africa and betook themselves to Rome for refuge.

<margin>Leo the Great forbids all communion with Manichaeans in both divine and human affairs.</margin>
XLVI. Furthermore, Leo decreed that there should be no association, no union, and no communion whatsoever between Catholics and Manichaeans in either divine or human matters. Instead, there should be a total estrangement and separation, lest that pestilential and impious breed contaminate and corrupt the healthy body of the Christian people with the contagion of their foulness and impieties (1):

> *“By my command,” he says, “let no Christian have anything in common with men of this sort; let there be no association or fellowship with such people.”* <note>original: "Nihil, jubendo inquit, cum hujusmodi hominibus commune sit cuiquam christiano, nulla cum talibus habeatur societas, nullumque consortium."</note>

Leo himself testifies in these words that the Holy Pontiff devoted all his care, anxiety, thought, and all his effort to extinguishing the Manichaean heresy by investigating, uncovering, restraining, punishing, and healing (2):

<margin>Leo the Great assigns repentant Manichaeans to public penance.</margin>
> *“Our investigation has uncovered many followers and teachers of the Manichaean impiety in the city; our vigilance has exposed them, and our authority and judgment have restrained them. Those we were able to reform, we corrected. We compelled them to condemn Manichaeus along with his teachings and rules, through a public profession in the Church and by the signature of their own hand. Thus, we have lifted those who confessed from the abyss of their impiety by granting them penance.”*

In these final words, St. Leo indicates clearly enough that he assigned the Manichaeans who were recalled from heresy to <term>public penance|A rigorous and public process of atonement required by the early Church for grave sins before a person could be readmitted to full communion</term>, as was the custom at that time. However, the Holy Pontiff does not clarify here whether this penance was to be lifelong (excepting only the moment of death), following the example of his predecessor Siricius, or if it was only for a set period of time. Indeed, St. Innocent I—who followed Siricius but preceded Leo—[maintained] that no one who sincerely repented should be denied [reconciliation] when near death, regardless of how terrible their public [sins] might be...

-># AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS.<-

The <term>New Manichaeans</term> <note>These are the Paulicians, a medieval Christian sect often accused by their contemporaries of being a revival of the ancient Manichaean dualist heresy.</note> greatly disturbed the Church of Christ, primarily in the 8th and 9th centuries, as they were nearly contemporaries in age. <margin>Peter of Sicily was an eyewitness and earwitness, and is the most reliable writer on the Paulician heresy.</margin>

*While I remained for a long time among the Paulicians at Tibrica for the sake of carrying out my embassy,* he says, *I frequently engaged in disputes with them, and I even carefully investigated all their secrets through the Catholics living there.* At the conclusion of his history of the Paulicians, Peter of Sicily adds the following (2): *Having spent nine months at Tibrica, I accurately examined and curiously inquired into those things which I have recorded above; and in obedience to the most holy commands of the pious and orthodox princes, though I am the least and most unworthy, I have striven to make them known to everyone.*

<margin>Photius left to posterity a history of the old and new Manichaeans (that is, the Paulicians), drawn from the most reliable records.</margin>

Furthermore, Photius was edited in Latin from a Greek manuscript in the Coislin Library (formerly the Seguier Library in Paris) by the venerable Montfaucon in the year 1715. He produced a summary history of the Manichaeans, both the old and the new (that is, the Paulicians), from the 3rd century through to the 9th, which is the century of the Paulicians. He drew his information on the Paulicians from the most abundant witnesses and certain reports of his own age, while his information on the ancient Manichaeans was borrowed from <term>Cyril of Jerusalem</term>, <term>Epiphanius</term>, and other writers whom he himself cites (3). # AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS.

The Church of Christ was greatly disturbed, especially in the 8th and 9th centuries, by groups who were nearly contemporaries of one another. For John of Damascus flourished in the 8th century, while Photius and Peter of Sicily flourished in the 9th. <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749) was a prominent Syrian Christian monk; Photius (c. 810–893) was the Patriarch of Constantinople; Peter of Sicily (fl. 870) was a Byzantine diplomat and historian.</note> Indeed, Peter of Sicily—whose work was translated into Latin with annotations from a manuscript in the Vatican Library by Matthew Rader <note>Matthew Rader (1561–1634) was a Jesuit scholar known for his editions of early Christian texts.</note> of the Society of Jesus, and is found in volume 14 of the *Library of the Fathers* <note>original: "Biblioth. PP." or *Bibliotheca Patrum*.</note>, Paris edition—relates in his *History of the Vain and Foolish Heresy of the Manichaeans* (dedicated to the Archbishop of the Bulgarians) that he was sent as an envoy by the Emperors Basil, Leo, and Constantine to the Paulicians. <note>The Paulicians were a medieval Christian sect often labeled as "New Manichaeans" due to their dualistic beliefs.</note> These Paulicians held the town of Tibrica in Armenia; Peter was delegated there to ransom captured military leaders, and he affirms that in that town he learned all the mysteries of the Paulicians (1).

<margin>Peter of Sicily is an eyewitness and earwitness, and a most reliable writer on the Paulician heresy.</margin>

He says: *"While lingering at Tibrica for the purpose of fulfilling my embassy among the Paulicians, I frequently engaged them in debate, and I carefully investigated all their secrets through the Catholics also living there."* At the conclusion of his history of the Paulicians, Peter of Sicily writes (2): *"I, having spent nine months at Tibrica, accurately examined and curiously inquired into those things mentioned by us above; and, having obeyed the commands of the most holy, pious, and orthodox princes—although I am unworthy and the least [of servants]—I have striven to make them all known to the public."*

<margin>Photius committed to posterity a history of the old and new Manichaeans—that is, the Paulicians—extracted from the most certain records.</margin>

Photius, moreover, was published in Latin by the venerable Montfaucon <note>Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741) was a Benedictine monk and a founding father of the study of archaeology and paleography.</note> from a Greek manuscript in the Coislin Library (formerly the Seguier Library) in Paris in the year 1715. He produced a summary history of both the old and new Manichaeans (that is, the Paulicians) from the 3rd century up to the 9th, which is the century of the Paulicians. Indeed, he drew his account of the Paulicians from the most reliable witnesses and certain reports of his own age, while the history of the ancient Manichaeans he borrowed from Cyril of Jerusalem, Epiphanius, and other writers whom he himself mentions (3). "If any wish," he says, "to know of the ancient Manichaeans and their impiety from the beginning, and..."

*To observe where the first seeds were sown, Cyril—to whom the governance of the holy city (Jerusalem) was entrusted—will be our guide through the history itself; <note>Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313–386 AD) was a bishop and theologian whose writings provided early descriptions of Manichaeism.</note> as will Epiphanius, great in miracles, <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD) was a renowned "heresy-hunter" who detailed dozens of sects in his work, the *Panarion*.</note> and many others who have adorned Ecclesiastical histories. Also Titus, Bishop of the Bostrians, <note>Titus of Bostra (died c. 378 AD) wrote a significant treatise against the Manichaeans.</note> and Serapion of Thmuis, as well as Alexander, who held the Archbishopric of Lycopolis. Moreover, beyond these, there is one who triumphed boldly over all of them and refuted this very impiety in question: Heraclianus, Bishop of Chalcedon, who established battles against their apostasy in twenty books. Most distinguished, however, is the dialogue of St. John of Damascus <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749 AD) was a Syrian monk and a key defender of icons during the Byzantine Iconoclasm.</note> against the Manichaeans, about which his translator Jacques de Billy <note>Jacques de Billy (1535–1581) was a French Benedictine scholar who translated Greek patristic texts into Latin.</note> has some doubts; however, the venerable Father Le Quien, <note>Michel Le Quien (1661–1733) was a Dominican scholar and the definitive editor of the works of John of Damascus.</note> the most recent editor and illustrator of Damascus’s works, rightly and deservedly attributes that work to Damascus and defends it most unbeatably. He teaches, in a warning joined to the work, that Damascus wrote this dialogue against the Manichaeans when they had begun to spread and strengthen in parts of Syria under the name of "Paulicians" during the reign of Emperor Leo the Isaurian.* <note>Leo III (reigned 717–741 AD), known as "the Isaurian," was the Byzantine Emperor who initiated the first period of Iconoclasm.</note>

<margin>From where the name of the Paulicians flowed down to the Armenian Manichaeans.</margin>

XLIX. Regarding the origin of the Paulicians from a certain Paul of Samosata (whose homeland was Samosata of Euphratean Syria), the name "Paulician" did not come to the Manichaeans from that famous 3rd-century Bishop of Samosata <note>original: "Episcopo Samosateno". champions. <margin>The Paulicians, like the ancient Manichaeans, deny that humans have free will.</margin>
Now, concerning the mixture of the good and evil principles from which human beings proceeded: he soon emphasizes and concludes again (1): *“From the portion of good, souls were produced, and from the substance of evil, bodies were produced.”* Moreover, since the Paulicians had established that only good fruits can be procreated from the good principle, and only evil fruits from the evil principle, they affirmed that, for this reason, the good actions of a human being proceed from the good principle; while, on the other hand, the evil actions of a human being proceed by an inevitable necessity of nature from the evil principle. Furthermore, by establishing contrary principles of this sort that impose necessity, they fundamentally overturned the free will <term>liberum arbitrium: the capacity of an agent to make choices free from certain kinds of constraints</term> of man.

->LI.<-

It remains for us to briefly examine a few points regarding the life, morals, and customs of the Paulicians, by which the Paulicians revealed themselves to be true and genuine Manichaeans. And although the public display of piety and holiness, and the exhibition of a more severe doctrine and discipline, is a very notable mark of all heretics of all times, it showed itself much more brilliantly in the ancient and new Manichaeans, such as the Paulicians were. Indeed, it was the custom of the Paulicians in their encounters with Catholics to put forward a certain singular and admirable holiness, to proclaim themselves as Catholics, and to profess themselves as wonderful admirers and practitioners of Catholic doctrine (2).

<margin>The Paulicians, like the ancient Manichaeans, falsely and deceitfully simulate the Christian life and doctrine, as well as a severity of morals.</margin>

</margin>

*“They study this especially,”* Peter of Sicily says of the Paulicians, *“so that they do not announce their sacred rites and heresies everywhere to everyone, even their own—I do not say to strangers, but even to their families. They communicate them only to the few whom they know have advanced more than others in impiety.”* Anyone who desires more details about the Paulicians—their expansion, the towns they founded, their civil and military affairs, their princes, leaders, raids, battles, slaughters, and punishments—should consult, besides the previously mentioned Photius and Peter of Sicily, Zonaras, Cedrenus, Euthymius in his *Panoplia* <note>Euthymius Zigabenus (died c. 1118) was a Byzantine monk whose *Panoplia Dogmatica* was a massive encyclopedia of heresies and orthodox defenses.</note>, and other writers of ecclesiastical history. 

<margin>
The Paulicians, like the ancient Manichaeans, taught two opposing, determining principles, by which they utterly overturned human free will.
</margin>

It is enough for us to have shown that the Paulicians were the successors of the Manichaeans, especially in their most fundamental error regarding the <term>dual principles</term> <note>The belief that there are two co-equal powers of Good and Evil in the universe, rather than one supreme God.</note> which impose necessity: which being established, they both fundamentally overturned and radically uprooted human <term>free will</term> <note>original: "liberum arbitrium." The author argues that if two cosmic forces control everything, humans cannot truly choose between good and evil.</note>.

### AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS.
M
<meta>catchword: infe- [inferre - to bring in]</meta>

...in France; in Italy, however, they were called **Patarines**, perhaps from "patience," or rather from the "hardness" <note>original: "duritia"; likely referring to their ascetic endurance or stubbornness</note> which they displayed, and they were called by other names in other places. The Third Lateran Council (1) indicates that they were referred to by many names: *"In Gascony, the Albigensian region, and the districts of Toulouse,"* it says, *"and in other places, the damned perversity of heretics has grown strong—heretics whom some call **Cathars**, others **Patarines** or **Paterenes**, others **Publicans** (perhaps 'Populicans' <note>A corruption of 'Paulicians' or 'men of the people'</note>), and others by different names."*

<margin>In the 9th century, the Paulicians planned to break into Bulgaria from Armenia.</margin>
For a long time now—specifically since the 9th century—the Paulicians, according to the testimony of Peter of Sicily, planned to break out of Armenia into Bulgaria (2). *"I learned from these same impious and delusional men about the Armenian Paulicians,"* he says, *"that they were going to send people from their secret assembly <note>original: "conciliabulo"</note> who would turn whoever they could in Bulgaria away from the Catholic religion to their own cursed and wicked sect."*

<margin>The Paulicians, who are also called Manichaeans, moved from Syria into Bulgaria and Thrace in the 8th century under Constantine Copronymus.</margin>
Furthermore, the venerable Father Lequien is the authority (3) stating that in the 8th century, while Constantine Copronymus <note>Constantine V (reigned 741–775), an Emperor often accused by later historians of favoring heretics due to his Iconoclasm</note> was the patron of the Manichaeans, the Manichaeans penetrated into Bulgaria and Thrace from Syria. Peter de Marca (4) records that the errors of the Paulicians, or Manichaeans, reached France from Bulgaria and the nearby region of Thrace through this specific route and opportunity.

<margin>The Paulician or Manichaean heresy was brought from Bulgaria into France by Frankish merchants at the beginning of the 12th century; hence the Albigensian heretics were commonly called "Bulgars."</margin>
For when the Franks took possession of Jerusalem at the end of the 11th century, and because they had frequent contact with the Bulgarians for the sake of trade, they absorbed the errors of the Bulgarians and carried them back to France. At the beginning of the 12th century, they infected the people of Toulouse, Aquitaine, and Orléans with the "Manichaean plague." Therefore, because the errors of the Paulicians or Manichaeans had arrived in France from Bulgaria, it came to pass that the **Cathars** or **Albigensians** were popularly and commonly called "Bulgars" <note>This ethnic label eventually became a general term for heretics in Western Europe</note>. Regarding Philip Augustus, who reigned in France at the end of the 12th century, a monk of Auxerre (5) left this record for posterity: *"He strove mightily against the heretics whom they call Bulgars..."*

### DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS
<meta>catchword: lorum</meta>

<margin>The heresy of the Albigensians (also called Bulgarians) and the Cathars is identical to the heresy of the Paulicians or Manichaeans.</margin>
...to harass <note>original: *insectari*; likely referring to the persecution of these groups</note>. Regarding the Bulgarian heresy, which spread most aggressively through France during the age of Philip Augustus <note>Philip II (reigned 1180–1223), the first French king to use the title "King of France"</note>, the author writes: *“During this same period, the detestable Bulgarian heresy—the final dregs of all errors—crept through many places, being all the more harmful because it was more hidden. But it had grown especially strong in the land of the Count of Toulouse and the neighboring Princes.”* <note>The Count of Toulouse at this time was Raymond VI, whose lands became the primary target of the Albigensian Crusade</note>. Therefore, since the Bulgarian heresy was the same as the Manichaean heresy, and the errors of the Albigensians were the same as those of the Bulgarians (who were called "Bulgars" for that very reason), it can now be deduced that the Albigensian heresy was the same as the Manichaean one; they were twin offspring and the hereditary successors of the ancient Manichaeans. This is a very common opinion, defended above all by the eminent Bossuet <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, a powerful 17th-century French bishop and theologian</note> in volume 2 of his *History of the Variations of the Protestant Churches*, book 11, page 124 and following; by the Reverend Father Thomas Augustine Richinius in his first dissertation on the Cathars, chapter 1; and by Father Peter Lazerius of the Society of Jesus <note>S.J., the Jesuits</note> in his study on the Albigensian heresy.

<margin>The Albigensians, like the ancient Manichaeans, taught two Gods: one good, the cause of all good things, and another evil, the cause of all evil.</margin>
LIII. Furthermore, from the total consistency and agreement of their doctrine, it is easy to demonstrate that the Albigensians (or Cathars) proved themselves to be the true and legitimate brothers of the Manichaeans. Indeed, as witnessed by Moneta <note>Moneta of Cremona (c. 1240), an inquisitor whose writings are a primary source for Cathar beliefs</note>—who lived at the same time as the Cathars and whose excellent work against them was brought out of long-standing darkness into the desired light by the Reverend Father Thomas Augustine Richinius for the good of the Christian world, and illustrated with highly learned dissertations and notes—the Albigensians, just like the Manichaeans, taught that there were two contrary Gods and two contrary principles. One was good, from whom all good things come; the other was evil, from whom all evil things come. This fact is clear and well-researched. For according to Moneta, this was the doctrine of the Albigensians (1): *“That there are two Gods: one the principle and cause of things invisible to us and of all good things; but the other the principle and cause of all things visible to us here, and of all evil things.”*

### AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS.

Wickedly contradicting the venerable Sacrament of baptism, the heretic says, *That it confers nothing upon a man toward salvation.* For he claims that neither the remission of sins nor the grace of the Holy Spirit is conferred through it. Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay <note>Petrus Vallis Cernaii (c. 1182–1218), a Cistercian monk and chronicler who documented the Albigensian Crusade from a pro-Church perspective.</note> records these things concerning the Albigensians of his own age (1): *They annulled the Sacraments of the Church to such an extent that they publicly preached that the water of holy baptism was no different from river water.*

<margin>The Albigensians, like the ancient Manichaeans, loathed marriage.</margin> Regarding Marriage, the Albigensians agreed with the ancient Manichaeans. Let Moneta <note>Moneta of Cremona (c. 1180–1240), an inquisitor and author of a major treatise against the Cathars and Waldensians.</note> be heard (2): *Now we must see,* he says, *concerning Marriage, which is the legitimate union of male and female, maintaining an inseparable way of life.* The heretics themselves, however, call this custom illegitimate—that is, *against God’s law*. Their error is derived from a filthy source <note>original: "canoso fonte," likely a variant of "caenoso," meaning swampy or foul.</note>, because they believe the body of the male and female was made by the devil, along with the distinction of the reproductive organs; for this reason, they say that all carnal intercourse is damnable.

<margin>The Albigensians, like the ancient Manichaeans, taught the Pythagorean Transmigration of Souls.</margin> Finally, the Albigensians, along with the ancient Manichaeans, taught Metempsychosis <term>Metempsychosis|The philosophical concept of the soul's reincarnation into a new body after death, often associated with the Greek philosopher Pythagoras.</term>—that is, the transfer of souls from body to body—which had Pythagoras as its author. For Moneta (3) records these things about the Albigensians, who are also called Cathars: *Distinguishing between the Soul and the Spirit, they say that the Spirit does not go from body to body, but the Soul does.* Therefore, they speak against themselves when they say that the Spirit which had been in that body (of Elijah) was later in the body of John the Baptist. Furthermore, among the anathemas <note>Formal ecclesiastical curses or denunciations used when a heretic renounced their errors to rejoin the Church.</note> prescribed to be pronounced by Albigensians returning to the Church, this is also read in the work of Tollius (4): *I anathematize those who admit Metempsychosis.*

<margin>The Albigensians and the ancient Manichaeans, neglecting the feast of Easter, celebrated the anniversary of Mani’s death with magnificent preparation.</margin>

<margin>The Albigensians abstained from the same foods as the ancient Manichaeans.</margin>
In their abstinence from foods which they believed were evil by nature, they imitated the ancient Manichaeans in no small way. Hence that pledge which they demanded from new disciples being received into their flock, concerning which Reinerius <note>Reinerius Sacconi (c. 1210–1258), a former Cathar leader who became a Dominican inquisitor and wrote a famous treatise on the sect's rituals.</note> writes in Martène’s collection (2): *“Do you promise that hereafter you will not eat meat, nor eggs, nor cheese, nor any sustenance except from water and wood?”* 
And by "water" they understand fish, and by "wood" they mean oil <note>The Albigensians avoided animal products resulting from sexual reproduction (meat, eggs, dairy). Fish were then believed to be born of water without mating, and olive oil was a plant product from trees.</note>.

<margin>The lust of the Albigensians, like that of the ancient Manichaeans, was most unrestrained.</margin>
Lucas of Tuy (3) <note>Lucas Tudensis (d. 1249), a Spanish bishop and historian known for his polemics against heresy.</note> declares the Albigensians' most unrestrained lust for every disgrace—even against and contrary to nature—in no different way than that of the ancient Manichaeans, with these words: *“They are carried away unrestrained through various desires of the flesh, and there is no harmful pleasure that their luxury does not pass through. The son abuses the mother, the brother the brother, and the father commits foulness with his daughter.”*
What is most impious and sacrilegious is that, following the example of the ancient Manichaeans, they crowned their most excessive lust for every pleasure with execrable sorceries, the summoning of demons, and incantations.

<margin>The Albigensians, like the ancient Manichaeans, were addicted to sorceries, the worship of demons, and familiarity with them.</margin>

<margin>The error of the Predestinarians is closely related to the error of the Manichaeans.</margin>
...and it teaches that this error flowed down from the Basilidians <note>A Gnostic sect from the 2nd century founded by Basilides.</note> to the Cathars <note>A medieval dualist sect, also known as the Albigensians, who believed in two opposing principles of good and evil.</note>. For the error of the Predestinarians <term>Predestinarians</term> <note>Those who believe God has unalterably determined the fate of every soul regardless of their actions.</note> is a neighbor to the error of the Manichaeans. If, as the Manichaeans wildly imagined, there are two contrary and necessitating principles—one toward good and the other toward evil—to which humans are subject, then once these are established, no place is left for the free choice of the human will. The Cathars, who held these views along with the Manichaeans, fell into the Predestinarian abyss not just by an easy path, but by one that was slippery and headlong. But let us not get stuck on the word itself, since our entire controversy concerns the reality of the matter. <margin>The errors of the Predestinarians: that God is unwilling to save any except the predestined; that the death of Christ the Lord was for the predestined alone; that predestination and reprobation are by necessity; and that free choice is removed from both the predestined and the rejected.</margin>
I. Who teach that God does not wish, with a serious and sincere will, for other men to be saved, except for the Predestined alone.
II. Who teach that Christ the Lord did not die for other men, but for the Predestined alone.
III. IV. Who teach that no free choice of the will <note>original: "arbitrium"</note> remains for the Predestined to attain salvation, nor for the rejected to avoid damnation, as the will is free from neither the antecedent nor the insurmountable necessity. I demonstrate from the same Moneta that such were the Cathars, the successors of the Manichaeans against whom the Venerable Moneta wrote—if not all of them, then certainly many.

# DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS #

...both the predestined and the rejected <note>original: *reprobi* — those who are not chosen for salvation and face damnation</note>, as the Apostle witnesses, died originally in Adam. Therefore, as far as the sufficiency of the price—which the Son offered to the Father who accepted it—and the benevolence of the Redeemer are concerned, it is consistent with the benevolent will of the Father, who wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Thus, Christ the Lord died for absolutely all men, with no one excepted, including both the faithful and the unfaithful, and both the predestined and the rejected. Where, however, it is said that Christ the Lord gave a redemption for *many*, and that the Blood of Christ was to be shed for *many* (1): *It is said so*, says Moneta, *because even if it is sufficient for all, it did not benefit all.* Therefore, the death of Christ the Lord and the most precious shedding of His Blood is not fruitful in justifying grace for the obstinate unfaithful due to their own fault, but only for the faithful, who are not few, but many. Nor is it fruitful for eternal salvation for the impenitent rejected due to their own fault, but only for the predestined, who are also not few, but many. Nevertheless, by the benevolent will of the Father who admits it, it is sufficient for salvation for absolutely all men.

<margin>The Albigensians, like the ancient Predestinarians, taught that those predestined for salvation and those rejected for destruction were irresistibly necessitated to their ends.</margin>

# AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS. 101 #

<margin>The third error of the Albigensian Predestinarians attacked by Venerable Moneta.</margin>
...salvation and perdition <note>original: *salus, & perditio*</note> consist, and not in such a "necessitating" Predestination as those people (that is, the Cathars) propose. However, Moneta completely rejects "predestination to guilt," as it is utterly repugnant to divine justice and holiness; along with Augustine, he admits only "predestination to punishment," and even then, only because of guilt that was foreseen beforehand.

<margin>Predestination to punishment arises from foreseen guilt; however, there is no Predestination to guilt itself.</margin>
For he teaches these things against the Predestinarians (1): *God prepared some for punishments, yet He did not prepare them to commit sins. God prepared what divine equity would render, not what human iniquity would do. This rule of Augustine must be held unshakably: Sinners were foreknown in their sins, but not prepared for them; however, the punishment was prepared, just as they were foreknown.* That man is pressed by no irresistible necessity of sinning or perishing is demonstrated by this excellent writer from the free power of choosing, which man relies upon without any irresistible determination toward one specific outcome. This is due to the choice of human freedom <note>original: *humanæ libertatis arbitrio* — what we commonly call "free will"</note>, which is entirely free from any preceding necessity. It arises from that active and elective freedom called the <term>liberty of indifference</term> <note>The theological idea that the human will is not naturally forced to choose one side over another, but remains free to pick between alternatives</note>, which he shows remains in man even after the fall of Adam through many illustrious testimonies.

<margin>There is no necessity of perdition, because the power of choosing is free.</margin>
But let Moneta himself be heard (2): *You see that here the necessity of fate or perdition presses no one, because the power of choosing is denied to no one. Predestination does not pull only in one direction where the choice of either side is offered.* These are the divine testimonies that Moneta brings forth to demonstrate this matter: Ecclesiasticus <note>Also known as the Book of Sirach</note>, chapter 15, verses 14 through 18.

<margin>The liberty of indifference is declared immune from all irresistible necessity.</margin>
*God from the beginning established man, and left him in the hand of his own counsel. He added his mandates and precepts: if you wish to keep the mandates, they shall preserve you, and to perform faithful service that is pleasing forever. He set before you water and fire; stretch out your hand to whichever you wish. Before man are life and death, good and evil: whatever pleases him shall be given to him.* Again, Deuteronomy, chapter 30, verse 19: *I call as witnesses...*

<margin>Once free will is established, no one is saved by necessity, and no one is damned by necessity.</margin>
LX. Once free will <term>liberum arbitrium; the capacity of a rational being to choose between different courses of action without being forced by necessity</term> has been posited, established, and demonstrated, it follows necessarily—according to the author Moneta—against the Predestinarians, that no one who possesses reason is saved by necessity, nor is anyone damned by necessity. Moneta shows this frequently (1): *Free will,* he says, *exists in men; however, free will would be in vain if man were saved by necessity. Nor would the equity of divine judgment stand; it would instead collapse (2):

<margin>The absurdities that follow from a "necessitating" Predestination and reprobation.</margin>
*If one person,* he says, *is destined for life by necessity, and another for death, we are not born to be judged, but judged already, and there will be no equity in judgment.* Therefore, God’s predestination remains—and it is indeed most certain—but it does not tear away or overturn the truly free choice of our will toward either side; rather, it is most excellently and amicably reconciled with it (3): *We do not deny,* says Moneta, *that some are pre-ordained by God to eternal life, but they are not ordained to possess it without free will.* Turning then to interpreting that passage of Revelation <note>original: *Apocalypsis*</note>, where those predestined for life are called "the Sealed" <note>original: *Signati*</note>, he teaches that they are not [sealed] for that reason...

<meta>This page continues the theological refutation of the "New Manichaeans" (likely referring to the Cathars or similar dualist sects), focusing on the relationship between God's foreknowledge and human free will.
