### AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS. ###

They are called by that name <note>The "Marked" or "Signed".</note>, not because they are marked by some sign of necessity for being saved, but because they are distinguished from the reprobate <note>Those rejected by God.</note> who will not use grace well. The rejection of these individuals is not to be traced back to any necessity of sinning or perishing, but rather to their own free abuse of grace (1): *They are called "marked,"* he says, *not by a sign of necessity for salvation; but marked, that is, distinguished from others who will not use grace well.*

<margin>Predestination is the foreknowledge of salvation; reprobation is the foreknowledge of damnation.</margin>
Furthermore, it is most vigorously shown from the definition of both terms—which Moneta <note>Moneta of Cremona (c. 1180–1240), an influential Dominican theologian who wrote against the Cathar and Waldensian heresies.</note> draws from Ambrose and proves—that neither predestination nor reprobation brings any preceding necessity of salvation or damnation (2): Ambrose says (these are Moneta's words), *that to predestine someone is the same as to foreknow that they are to be saved; Predestination, therefore, is the foreknowledge of salvation. In the same way, God rejects someone—the meaning being—that is, he foreknows that they are to be damned; hence reprobation is the foreknowledge of damnation.*

<margin>Both types of foreknowledge are consequent; neither is an antecedent necessity of salvation or damnation.</margin>
Now truly, the foreknowledge of both salvation and damnation is nothing other than a **consequent necessity** <note>In medieval logic, this refers to a necessity that follows from an event happening, but does not cause the event to happen (e.g., "if I see you walking, you must be walking," though my seeing you does not force you to walk).</note>. For the foreknowledge of salvation to be carried out, as God predestines it, follows the foreknowledge of final perseverance <note>The theological concept of remaining in a state of grace until death.</note>; while the foreknowledge of damnation follows the foreknowledge of final impenitence. For God foreknows that one person is to be saved in practice because He foreknows that person's final perseverance; similarly, God foreknows that another is to be damned because He foreknows that person's final impenitence. These latter are the final and most certain causes of future salvation and damnation.

<margin>The foreknowledge of God takes away neither liberty from coercion nor liberty from simple necessity.</margin>
Since, however, active final perseverance and active final impenitence are free actions of man, both instances of foreknowledge are merely a consequent necessity. This not only does not take away, but actually confirms the **freedom of indifference** <term>libertatem indifferentiae; the power of the will to choose between different options or to refrain from acting at all, even when all conditions for acting are present</term>. Regarding this kind of foreknowledge, Moneta teaches the following (3): *The foreknowledge of God does not take away the freedom of the will; lest anyone should say: even if*

LXI. > *Augustine says in Book 3 of "On Free Choice of the Will," chapter 3: We cannot perceive anything else to be in our power except that which we do when we will it. Therefore, the will itself is most of all in our power.* <note>original: "Ea enim prorsus nullo intervallo, mox ut volumus, præsto est... Ergo ipsa voluntas maximè est in potestate nostra."</note>

Our will is placed in our power in such a way that it is fixed to no side and bound to no party; rather, it is entirely within our power to bend, incline, or turn it to either side—whether by willing or not willing—as it pleases us. Moneta teaches that we have received such a will from God, one that can be turned in any direction at our command, with these words (2):

For he teaches that he does not indeed reject "freedom from compulsion" <note>original: "libertatem a coactione" — the state of acting without being physically or externally forced</note>, which is incompatible with voluntary action, but only rejects the "freedom of indifference" <note>original: "libertatem indifferentiæ" — the power of the will to choose between two different options without being determined by one</note>, which is free from insurmountable necessity. For whatever the human will does, whether good or evil, it does not do it unwillingly or by force (which would be entirely contradictory), but willingly and gladly; and it does so with a sweetness and delight that draws it along (2). *The will*, he says, *if it were forced, would not be a will. For compulsion is rather, so to speak, an **Un-will**.* <note>original: "Noluntas" — a play on words; since "Voluntas" comes from the verb "to will" (velle), Luther invents "Noluntas" from the verb "to be unwilling" (nolle).</note> Likewise (3), *The will, whether divine or human, does what it does by no compulsion, but by mere pleasure or desire, as if truly freely, whether it be good or evil.* From this most filthy and polluted sewer of Luther’s, Jansenius <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), a French-Dutch theologian whose work on St. Augustine led to the "Jansenist" controversy regarding grace and predestination.</note> drew two errors and offered them to his disciples: one regarding the admission of only freedom from compulsion and the denial of so-called "freedom of indifference"; the other regarding the twin delights—one for good, the other for evil—necessitating the will irresistibly.

<margin>
Freedom of indifference for natural acts is permitted by Luther, but for salvific acts it is utterly denied.

You might perhaps rightly attribute some "choice" to man; but "free choice" in divine matters is too much.* And in another place, much more clearly (4): *Toward God*, he says, *or in things pertaining to salvation or damnation, man does not have free choice, but is a captive, subject, and servant of either the will of God or the will of Satan.*

Under this irresistible command, according to Luther, unbelievers are constantly oppressed; and because they are impious, all works of such men are sins (1). *The impious man,* he says, *sins against God whether he eats or drinks, or whatever he may do.* This error of Luther—blown from the same set of pipes—is entirely consistent with that condemned refrain of the Bajanists and Jansenists: <note>Michael Baius (1513–1589) and Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638) were theologians whose views on "total depravity" and grace were condemned by the Catholic Church for being too similar to those of the Reformers.</note> *All works of unbelievers are sins, and the virtues of philosophers are vices.*

LXV. Furthermore, regarding the Manichaean <note>Manichaeism was an ancient religion that taught a radical dualism between good and evil; Catholic polemicists often accused Luther of being a "New Manichaean" because he taught that the will is controlled by external forces.</note> principles that necessitate either good or evil—which, if accepted, completely overthrows <term>free choice</term> <note>Latin: "liberum arbitrium." This refers to the human capacity to choose between different courses of action without being determined by necessity.</note>—Luther teaches similar things. For he asserts that both the foreknowledge of God and the omnipotent will of God bring a necessity to our actions, and therefore fight directly against the doctrine of free choice (2). <margin>According to Luther, God’s omnipotence, foreknowledge, will, and predestination are necessities that remove free choice.</margin> *Foreknowledge,* he says, *and the omnipotence of God are diametrically opposed to our free choice. This omnipotence and foreknowledge of God, I say, fundamentally abolish the dogma of free choice.* Indeed, with his usual boldness, he calls the force and excellence of divine foreknowledge and will a "thunderbolt" <note>original: "fulmen." Luther used this vivid imagery in his famous work "The Bondage of the Will" (De Servo Arbitrio) to describe how God's sovereign power crushes human pride in their own will.</note> by which free choice is consumed (3). *By this thunderbolt,* he says, *free choice is laid low and utterly crushed.* When he openly and freely professes what he himself believes and feels regarding divine foreknowledge, the predestining will of God, and the free choice of human and angelic nature (4), he says: *We believe it to be true that God foreknows and preordains all things; then, that His foreknowledge and predestination can neither be deceived nor hindered; and finally, that nothing happens unless He Himself wills it; (therefore) there can be no free choice in man, or Angel, or any creature.* He provides an example of this "extinguished" freedom under divine foreknowledge—not by coercion, but by a simple...

simple necessity of choice regarding the traitor Judas, he boasts of presenting himself with this childish reasoning (1): *If God foreknew that Judas would be a traitor, Judas necessarily became a traitor, nor was it in the hand of Judas, or of any creature, to do otherwise, or to change his will, although he did so by willing it, and was not coerced.* <note>original: "Si præscivit Deus Judam fore proditorem... non coactus." This is a central argument in Luther’s debate with Erasmus: if God is all-knowing, can anything happen differently than He sees it?</note> What he teaches concerning foreknowledge, he confirms with even greater impiety regarding the divine will, by which he says God so hardens us that by His own will He necessitates us irresistibly toward pertinence and obstinacy in evil (2). *The will of God,* he says, *imposes necessity upon us. It is not in our power to change His will, much less to resist it, when He wants us hardened; by which will we are compelled to be hardened, whether we wish it or not.* Nor does the divine will necessitate us only toward evil actions, but toward all our actions whatsoever, of every kind, according to Luther (3). *All things that we do,* he says, *happen necessarily and unchangeably, if you look to the will of God.*

LXVI. Nor does Luther contend that the human will is enslaved only to the necessitating will of God, but also to the necessitating will of Satan. Furthermore, to explain the utterly bestial condition of the human will, its liberty having been completely lost, he seeks an example from the most dull-witted of all beasts. He therefore compares the human will to a pack animal <note>Latin: *jumentum*. This is one of Luther's most famous and controversial metaphors, suggesting humans have no more agency over their spiritual direction than a donkey has over its rider.</note>, which must go wherever the rider wishes. If God sits upon it, it goes where God wills; but if Satan sits upon it, it goes where Satan wills; like a sluggish pack animal, the human will is necessarily carried along (4). <margin>The will of God and the will of Satan, according to Luther, are a double necessity of good and evil for us.</margin> *The human will,* he says, *is placed in the middle, like a pack animal. If God sits upon it, it wills and goes where God wills; if Satan sits upon it, it wills and goes where Satan wills.* In addition to these external factors mentioned above, there are also two contrary internal principles necessitating one toward good and the other toward evil...

...just as the Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans were followers of the prophet Mani; they believed the world was a battlefield between a good spiritual realm and an evil material realm, leaving humans with little choice in their actions.</note> do, Luther teaches: namely, that <term>original sin</term> <note>The Christian doctrine that all humans are born with a corrupted nature inherited from Adam.</note> remains in baptized men even after baptism, although he contends it is not imputed to them by God. The capacity of the human will to choose between good and evil.</note> absolutely no power, except to sin and be damned.*

<margin>According to Luther, original sin is for us a necessity of sinning; God's grace, however, is for us a necessity of living rightly.</margin>

On the other hand, he asserts that by interior divine grace—such as heavenly illumination—a man is snatched to Christ by a "most sweet snatching" indeed, but one that is entirely irresistible. By this, he denies liberty from necessity, though he claims to free the will from outward coercion. For he holds these views (3): *By the illumination of the spirit, man is snatched to Christ by a most sweet snatching <note>original: "suavissimo raptu." This implies an ecstatic, overwhelming experience where the soul is "carried away" by God.</note>, and he is a passive listener to the teacher speaking and to God drawing him, rather than seeking and running himself.* And again in another place, he asserts that Christians are driven not by free will, but by the Spirit of God—that is, by the interior grace of God—like a saw and an axe, which are unable to resist the craftsman, but are acted upon and snatched away (4): *Christians,* he says, *are driven not by free will, but by the Spirit of God. To be driven, however, is not to act, but to be snatched away, just as a saw and an axe are driven by a craftsman.* <note>original: "quemadmodum serra & securis a fabro agitur." This is one of Luther's most famous metaphors for the "bondage" of the human will: we are merely tools in the hands of either God or the Devil.</note> Finally, according to Luther, as long as the grace of God is present to a man, fixing his will toward desiring the good, no freedom is left to him to turn elsewhere—that is, toward evil—nor anything else besides...

This blind and impudent man even dared to affirm that they were wandering in the thickest darkness of ignorance (4). *In the same way,* he says, *Clement of Alexandria asserts free will everywhere, so that it appears not only were all the teachers of that age in such darkness, but that these things grew even more in later times.*

LXXI. As for the other theologians of the Catholic Church whom our adversary brings against us—especially St. Thomas—I pass over the others, who also deserve a kind interpretation. Even if the Angelic Doctor had taught this, he would still be very far from the <term>Manichaeans: followers of a dualistic religion who believed humans were composed of a naturally good part and a naturally evil part</term>, who claimed that man consists of one part good and one part naturally evil; and who believed, most seriously, that this evil nature drives us to sin by an irresistible necessity. Now, St. Thomas in his *Summa Theologiae* <note>First part of the second part, question 82, article 1</note> teaches that original sin, taken in a broad sense as including both the fault and the punishment, is a certain "corrupt habit" <note>original: "habitum quemdam corruptum"</note>. But in the following <note>Article 3</note>, he divides this corrupt habit into two parts: namely, the turning away of the mind from God, and the rebellion of the lower part of the soul. He teaches that this turning away of the soul from God is the "formal" aspect of original sin—that is, original sin itself. The rebellion of the lower part—"because there is in it," as Augustine says, "disobedience against the mastery of the mind"—is the "material" aspect <note>the physical or secondary component</note> of original sin.

<margin>
Original sin, properly understood by St. Thomas and other theologians, is that turning away of the soul from God which was a specific act in Adam, but is only a "habit" in Adam’s descendants from the moment they are conceived and naturally born.
</margin>
Therefore, the Angelic Doctor—and with him Bellarmine and many other theologians of the Catholic Church—locates original sin in this turning away of the soul from God. This act occurred in the first man, who was divinely established as the natural and moral head of all future people; this state exists as a "habit" <note>a spiritual disposition or orientation</note> in all human beings as soon as they are naturally conceived and propagated. For the loss of "original justice"—that is, the habitual orientation of the soul toward God from birth—was followed by a habitual turning away of the soul from God in all of us, the descendants of Adam. <meta>This page continues the defense of Catholic theology against accusations of Manichaeism. The previous page discussed the Lutheran scholar Wolf's critiques; this page specifically addresses the hypothetical "state of pure nature"—a concept used by theologians to describe what human nature would be like without supernatural grace—and argues that this view does not promote the dualism or determinism associated with Manichaean heresy.</meta>

<page-num>122</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS</header>

<note>original: "Manichæismum"</note> Manichaeism is a reproach thrown at our theologians because, by teaching that the <term>state of pure nature: a hypothetical state of humanity possessing only natural faculties without supernatural grace or original sin</term> is not a contradiction, they supposedly establish two contrary principles within it. Furthermore, the critics claim that in such a state, our theologians make God the author of sin—a suspicion that even the <term>Manichaeans: followers of a dualistic religion that believed in two eternal, equal powers of Good and Evil</term> did not dare to entertain. 

Now, however, these two "contrary principles" in the state of pure nature, as described by our theologians, are simply these: on one hand, there is the <term>sensitive appetite: the part of human nature that experiences physical desires and emotions</term>, which lacks the "bridle of integrity" <note>This refers to a supernatural gift of perfect self-control that Catholic theology teaches was lost after the Fall of Adam.</note> and is thus prone to pleasure and inclined toward what is perceived as delightful. On the other hand, besides natural reason, there are natural aids supplied by God that would allure the soul toward virtue and honorable goodness. 

But absolutely none of our theologians has ever taught that it would inevitably happen that either the sensitive appetite, being free from that bridle of integrity, would irresistibly force a person in a state of pure nature toward vice and misdeeds, or that those natural aids—supplied by God in place of a bridle—would irresistibly force a person toward virtue and good deeds. Such monstrosities were taught by the ancient Manichaeans, who were the destroyers of free will. And currently, the <term>Lutherans, Calvinists, and Jansenists: Protestant and dissenting Catholic groups who, in the author's view, held overly deterministic views on grace and sin</term> teach the same, agreeing with the Manichaeans in this regard.

<margin>
In the state of pure nature, neither the sensitive appetite (lacking the bridle of integrity) would necessitate a person to sin, nor would the natural aids supplied by God necessitate a person to live well.
</margin>

Therefore, in humans of a "pure nature," liberty would persist intact. There would always be at hand a completely free power both of consenting to and of dissenting from the movements of the sensitive appetite, should they ever allure one toward vice and baseness. Likewise, one would have the power to consent to or dissent from the natural aids supplied by God (as the author of such a nature), which allure one toward virtue and honor. If such a nature were to sin, God would in no way be the author of that sin. For God would have granted nothing to a nature of this kind that would irresistibly force it to sin; on the contrary, He would have supplied natural aids by which a person could both restrain the movements of the sensitive appetite and abstain from sin, if they so willed.

From these points, it becomes manifest that the defenders of the state of pure nature are entirely removed from the Manichaeans and stand very far apart from them. Moreover, regarding the existence of two principles contrary to each other—one good and the other evil—in our actual state of fallen nature, the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, specifically in the Epistle to the Romans.</note> testifies to this without being a Manichaean himself. One of these he calls the "law of sin" and the "concupiscence of the flesh" <note>original: "concupiscentia," the inclination toward sin.</note>;

**LXXIII.** In order for Wolf to appear to distance himself far from the error of the Manichaeans—into which, as we saw above, he actually fell—he runs into another fatal error. Therefore, they are not spirits, but belong to the category of matter. Consequently, they are not immortal by nature, but mortal.

<margin>Wolf’s slanders concerning Catholics deriving the origin of sin from the condition of matter are exposed and refuted.</margin>

*“The Papists,”* he says, *“along with their Scholastics, follow in the footsteps of Marcion, Hermogenes, and the Manichaeans, while they derive the origin of sin from the condition of matter.”* Now, in truth, Catholics do not trace the cause of the soul's original corruption to matter, and much less to God, who is the author of matter. For it is impossible for matter to corrupt the spirit—which is of an entirely different and more excellent nature—through some kind of "contagion." Therefore, the soul is indeed corrupted by original corruption *within* matter, that is...

...immediately when it is created by God in matter; it is by no means corrupted by matter. For it is one thing to be corrupted *in* matter, and quite another—far different—to be corrupted *by* matter. As we say in the study of physics: insects are indeed generated *in* rot, but by no means are they generated *from* rot <note>The author uses a common (though now debunked) early modern scientific belief in "spontaneous generation" to argue that the environment where something begins does not necessarily define its source or nature.</note>. Moreover, God is the cause or author of original sin neither insofar as He is the creator of the soul, nor insofar as He is the author of matter, nor insofar as He is the joiner of the soul within matter. For the nature of the soul is good, the nature of matter is good, and the union of the soul with matter is good—all of which have God as their cause and author.

On the contrary, the original vices of the soul are evil, and the original vices of matter are evil, and of these God is neither the cause nor the author. Rather, the cause is the sin of the first of all parents <note>Referring to Adam.</note>. It was he who, through that offense of transgression—as the Council of Trent <note>original: *Tridentinum*; referring to the mid-16th century ecumenical council that defined Catholic doctrine in response to the Reformation.</note> states in *Session 5, Decree on Original Sin*—was changed for the worse in both body and soul. He poured out onto all men death, the punishments of the body, and sin—which is the death of the soul—just as the Apostle says (1): *Through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin: and so death passed upon all men, in whom all have sinned.*

**LXXIV.** Adam existed, therefore, and we were all in him, as if in the head of all humanity both naturally and morally. For by His most just judgment, God established the first man such that if he obeyed God’s command, his obedience would be granted as merit and reward to all humans naturally descending from him. Conversely, if he violated God’s precept, his transgression <term>prevaricatio: a legalistic term for a breach of duty or a transgression of a command</term> would be ascribed as guilt and punishment to all humans naturally born from him. And yet Adam sinned, he transgressed, and he violated the command of God. Therefore, in Adam we have all sinned; in him we have all transgressed; we have all violated the command of God in Adam, we who have risen from him through natural propagation...

<margin>How original sin is contracted and removed is explained by a comparison that is not entirely unfitting.</margin>

For this most abstruse and deeply hidden matter, I seek an example from the likeness of a Lunar Eclipse or failure: though it is not entirely apt, nor perfectly fitting to the rule, it is nonetheless not entirely unfitting. For just as the Moon, in its failure and eclipse, enters the shadow of the earth, takes on a blackish spot, and is seen stained with a dark color, and being turned away from the Sun, lacks the brilliance of the Solar light; on the other hand, as soon as it emerges from the shadow of the earth in which it was submerged, it puts off the dark color, casts off the blackish spot, and being turned toward the Sun, shines brightly, bathed in the brilliance of the Solar light; so, as soon as the soul is created in a human fetus according to its necessity, it enters the "shadow," so to speak, of the sin of our first parent. It is turned away from God, the Sun of Justice; it is infected by the stain of original sin and lacks the light of Divine grace. But where it is washed by the baptism of Christ, it emerges from the shadow of the first parent's sin; the stain of original sin is wiped away, and being turned toward God, the Sun of Justice, it puts on the brightness of radiating grace. Furthermore, just as neither the Sun nor the Ether <note>original: *Ether*; the substance once thought to fill the upper regions of space.</note> in which the Moon floats and is contained is the cause of the lunar failure, but rather the opposition and turning away of the earth from the Sun—into whose shadow the Moon runs in its natural course—so neither God, the Sun of Justice, nor matter, in which the soul is created, is the cause of original sin, but rather the opposition and turning away of the will (the arbiter of all) from God, such as...

### CHAPTER XV.

->On the Calvinians as the Successors of the Manichaeans.<-

<margin>The Calvinians are the successors of the Manichaeans in establishing principles that impose necessity, and in denying free will.</margin>

75. Since the matter has been sufficiently explained and is clear, that the Calvinians are the true and genuine successors to the Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans were followers of Mani (3rd century AD) who believed in a cosmic struggle between a good spiritual world of Light and an evil material world of Darkness. Here, the author accuses Calvinists of sharing their "fatalistic" views.</note> in their most fundamental error, we shall be content—setting aside all others—with the one Master and Leader of them all: Calvin. Indeed, Calvin agrees with the Manichaeans with the highest degree of consensus, both in the idea that certain principles predominate over man which irresistibly compel him <note>original: *necessitent*; to impose a logical or divine necessity that removes choice.</note> to sin on the one hand, or to live piously on the other; and in the idea that there is no free choice of the human will, as there ought to be. I begin with the external principles, and shall soon move to the internal ones, finally coming to rest on the destruction and death of human liberty. Regarding what pertains to principles external to us, Calvin establishes such a version of predestination that predestination to life irresistibly compels us toward living piously and attaining eternal salvation; conversely, predestination to death irresistibly compels us toward sinning and undergoing eternal punishment (1):

> *We call predestination,* he says, *the eternal decree of God, by which He has determined within Himself what He willed to happen to every single person. For not all are created in the same condition; rather, eternal life is foreordained for some, and eternal damnation for others. Therefore, as each person is created for one or the other end, so we say he is predestined either to life or to death.* And again (2): *We say that by an eternal and immutable plan, God once determined those whom He would one day take up...*

Therefore, to achieve this end, he creates some so that they may go irresistibly into damnation; others, however, so that they may descend <note>The Latin *discendant* suggests a movement or transition into a state of life.</note> irresistibly to eternal life. From this, for the same purpose and by the same necessitating will, he blinds and hardens those predestined to death, while offering mercy to those predestined to life. From these points, according to Calvin, it follows that those predestined to piety and good deeds are irresistibly necessitated; while on the contrary, the reprobate are irresistibly necessitated to impiety and crimes.

Calvin traces <term>reprobation</term><note>The theological concept that God has rejected certain individuals from eternity, predestining them to damnation.</note> back to the secret counsel of God, to the sovereign will of the Supreme Lord, and to the illustration of the glory of Divine justice. While the Church Fathers and theologians maintain that God’s foreknowledge precedes the decree of punishment—thereby keeping God's holiness, justice, and goodness intact, as well as human freedom—Calvin insists that God’s decree precedes his foreknowledge. In this view, God does not merely foresee a person's actions; rather, God irresistibly decrees not only the punishment, but the very guilt itself. Regarding these impieties, which cause pious ears to shudder, I produce Calvin himself as a witness (1): *Those whom God passes over,* he says, *he reprobates; and for no other cause than that he wishes to exclude them from the inheritance which the Son predestines for his own... Yet it is by no means consistent to attribute the preparation for destruction to anything other than the secret counsel of God.* <note>original: "Quos, inquit, Deus præterit, reprobat... Minimè tamen consentaneum est, præparationem ad interitum aliò transferre, quam ad arcanum consilium Dei."</note> Not hiding the horror of his own opinion, he adds (2): *I admit,* he says, *it is a horrible decree; yet no one can deny that God foreknew what end man was going to have before he created him; and he foreknew it precisely because he had so ordained it by his decree.* <note>original: "Decretum, inquit, horribile fateor... et ideo præscierit, quia decreto suo sic ordinarat."</note>

Therefore, let this summary of the distinction be observed: that man, as he was corrupted by the Fall, indeed sins willingly, not against his will nor by compulsion; with a most prone affection of the soul, not by violent force; by the movement of his own lust, not by external compulsion; yet because of the depravity of his nature, he cannot be moved or driven except toward evil. I shall proceed no further on this, as I am not here to attack, but to narrate.

<margin>
Calvin teaches that sin is both voluntary and necessary by an irresistible necessity: inevitable, and yet at the same time imputable toward the merit of guilt and punishment.
</margin>

LXXX. Calvin frequently hammers the same anvil concerning this internal and irresistible necessity of sinning, yet without any violent compulsion. I provide a few examples, though many more have been omitted (1): *“For by the dominion of the devil,”* he says, *“to which the will of the natural man <note>original: "animalis hominis," referring to the unregenerate human state</note> is said to be subject so that it is driven by it, it does not mean that the will itself, struggling and resisting, is driven to obedience—just as we compel unwilling slaves by the right of mastery to carry out our orders—but that, fascinated by the tricks of Satan, it necessarily yields itself obedient to his every leading.”* And yet, the force and action of this "fascination" is internal, by which men are so bound that they are not free. And again (2): *“The distinction was made between compulsion and necessity, so that it would be clear that while man necessarily sins, he nevertheless sins voluntarily.”* Furthermore (3): *“I deny,”* he says, *“that sin ought to be imputed any less because it is necessary: I deny again the consequence they infer, that it must be avoidable because it is voluntary.”* Calvin teaches here that sin is indeed voluntary, yet it is necessary and inevitable; and at the same time, it is imputable to a man for the "merit" of punishment, even though he is driven to sinning by an internal and irresistible necessity. Finally, he concludes (4): *“Therefore, let this truth stand for us as indubitable, which can be shaken by no engines.”*

Calvin (1): *“But when elsewhere [Augustine] says that grace does not take away the will, but rather changes it from a bad one into a good one, and helps it once it has become good; he means only that man is not dragged along in such a way that he is carried by an external impulse without the movement of his heart; but rather that he is so affected inwardly that he obeys from the heart.”*

Indeed, if it is not in our power to resist or obey God's grace, and to agree or disagree with it, grace of this kind is so effective that it irresistibly forces us to give our consent.

Calvin taught this error long ago, and Jansenius <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), whose writings on grace sparked the Jansenist controversy in the Catholic Church</note>, having taken it from Calvin, restored it once more. This is the second part of his own fourth condemned proposition: *“In this the heretics [the Semi-Pelagians] err, in that they would want grace to be such that the human will could either resist or obey it.”*

<margin>Jansenius’s opinion on efficacious grace—that it irresistibly necessitates us to give our consent—is entirely the same as Calvin’s opinion.</margin>
In order to maintain that God's efficacious grace was an irresistible necessity for our consent, Calvin called it EFFICACIOUS BY ITSELF. By this new title, he maliciously attempted to introduce a grace that necessitates us irresistibly.

But those theologians <note>Likely referring to Thomist or Molinist theologians who used similar terms but maintained a role for free choice</note> who defend the idea of grace being "efficacious by itself" are far removed from Calvin’s error. For Calvin, by the term "grace efficacious by itself," understood nothing other than a grace that necessitates us beforehand, which excludes the freedom of indifference <term>libertas indifferentiae: the capacity of the will to choose between two opposites, such as acting or not acting</term>, and is only compatible with a freedom that is free from external compulsion <term>coactio: physical force or coercion</term>.

### LXXXIII.

Perhaps someone might say that Calvin, in the four books of his *Institutes*, frequently refutes the errors of the Manichaeans. I admit this. But which errors, and of what kind? Does he refute the error of the double principle that necessitates us irresistibly? Does he refute the total destruction of the free choice of the human will? Certainly not. Indeed, Calvin not only seized upon these Manichaean errors, but he nourished, fostered, and strengthened them. Therefore, the errors of the Manichaeans that Calvin *does* reject are those concerning the Devil as an eternal "evil principle" (the creator of evil natures and nearly equal in power to God); the human soul being a "particle of God" that fell into a human body; the "airy" or phantom body of Christ the Lord; and human flesh being naturally evil (like that of other animals) and thus not to be called back to life at the final end of the world. He is only occasionally occupied with attacking Manichaean absurdities of this sort.

## CHAPTER XVI.

### *On the Jansenists as successors to the Manichaeans.*

<margin>The Jansenists as successors to the Manichaeans.</margin>
LXXXIV. **Jansenius** <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), a Catholic bishop whose book "Augustinus" emphasized the power of God's grace and the total depravity of man after the Fall, leading to a major theological movement known as Jansenism.</note> teaches, and all his **Jansenist** disciples agree, that we are moved by two opposing and contrary affections: one is called **heavenly delight**, **charity**, and **healing grace** <note>original: "gratia medicinalis"</note>, which Christ the Lord brought to us; the other is **earthly delight**, **cupidity** <note>A term for worldly desire or lust.</note>, and the disease or sickness of the soul, which **Adam** brought upon us by sinning. Neither is within our power, but both are involuntary and not chosen by us. For we are not able to have them, or not to have them, by our own will. Let Jansenius be heard (1): *The delight,* he says, *which precedes consent and follows suggestion, is nothing other than an illicit, unchosen desire by which the soul, even while resisting, longs for sin; or certainly it is the first movement of concupiscence itself, like a certain unchosen love, through which a man is pleased to sin even against his will, even if consent does not follow (2).* Likewise: *The will,* he says, *was cast down into the rule of lusts through the sin of the first man; from this it happens that in all actions before grace, it is provoked by a certain preceding and tickling lustful delight, by consenting to which it sins.* Furthermore—and here the deformity of the Jansenist doctrine begins to appear more clearly (3): *The weight,* he says, *by which the will is now pressed down and—when grace is absent—is delightfully, and indeed insuperably, drawn to sinning, did not come to that faculty from God's creation, but from the punishment of the first evil will... And so Saint Augustine always refers to sins of this kind, which happen from that contracted necessity of sinning, as*

LXXXV. > *That battle is waged, he says, insofar as two delights, those of the flesh and of the spirit, contend with each other to see which of the two will overcome the other and draw the soul's consent after itself.... These struggle against each other with contrary concupiscences <note>original: "concupiscentiis" — in this context, strong worldly desires or passions that pull the soul away from God.</note>, or desires, so that they may snatch away the soul's consent.*

And again (2):

> *(The human will) in this life, after receiving grace, serves as a soldier for God; as the delight of the creature and of the Creator alternate, it acts now rightly, now wrongly, according as the delight of heaven or of earth has snatched away its consent.*

Therefore, according to Jansenius, the power of either delight is relative—that is, it depends on whether its strength is greater or lesser than the delight opposing it. Thus, if the heavenly delight is superior in strength to the earthly delight, it overcomes the earthly one and at the same time irresistibly pulls the will to a good assent. Conversely, if the strength of the earthly delight is greater than the strength of the heavenly delight, the earthly overcomes the heavenly and simultaneously snatches the will away with it, thrusting it irresistibly into an evil consent; it leaves nothing to the will except certain weak, unfinished, and hollow good desires.

<margin>According to Jansenius, the effective grace of God is an unchosen good delight that is "relatively victorious"—that is, one which overcomes the evil delight by its strength and irresistibly obtains a good assent from us.</margin>
It is better to hear Jansenius himself, whose words these are (3):

> *The victorious delight, which for Augustine is effective help <term>efficax adjutorium</term> <note>This refers to "efficacious grace," the divine help that actually produces the intended result in the person.</note>, is relative. For it is victorious only when it overcomes the other. But if it happens that the other (earthly) delight is more burning, the soul will remain stuck in mere ineffective desires; nor will it ever effectively will what ought to be willed.*

Again (4):

> *In that struggle with temptations, a great—and therefore greater and victorious—heavenly delight is necessary so that the earthly delight may be overcome; because otherwise the will cannot apply such great powers of willing, or as the School <note>A reference to the Scholastic theologians, the academic philosophers and theologians of the Middle Ages.</note> says, will so intensely and strongly.*

LXXXVI. <margin>According to Jansen, if an indeliberate evil delight is greater than the good, an irresistible necessity of sinning is upon us; if an indeliberate good delight is greater than the evil, an irresistible necessity of living rightly is upon us.</margin> Hence, according to the author Jansen, a double necessity weighs upon our will regarding both good and evil assent, which for us is entirely insuperable and irresistible; and likewise, there is a similar impotence regarding the opposite choices. For according to the teacher Jansen, a greater preceding good delight over an evil one is an irresistible necessity for us toward a good assent, and a similar impotence toward an evil assent. Similarly, according to the same Master, a greater evil delight over a good one is an irresistible necessity for us toward an evil assent, and a similar impotence toward a good assent. For these things correspond to each other equally and in the same way. Jansen strives to support this most absurd doctrine by the authority of Augustine, especially by that maxim which he proposes as the foundation for his entire poorly constructed edifice. Although this statement was made by Augustine when he was not yet a Bishop, and before the Pelagian war <note>The "Pelagian war" refers to the theological conflict between St. Augustine and Pelagius over the nature of grace and free will in the early 5th century.</note> had even begun, Jansen nevertheless extols it to the heavens with the highest praises, repeating it six hundred times—not just to the point of satiation, but to the point of disgust. It is found in the *Exposition on Chapter 15 of the Epistle to the Galatians, number 49, volume 3*: *It is necessary that we act according to that which delights us more* <note>original: "Quod amplius nos delectat, secundum id operemur ne- cesse est"</note>. Although this is clearly about voluntary and deliberate delight, and about a merely consequent necessity of action—which is perfectly compatible with the indifference of freedom—Jansen maliciously interprets it...

...which is pulled by a heavier weight: likewise, if the weight of heavenly delight is heavier than the weight of earthly delight, the heavenly necessarily draws the will toward a good assent; but conversely, if the weight of earthly delight is heavier than the weight of heavenly delight, the earthly necessarily thrusts our will down into an evil assent. Whichever of these happens, our will is never free with the <term>liberty of equilibrium</term> <note>The idea that the will is a neutral "balance" that can choose between two options regardless of external pressure.</note> and indifference; instead, by a perpetual alternation, it is carried from one irresistible necessity to another equally irresistible necessity. Such is the opinion devised by Jansen <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), the theologian who argued that humans are essentially puppets of either divine grace or sinful desire.</note> concerning the "dual delight" that is relatively victorious.

<margin>The difference between the equilibrium and action of a balance scale, and the equilibrium and action of the will, is shown against Jansen.</margin>
Although this is not the place to refute Jansen, I will say briefly and in passing that the indifference and equilibrium of our liberty differ most significantly from the equilibrium and indifference of a scale. For the indifference of a scale is merely passive; it does not determine itself to descend on one side or ascend on the other by its own force, nature, or choice; instead, it is necessarily determined to such movements by the heavier weight of matter itself. In contrast, the indifference of our will is not merely passive, but is entirely active. Under any weight of delight—whether earthly or heavenly—no matter how heavy, it actively and freely determines itself to either assent or dissent by its own force, nature, and choice. A balance scale certainly lacks moral equilibrium and indifference, for it is an inanimate machine. But in our will, besides the active and physical indifference, there is also a moral indifference, by which it frequently inclines toward neither of the two opposing sides.

<margin>Applying the mechanism of a scale to the will is true <term>Manichaeism</term> <note>A dualistic heresy that viewed humans as caught between two equal and opposite forces of Good and Evil, lacking true personal agency.</note>.</margin>
This moral indifference and, so to speak, moral equilibrium of our will is removed by those preceding, indeliberate stirrings of the soul <note>original: "permotionibus," referring to sudden impulses or emotions that arise before the mind has time to reflect.</note>, which cause the will to incline and lean more toward one side or the other. But despite these, it is always within the free power of the will to [deal with] such affections and stirr-

<margin>Why Jansen exerted such great effort to establish the system of the two delights.</margin>
90. But now I return to the history, from which I have slightly wandered. Since Jansen proposed in his lifelong work to remove the <term>liberty of indifference</term> <note>The ability of the will to choose between two options without being forced by external or internal necessity.</note> for this current state of fallen nature, and to introduce in its place an insuperable necessity of acting well or poorly, he believed that no argument could be used to achieve this more certainly or more powerfully than his twin "indeliberate" delights—which are not absolutely, but relatively victorious. For this reason, he fights "with sails and horses" <note>original: "velis equisque"—a Latin idiom meaning to fight with all one's might or with every possible resource.</note> to establish, confirm, and strengthen these kinds of delights, declaring their power and persuading us of this insuperable way of acting. Otherwise, the liberty of indifference, which Jansen so stubbornly and stiffly denies for the state of fallen nature, he very willingly attributes both to the first man in his state of upright and innocent nature, and also—even more so—to all the Angels while they were still <term>on the way</term> <note>original: "in via"—the theological term for a soul still on its journey toward God, before its final state is fixed in heaven or hell.</note> (1).

<margin>The liberty of indifference for the state of unfallen nature admitted by Jansen.</margin>

<margin>The liberty of indifference for the state of fallen nature denied by Jansen.</margin>

<margin>For this state [of fallen nature], Jansenius admits only freedom from coercion, following Calvin.</margin>

XCII. Therefore, having rejected the freedom of indifference—or freedom from simple necessity—which Jansenius claims was lost through the sin of the first man, he teaches (alongside <term>Calvin</term> <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the French reformer whose views on predestination and the "total depravity" of the human will were often compared to Jansenism by their Catholic critics.</note>) that no other freedom remains for us in our state of fallen nature except that which is called **freedom from coercion**. This concept is perfectly compatible with simple necessity and only opposes violence; it suggests that "freedom" only means we are not being physically forced to act against our will, rather than having a real choice. Therefore, to preserve the "freedom" of an act—at least the kind necessary for earning merit or blame—it is enough for Jansenius that the action is not coerced but voluntary, even if it is necessary by a necessity that is for us insurmountable and invincible. This doctrine of his, which he rashly and shamelessly peddles as having Augustine as its author, being a new and unheard-of thing...

# DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS
->156<-

Item (1): *So great is the silence in <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the most influential theologian on the topics of grace and free will.</note> regarding that "indifference of contradiction" <note>The philosophical concept that true freedom requires the ability to choose either to act or not to act, or to choose between opposites.</note>—viewed as necessary for liberty, over which there is now such fierce debate—that in all his intellectual works written against the <term>Pelagians</term> <note>Followers of Pelagius, who argued that humans could achieve salvation through their own will without needing divine grace; Augustine's primary theological opponents.</note>, he never once employed it to safeguard the freedom of choice under grace. One might rightly suspect that this definition of liberty, so heavily contested today, is the offspring of mere Philosophy. It was never championed, required, or even recognized under the name of "freedom of choice" by any of the ancient defenders of grace, such as Augustine, <term>Prosper</term>, or <term>Fulgentius</term>.* <note>Prosper of Aquitaine and Fulgentius of Ruspe were 5th- and 6th-century theologians who strictly followed Augustine’s teachings.</note>

Again (2): *Regarding "indifference," as certain <term>Scholastic</term> <note>Medieval theologians who used logic and Aristotelian philosophy to explain faith.</note> thinkers require it, the <term>Holy Doctor</term> <note>A traditional title for St. Augustine.</note> is not concerned at all, provided that the action is not alienated from one's own will... He establishes the harmony of grace and free will on this sole basis: that the power of choice does not sit idle like a dead log, nor is it forced against its will.*

Once more (3): *Augustine, when responding to the Pelagians who complained that freedom was violated by grace, never touched upon this method of reconciliation—the idea that the will "wills" through grace in such a way that it is also "able not to will." Instead, he always maintained that by the operation of grace, we are not moved like a dead log by God, but are carried toward the good.*

Again (4): *Hear what Augustine replies, and how he teaches that liberty remains intact: not because we are moved like stones, but because we also act simultaneously by our own will.*

Soon after (5): *Augustine reconciles grace with liberty in no other way than by stating that grace makes the will desire to act, without worrying at all about the presence or absence of indifference.*

Then (6): *The will is always free, whether in doing good or evil, whether under grace or under sin; because it is devoid of violence and compelling necessity.*

Finally (7): *No efficacy of grace, no necessity of...*

XCIV. <note>Section 94.</note> <term>Jansenius</term> <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), a Catholic bishop whose posthumous work *Augustinus* sparked the Jansenist controversy by arguing for a strict interpretation of St. Augustine’s views on grace.</note> was not unaware that this way of reconciling God's <term>efficacious grace</term> <note>Grace that is so powerful it effectively ensures that the person acts in accordance with God's will.</note> with human liberty neither differed from the opinion of <term>Calvin</term> <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the Protestant Reformer whose doctrines on predestination and the "bondage of the will" were condemned by the Catholic Church.</note> on the same matter, nor fit aptly with the doctrine of the <term>Council of Trent</term> <note>The 16th-century Catholic council that defined Church doctrine in response to the Protestant Reformation.</note>. Therefore, he proposed to resolve this very troublesome difficulty for himself with these words (1):

> Perhaps it is objected against this harmony of grace and free will that it does not differ from the opinion of Calvin. For in this way, he [Calvin] reconciles both to each other, so as to say that man is not drawn by the force of grace in such a way as to be carried along without the movement of the will, as if by an external impulse; but is affected inwardly, so that he obeys by his own will. That is, the will flows into good works only voluntarily, not freely. This opinion is at odds with the Council of Trent.

Now, let us hear a "brilliant" solution, and one worthy of Jansenius: He responds, *Not everything that heretics teach is heretical.*

<margin>Jansenius confesses that his opinion on the harmony of efficacious grace with only the "freedom from coercion" is the same as Calvin’s opinion; he affirms that Calvin does not err in this, but rather feels perfectly in line with Augustine.</margin>

He further adds that Calvin thought well alongside <term>Augustine</term> and the ancient Fathers, namely by denying <term>freedom of indifference</term> <note>The ability of the will to choose between opposites or to choose not to act at all.</note>—or freedom from simple necessity, however irresistible—under efficacious grace; and by teaching only "freedom from coercion." In this matter, Jansenius argues, one should not be indignant with Augustine because of a hatred for Calvin; rather, because of the love and honor due to Augustine, one should instead congratulate Calvin. Behold the words of Jansenius (2):

> If in any matter Calvin agreed with Augustine and the ancient Fathers, one should not be indignant with Augustine because of Calvin; rather, one should congratulate Calvin because of Augustine.

Jansenius therefore confesses that Calvin—to whom he could have added <term>Luther</term> <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the initiator of the Protestant Reformation.</note>, as we demonstrated in Chapter XIV—is of the same opinion as himself regarding the destruction of the freedom of indifference and freedom from simple necessity, and regarding the only remaining liberty being "freedom from coercion" under efficacious grace. ### DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS
->158<-

...with the following Fathers, <term>Jansenius</term> <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), whose work *Augustinus* argued that human nature is so corrupted by sin that it requires a specific kind of "efficacious" grace to do good.</note> contends that, in his judgment, we should not abandon <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the Church Father whose writings on grace and predestination are central to this entire theological debate.</note> just to oppose <term>Calvin</term> <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the Protestant Reformer. Catholic authors of this period often used "Calvinist" as a term of reproach for any doctrine that seemed to deny human free will.</note>. But let us hear Jansenius himself (1):

> *Is it therefore to be denied,* he says, *what is most evident and certain: namely, that Augustine, his disciples, and the holy Fathers who followed him, reconciled grace with free will in such a way that grace does not violently compel the will, but sweetly grants it the power to will? Thus, the will does not act like a stone, but even cooperates by its own motion. Should this, I say, be denied as something Augustine felt and taught, simply because Calvin also seems to have wanted to place liberty in the "immunity from coercion"?* <note>original: "immunitate coactionis." This refers to the idea that a person is "free" as long as they aren't being physically forced, even if their choice is internally necessitated by grace or sin.</note>

These final words are clever and malicious. For it does not merely "seem" that Calvin wanted to place liberty in the "immunity from coercion," as Jansenius phrases it; rather, it is absolutely certain, clear, and well-established that Calvin placed liberty—the same liberty supported by Jansenius—solely in that immunity from coercion. Therefore, it appears instead that Jansenius, by this response, wished to distance himself, if possible, from the brand, infamy, and shame of Calvinism.

XCV. <note>Section 95.</note> Now, as for what pertains to the <term>Council of Trent</term> <note>The Catholic Council (1545–1563) that defined Church doctrine in opposition to Protestantism. It affirmed that human free will remains active and must cooperate with God's grace.</note>, which Jansenius had earlier raised as an objection against himself, he indeed says many things and turns himself in every direction; but **he is stuck in the mud**, as the saying goes. <note>original: "aqua hæret," literally "the water stops," a Latin idiom meaning to be at a standstill or in a difficult position.</note> It is helpful here to bring forward the authority of Trent (2):

> *If anyone says that man’s free will, moved and awakened by God, does not cooperate by assenting to God who awakens and calls him, so as to dispose and prepare itself to obtain the grace of justification; and that it cannot dissent if it wishes, let him be <term>anathema</term>.* <note>"Anathema" is a formal curse or excommunication by the Church.</note>

Likewise, the Council declares (3):

> *The beginning of justification in adults must be derived from the prevenient grace* <note>Grace that comes "before" any human action to stir the soul.</note> *of God through Christ Jesus; so that they, who through sins were turned away from God, may be disposed to turn themselves toward their own justification by freely assenting to and cooperating with that same grace which awakens and assists them.*

### AND THE NEW MANICHAEANS.
->159<-

<margin>It is demonstrated that the Council of Trent, Session 6, both in Canon IV and Chapter V, does not speak of sufficient grace, but of efficacious grace.</margin>
...so that when God touches the heart of man through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, man himself is not entirely inactive while receiving that inspiration, since he is indeed able to reject it. Now it is entirely evident—and it strikes the eyes of anyone, unless they have gouged them out—that in the aforementioned canon and decree, the Council of Trent is dealing with and speaking not of <term>sufficient grace</term><note>Theologians define "sufficient grace" as grace that gives a person the power to do good, but which may not actually result in a good act if the person does not cooperate with it.</note>, but of <term>efficacious grace</term><note>In contrast, "efficacious grace" is grace that actually produces the intended effect or good work in the person.</note>. For it deals with the grace by which the free will of man, in reality and <term>in the second act</term><note>original: "in actu secundo." A scholastic term referring to the actual performance of an action, as opposed to the mere potential to act (the "first act").</note> as the schools say, disposes and prepares itself for its own justification. But grace of this kind is certainly not merely sufficient grace—by which no one actually disposes or prepares themselves for justification—but is efficacious grace. It deals with the grace of God that precedes, moves, excites, aids, illuminates, and inspires, with which the free will of man actually cooperates, and to which it actually assents. But it is entirely evident that God's grace—with which the human free will actually cooperates and to which it actually assents—is not merely sufficient grace (with which one neither cooperates nor assents), but efficacious grace.

<margin>Father Bellelli, praised by Father Berti, believes—though I do not agree with him—that the Council of Trent, in the passages mentioned, deals with merely sufficient grace.</margin>
But <term>Father Bellelli</term><note>Fulgentius Bellelli (1675–1742), an Augustinian theologian who sought to navigate the difficult path between Jansenism and its opponents.</note>, praised by <term>Father Berti</term><note>Gian Lorenzo Berti (1696–1766), another prominent Augustinian theologian.</note>—with whom I can by no means agree—interprets the Canon and Decree of Trent as referring not to efficacious grace, but merely to sufficient grace. These are his words (1): *We say that it was defined by the Synod of Trent that the free will, moved and excited by God through an interior sufficient calling which gives the "power" [to act], is able to resist if it wishes; and if it wishes to reject this grace, it indeed can, and sometimes even does reject it...* Therefore, the ecumenical Synod of Trent certainly sanctioned that the will can resist sufficient grace. 

<margin>From the Council of Trent, the free will of man can resist efficacious grace.</margin>
But it is evident that Trent is there dealing with and speaking of efficacious grace. Therefore, the ecumenical Synod of Trent certainly sanctioned that the human will can resist efficacious grace. <term>Augustine</term> however, continues Father Bellelli, *[spoke] not of sufficient grace, but of grace efficacious in itself, victorious, unavoidable, and insuperable,*

<margin>Words never used by Augustine.</margin>
...[the will], which gives both the willing and the performing, he wrote that the will is least of all able to resist. Let Father Bellelli <note>Fulgenzio Bellelli (1675–1742) was an Augustinian monk and theologian who defended the Order's views on grace against Jansenism.</note> point out to me a single place in all the works of Saint Augustine in which the Holy Doctor even once uses these words: *Grace efficacious by itself*; *Victorious grace*; *Unswerving grace*; *Insurmountable grace*. If he does, he will be a "great Apollo" to me <note>A Latin idiom meaning a person of supreme wisdom or an infallible oracle.</note>. Saint Augustine does indeed teach, and teaches most excellently in his book *On Rebuke and Grace* <note>original: "lib. de Correp. & Grat."</note>, chapter 12, number 38, volume 10, that the will of a person predestined by the gift and grace of <term>final perseverance</term><note>The theological concept of remaining in a state of grace until the moment of death, ensuring salvation.</note> cannot fail due to its own weakness; and therefore, he says that such a will is "unswerving" and cannot be overcome by any adversity, and thus this kind of will is "insurmountable." However, he never and nowhere teaches that the grace of God is "unswerving" or "insurmountable" by the human will in such a way that the free choice of our will cannot resist or disagree with the efficacious grace of God—for that would be contrary to the Council of Trent. Furthermore, I do not doubt that the interpretation of Trent used by Father Bellelli, and praised by Father Berti <note>Giovanni Lorenzo Berti (1696–1766), another Augustinian theologian often associated with the "Augustinian school" of thought.</note>, truly differs from the interpretation of Jansenius. Therefore, I both approve and venerate the mind and intention of both men (to which I have no personal access); however, I cannot at all approve of their words, as they sound to me.

### XCVI.

<margin>Jansenius tries in vain to extricate himself from the authority of Trent.</margin>
And so, having most amicably greeted Fathers Berti and Bellelli, I return immediately to Jansenius alone, with whom I have business. Jansenius denies that his doctrine—concerning the removal of the <term>liberty of indifference</term><note>The ability of the will to choose between contrary options (to act or not to act) under the same circumstances.</note> under the influence of efficacious divine grace—differs from the doctrine of Trent. Let us see whether he denies this rightly or wrongly.

<margin>It is demonstrated from Trent that human free will is able to resist and dissent from efficacious grace, and therefore the liberty of indifference persists under efficacious grace.</margin>
The Synod of Trent defines and decrees against the Lutherans and Calvinists that the free will of man assents to the efficacious grace of God in such a way that it can dissent from that same grace if it wishes. Therefore, the free will of man, instead of giving its assent, can, if it wishes, offer its dissent to the efficacious grace of God. Therefore, the efficacious grace of God is by no means an irresistible necessity for the free will of man to assent. The will of man, therefore, under the efficacious grace of God, is entirely free

Furthermore, the holy Synod teaches that "unjust men—specifically adults—who, through the benefit of divine <term>efficacious grace</term><note>Grace that successfully produces the effect of conversion or a good work in the soul.</note>, dispose themselves toward their own conversion, freely assent to that divine efficacious grace. It is therefore clear and well-proven that Jansenius's doctrine—which claims that liberty of indifference is destroyed under the influence of efficacious grace—is utterly repugnant to the doctrine of Trent. For Trent defines and decrees that under efficacious grace, our liberty of indifference persists and remains safe and sound.

XCVII. Beyond the "Calvinist stain," which Jansenius tries in vain to wash away, he also attempts, with repeated and useless effort, to repel the "Manichaean disgrace." Jansenius does not shudder at the <term>Manichaean</term><note>Followers of Manichaeism, an ancient dualistic religion that taught a radical struggle between good and evil and was often accused of denying human free will by claiming sin was an inevitable part of material nature.</note> monster as the horror it truly is; instead, he mocks it as a mere "Manichaean specter." He ridicules the idea that all freedom to do good has been taken from us and that an inevitable necessity of sinning weighs upon the human race—claims that he says make people shudder like children at a mask, specifically those people steeped in the profane rules of philosophers and less accustomed to Christian teachings and institutions. And they held that this lack of freedom happened because of the very design of our nature. Augustine, on the other hand, teaches that man's nature was originally created with the freest choice, without blindness, and without the weakness of resisting concupiscence; but by the evil use of this freedom, a necessity of sinning occurred. Thus, it follows that this necessity of sinning—which both the Manichaeans and Augustine noticed, admitted, and confessed to be in man—was not the nature of the original man, but the punishment of the condemned man.* Now indeed, I take up the comparison initiated by Jansenius between his own doctrine and that of the Manichaeans; I bring it to the scale <note>original: "ad trutinam revoco"; a metaphor for weighing or testing the validity of an argument</note>, and from it, I demonstrate that the Jansenists are involved in the same heresy as the Manichaeans.

<margin>
From Jansenius's own comparison, it is demonstrated that he agrees with the Manichaeans against Augustine.
</margin>

The Manichaeans taught, according to Jansenius's own testimony, that an evil nature was mixed within us, which would fashion sins in us without the freedom of our choice. Jansenius teaches that evil concupiscence, or an evil delight, is mixed within us; this we willingly grant. However—and here lies the error—this delight fashions sins in us by necessitating them, without any freedom of our choice from an irresistible necessity. Such freedom is what Catholics hold as necessary for <term>merit and demerit</term><note>The capacity for an action to be morally credited to a person as either good (deserving reward) or bad (deserving punishment).</note>. The Manichaeans, by the same witness, affirmed that this lack of freedom—specifically, freedom from irresistible necessity—happened from the very design of our nature. Furthermore, when a comparison is made between <term>Augustine of Ypres</term><note>Referring to Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), the Bishop of Ypres, whose book *Augustinus* sparked the Jansenist movement.</note> and the true <term>Augustine of Hippo</term><note>The famous 4th-century Saint and Doctor of the Church, whom Jansen claimed to be following strictly.</note>, it becomes clear that the "Augustine of Ypres" teaches an error against the Manichaeans. He claims that from the misuse of the first man's most free liberty, a physical and irresistible necessity of sinning occurred. However, the real Augustine of Hippo rightly teaches against the Manichaeans that from the misuse of that same liberty, nothing occurred except a moral and resistible necessity of sinning. This is because <term>concupiscence</term><note>Disordered desire or the inclination toward sin.</note>—once the bond of human integrity was loosened as a punishment for original sin—provokes and entices us to sin. We are able to resist this impulse, though not without the help of God’s grace and not without difficulty. Finally, Augustine of Hippo admitted only a moral and resistible necessity of sinning, which he affirmed was the punishment of the first condemned man. 

In contrast, Jansenius admits not a moral, but a physical and irresistible necessity of sinning. The Manichaeans also admitted such a necessity, though they traced it back to the very nature of how man was created; Jansenius, on the other hand, traces it back to the punishment of the condemned man. But whether this irresistible necessity of sinning and the loss of <term>liberty of indifference</term><note>The power of the will to choose between different courses of action without being determined by prior causes.</note> is said to arise from an "evil nature" mixed within us (as the Manichaeans held) or from an "evil concupiscence" mixed within us (as Jansenius holds)—and whether it is from the nature of man's design or from the punishment of the fallen—it remains the same execrable doctrine of the Manichaeans and the Jansenists alike.

### XCVIII.

Now indeed, if the defense Jansenius took up for his doctrine—in which he struggled to push away the shame of the Manichaean heresy—already sufficiently demonstrated above that he agrees with the Manichaeans, it appears even more clearly from the testimony of Saint Augustine. It is evident that the Jansenists do not merely smell and taste of Manichaeism, but are the genuine and true successors of the Manichaeans. They are restoring and rebuilding that poorly constructed and ruinous heresy once again. I here bring forth a few testimonies from Saint Augustine, though I shall later bring many more into the fray from the elite ranks of the Augustinian army...

[...contin]ued, in the very heat of the struggle against new and old Manichaeans (1). *“The Manichaeans say,”* says Augustine, *“that there are two souls, or two minds—one good, the other evil—engaged in a conflict between them, when the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh.”* <note>original: "Duas animas... But this conflict of flesh and spirit, of which the Apostle Paul speaks, is not a "Jansenist conflict." It is not like the Manichaean conflict where, as Jansenius describes it, two indeliberate delights—one good, the other evil—struggle against each other to see which will overcome the other and drag the consent of the will along with it. Augustine also records these details about the Manichaeans (2): *“The Manichaeans rave that there are two souls in one man, one good and one evil. They attribute all the good things of a man to that good soul, but all the evil things to that evil soul.”* <note>original: "Manichæi duas animas unam bonam, alteram malam in uno homine esse delirant. Et omnia quidem bona hominis illi bonæ animæ, omnia vero mala illi malæ animæ tribuunt."</note> Jansenius similarly raves that there are two delights in one man—one good and one evil—that irresistibly necessitate him toward good or evil. He attributes all a man's good deeds to the necessitating good delight, and all his evil deeds to the necessitating evil delight.

Furthermore, Augustine says this of the Manichaeans (3): *“They say they sin when the nature of evil prevails over the nature of God. This is the most filthy insanity of the Manichaeans.”* <note>original: "Tunc se peccare dicunt, (Manichæi) quando natura mali prævalet naturæ Dei. Hæc Manichæorum est immundissima insania."</note>

In this exact way, and no other, with Jansenius as their leader and teacher, the Jansenists say they sin when the evil delight prevails over their strength and is greater than the good indeliberate delight. This is the "most filthy insanity" of the Jansenists.

## CHAPTER XVII.

### Concerning Saint Augustine, once a Hearer of the Manichaeans.

<margin>Augustine as a Catechumen <note>A person receiving basic instruction in the Christian-faith before baptism.</note> was a "Hearer" <note>The lower rank of Manichaean followers who lived in the world, as opposed to the "Elect" who lived as ascetics.</note> from his nineteenth to his twenty-eighth year.</margin>

XCIX. Augustine, then a Christian catechumen and not yet a baptized believer, was nineteen years old and living in Carthage—where, as a young man himself, he was teaching the liberal arts to other youths—when he encountered the Manichaeans, by whose errors he was corrupted and led astray. He remained involved in that heresy for nine years, specifically from his nineteenth year until his twenty-eighth. This is attested by Possidius, the Bishop of Calama and a disciple of Augustine, who, as he himself testifies, lived in the closest friendship with him for forty years. He recorded these words concerning him (1): *“Indeed, at one time as a youth at Carthage, he had been seduced by the error of the Manichaeans.”* <note>original: "Verum aliquando Manichæorum apud Charthaginem adolescens fuerat errore seductus."</note> To this is added the testimony of Augustine himself,

Augustine teaches again in these words (1) that the entire Manichaean heresy was revealed to him while he was a Manichaean **Auditor**, and that the letter which they called the *Foundation* <note>Original Latin: "Epistola Fundamenti". He did this so effectively that the Manichaean Elect who were present at that judgment were entirely unable to deny it.

The most reliable witness is Possidius, Bishop of Calama <note>a close friend and biographer of Augustine</note>, who committed these details to writing (1): *At Carthage, through a certain steward of the royal palace named Ursus—a man of the Catholic faith—several Manichaeans, whom they call the "Elect" (both men and women), were discovered and brought to the Church. They were interrogated by the bishops, and their testimony was recorded in official records. Among those present was Augustine of holy memory, who knew that execrable sect better than others. By exposing their damnable blasphemies from the very books the Manichaeans accept, he led them to a confession of those blasphemies. And those unworthy and shameful things they were accustomed to doing among themselves in their evil way were revealed in those ecclesiastical records through the confession of those women of the so-called "Elect."*

<margin>Augustine, as a youth and a catechumen <note>a student of the faith not yet baptized</note>, quite unlearned in Christian doctrine, a slave to pleasures, eager for glory, and deceived by the outward piety and severity of the Elect, fell into errors.</margin>

Perhaps someone will wonder how it was possible that Augustine, relying on such a sharp intellect, could have agreed to so many and such great Manichaean myths—especially those so absurd and discordant. But if we investigate the reasons for his straying, the wonder will cease entirely. For when he fell in with the Manichaeans, Augustine was a youth, at an age where there is the greatest weakness of judgment; likewise, he was by nature very eager for new things and empty glory. Furthermore, he was captured by the allurements of pleasures and enslaved to lusts; and what is most critical, he was a quite negligent, soft, and lukewarm catechumen—almost a stranger and a traveler in Christian doctrine. Augustine himself testifies to what drove him more forcefully as a youth toward the Manichaean heresy: namely, the feigned piety, charity, restraint, and modesty of the Manichaeans—especially that certain wonderful severity of morals and doctrine which they preached. Although this is common to all heretics, it is especially true of the Jansenists <note>a 17th-century Catholic movement known for its moral rigorism, which the author here compares to ancient heresies</note>, who come to us in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are wolves.

<margin>Augustine, having been promised truth and certain, clear happiness by the Elect <note>the high-ranking "perfected" members of the Manichaean sect</note> in exchange for what they called blind, superstitious, and simple faith, becomes a Manichaean.</margin>

...he explains the matter more fully to his friend Honoratus, who was still persisting in Manichaeism, and whom the Holy Doctor <note>St. Augustine</note> is attempting to lead away from error (1). "You know," he says, Honoratus, "that we fell in with such men for no other reason than their claim that—setting aside terrifying authority—they would lead those willing to hear them to God by pure and simple reason, and free them from every error. For what else compelled me for nearly nine years, having scorned the religion planted in me as a boy by my parents, to follow those men and listen to them diligently, except their claim that we were being terrified by superstition and that faith was being demanded of us before reason? They, on the other hand, claimed they would press no one to believe until the truth had been discussed and unraveled. Who would not be enticed by such promises, especially the mind of a youth eager for the truth?" <note>original Latin: "Nosti... Quis non his pollicitationibus illiceretur, præsertim adolescentis animus cupidus veri?"</note>

But no torment was more powerful in shattering the weak and wavering mind of a youth and a <term>Catechumen<gloss>a person receiving basic instruction in the Christian faith but not yet baptized</gloss></term> than that very famous question raised by the Manichaeans: **WHENCE COMES EVIL?** <note>original: "UNDE MALUM?"</note> By no means, they said, does it come from a good God; therefore, it must come from an evil God, and thus from an eternal evil nature. This is the very question that has always twisted and exhausted the minds of even the most learned men. Furthermore, so that the origin of all evils would not be attributed to the sin of the first parent <note>Adam</note>, the Manichaeans rejected the Old Testament and claimed the New Testament had been corrupted by "new Christians" coming from Judaism; it was through the authority of these two volumes that original sin became known. To undermine the authority of the Old Testament, they presented such objections to the young Augustine that, at first sight, they greatly disturbed him and required a learned and wise interpreter. Let Augustine himself be heard in his reply to Evodius, who asked him (2): "Tell me, why do we do evil?" <note>original: "Dic mihi unde malè faciamus?"</note> To which Augustine replied, "You raise that very question which greatly troubled me in my youth and, having exhausted me, drove me into the hands of heretics and cast me down. By which fall I was so afflicted,"
