...and I was overwhelmed by such heaps of empty fables that, had the love of finding the truth not obtained divine help for me, I would not have been able to emerge from them and breathe again in that first liberty of seeking. And again, in another place (1), he says, *“I was moved to support [the Manichaeans], those foolish deceivers, when they asked me: **WHENCE COMES EVIL?** <note>original Latin: "UNDE MALUM?" – a central philosophical problem regarding how an all-good God could allow evil to exist.</note> And whether God enjoyed a physical human form, and had hair and nails? And whether those men <note>referring to Old Testament patriarchs like Abraham or David</note> were to be considered just, even though they had many wives, killed men, and sacrificed animals?”*

<margin>Having established an irresistible necessity for sinning, and thus removing the shame of sin and extinguishing the stings of conscience, Augustine—who was inclined toward lusts—clings to the Manichaeans.</margin>
CIII. But no bond was tighter in binding Augustine’s mind to the Manichaean sect than that "irresistible necessity of sinning," which followed logically from Manichaean principles. For the character of the young Augustine was such that he was strongly inclined and prone on one hand toward the praise of virtue and glory, and on the other toward lusts and the shameful pleasures of the body. Therefore, Augustine sought to join the splendor of virtue, if possible, with bodily pleasure. Consequently, to retain the praise and glory of virtue—and to maintain a tranquility of mind even in the midst of the waves of his own depravities—he persuaded himself, along with his Manichaean companions, that it was not he who sinned, but "something else" that was with him yet was not himself. He thought he would be excused because he did not sin by his own free will; rather, another nature within him sinned by necessity. He cast his guilt upon this nature—namely, that "evil soul" which the Manichaeans taught had been deeply admitted into us, forcing us irresistibly to sin. Thus, Augustine flattered himself alongside the Manichaeans, believing he was beyond fault when he sinned, because he did so not by free will, but by a necessity he could not resist. Augustine deplores this destructive and most capital error of his in these words (2): *“For it still seemed to me that it is not we who sin, but some other [nature] in us...”*

*...that our nature sinned in us; and it delighted my pride to be outside of fault; and when I had done something evil, not to confess that I had done it, so that you might heal my soul, because it sinned against you: but I loved to excuse it, and to accuse some other thing, which was with me, and yet was not I.* <note>original Latin: "nobis peccare naturam; & delectabat superbiam meam extra culpam esse... sed excusare eam amabam, & accusare nescio quid aliud..." – This is a quote from St. Augustine’s *Confessions*, Book 5, Chapter 10, describing his time as a Manichaean.</note>

<margin>
The error of the Jansenists <note>Jansenism was a theological movement that emphasized original sin and the necessity of divine grace, often accused by its opponents of denying free will.</note> concerning the indeliberate evil delight that compels one to sin, along with its consequences, is shown to be entirely similar to the error of the Manichaeans concerning an evil Soul as the necessary cause of sin, along with its consequences.
</margin>

In the same error, the Jansenists—the true, natural, and genuine successors of the Manichaeans—are involved. For it seems to them, to use Augustine's expression, that it is not they who sin, but another thing within them, distinct from themselves, which commits the sin: namely, an **indeliberate evil delight** <note>original Latin: "delectationem malam" – a spontaneous, unbidden pleasure or inclination toward sin that occurs before the mind consciously chooses.</note> that is greater than their **indeliberate good delight**. And it delights their pride that they are outside of fault; and when they do something evil, they do not confess that they have done it so that God might heal their souls (since they sin against Him). Instead, they love to excuse their souls and accuse something else—specifically, that "evil delight" which is greater than the "good delight," which exists within them but is not what they themselves truly are. 

The Jansenists say that they do not teach such things; however, one must not look at what they say, but at what is consistent for those to say who establish that it is impossible to resist a greater evil delight with a lesser good delight and to restrain oneself from sinning. Likewise, they claim it is not in the power of the sinner either to increase the strength of the good delight or to diminish the strength of the evil delight, so as to make the good delight greater than the evil one—which is the only case in which a person could abstain from sin. For both delights are "indeliberate" <note>Meaning they happen automatically or spontaneously, without the intervention of the person’s free will.</note> and do not depend on our plans or wills. 

Therefore, it must be that a person placed in such a state—into which he did not cast himself by his own will, and from which he cannot escape by his own will—it must be, I say, by an **irresistible necessity** that he sins. It is not, therefore, the person himself who sins (at least not in a way that sin could be imputed to him as guilt deserving of punishment); rather, it is that evil delight, or more likely the devil, the author of such delight, who sins within him. Therefore, in the Jansenist view, the excuse of the sinner is just, nor is the accusation of the greater evil de-

...or the devil, who is the author of such a delight. Someone might perhaps say: let him pray, so that he may obtain a good delight to avoid sinning, which would be greater than the evil delight to sin. But in the Jansenist view, he cannot pray unless he has a good delight to pray, which is greater than the evil delight not to pray. This greater good delight, however, is entirely outside the power of man. Therefore, by an irresistible necessity in the Jansenist doctrine, whoever sins, sins. Moreover, given this Jansenist necessity of sinning, we are plunged into the despair of salvation; all the sinews of honesty are severed; the reins are loosened for all evil desires; and finally, there is no crime, no evil deed, to which that Jansenist "indeliberate delight," being relatively victorious, would not impel one. Oh, holy doctrine of Christian severity and restraint! Oh, severe judges and censors of vices! <note>The author is being deeply sarcastic here, mocking the Jansenists' reputation for being strict moralists by arguing that their theology actually excuses all sin as inevitable.</note>

### CV.
There follow two books by the Holy Doctor <note>A title for Saint Augustine, recognized as a "Doctor of the Church" for his influential teachings.</note> against the Manichaeans, the first of which is titled *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, and the second *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*. The Holy Doctor finished these in Rome at the beginning of the year 388; however, he published them in Africa, as the Maurist editors <note>The Maurists were a group of French Benedictine monks in the 17th and 18th centuries who produced the definitive editions of the works of the Church Fathers.</note> believe, perhaps in the year 389. The reason for writing such books was the feigned and simulated severity and self-restraint of the Manichaeans, which they—in their most depraved lives, after the manner of other heretics—deceitfully displayed to deceive simple and unwary believers. I produce Augustine as a witness (1): *Already baptized,* he says, *when I was in Rome, and unable to bear in silence the boasting of the Manichaeans about their false and deceptive self-restraint or abstinence—by which they even prefer themselves to true Christians (to whom they are not to be compared) in order to deceive the unskilled—I wrote two books: one on the morals of the Catholic Church, the other on the morals of the Manichaeans.* <note>original: "Jam baptizatus... cum Romæ eſſem... ſcripſi duos libros..."</note>

<margin>Augustine’s book *On True Religion*, in the final part of which he refutes the Manichaeans.</margin>

Concerning this, Augustine says (2): *This book speaks especially against the "two natures" of the Manichaeans.* <note>The Manichaeans were dualists who believed the universe was a struggle between two co-eternal natures: Light (Good) and Darkness (Evil).</note>

They wildly suggest that both these souls, one good and one evil, exist in a single human being. They say this evil soul is the property of the flesh, which they also claim belongs to the race of darkness. The good soul, however, they claim comes from a part of God that arrived and fought with the race of darkness, resulting in a mixture of both. They attribute all the good deeds of a man to that good soul, and all the evil deeds to that evil soul.*

<margin>The first acts of Augustine the priest against the Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans followed a dualistic religion that saw the world as a struggle between equal forces of Light/Good and Darkness/Evil.</note>, preserved in his writings, consist of two disputes against Fortunatus, a priest of the Manichaeans, regarding the origin of evil. He refuted him excellently and compelled him to depart from Hippo.</margin>

*In that city of Hippo, the Manichaean pestilence had infected and penetrated many citizens and travelers, being seduced and deceived by a certain priest of that same heresy named Fortunatus, who was living and staying there. Meanwhile, the citizens of Hippo and Christian travelers—both Catholics and even Donatists <note>The Donatists were a schismatic Christian group in North Africa who disagreed with the Catholics over the validity of sacraments performed by "traitor" priests; it is notable here that they joined with Catholics to oppose the Manichaeans.</note>—approached Augustine the priest and requested that he meet with that Manichaean priest, whom they believed to be learned, and discuss the Law with him. Augustine did not refuse. But he inquired whether Fortunatus also wished for this to happen. They immediately brought the matter to Fortunatus himself, asking, encouraging, and demanding that he not refuse. Indeed, since Fortunatus had known Saint Augustine when Augustine was still held in that same error <note>Augustine had been a "Hearer" (a low-level member) of the Manichaean sect for nine years before his conversion to Christianity.</note> along with him, he was afraid to clash with him. However, compelled by the persistence of his own followers and overcome by shame, he promised he would come face to face and undergo the contest of debate.*

*Therefore, on the appointed day and place, they met together, with many studious men and curious crowds rushing in. And with the Notaries' tablets <note>Original Latin: "Notariorum tabulis." These were professional stenographers who recorded the debate in shorthand to ensure an accurate public record.</note> open, the dispute began on the first day and finished on the second. In this debate, that Manichaean teacher—as the record of the Acts <note>Original Latin: "Gestorum." This refers to the official transcript of the debate.</note> maintains—was neither able to dismantle the Catholic assertion nor prove that the Manichaean sect was supported by truth. Instead, failing in his response, he claimed at last that he would discuss with his superiors those points which he could not refute; and if they could not satisfy him on these matters, he would look to his soul's welfare. And so, by all those in whose eyes he had seemed great and learned, he was judged to have achieved nothing in the defense of his sect. Struck by this shame, he departed from the city of Hippo shortly thereafter and did not return again. And thus, through the aforementioned man of God, that error was removed from the hearts of all who were present or who learned of the events in their absence, and the Catholic religion was made known and retained. Thus far Possidius <note>Possidius was the Bishop of Calama and a close friend of Augustine who wrote his first biography.</note>. The same account of Augusti-*

## CHAPTER XIX.

### Concerning the Doctrine of Saint Augustine against the New and Old Manichaeans.

CXI. I believe I should entirely refrain from discussing those things which Augustine taught against the "old wives' tales" of the Manichaeans. For such inventions of the Manichaeans are so absurd, discordant, and utterly ridiculous that they do not require repeated refutation. However, I shall proceed to draw out the arguments with which Augustine overthrew their opinions regarding the "two principles" that impose necessity <note>The Manichaean belief that two primal forces, Good and Evil, exert a physical necessity over human actions</note>, and their denial of the "indifference" of our freedom <term>Liberty of Indifference: The philosophical concept that the human will is not pre-determined and has the power to choose between different courses of action</term>. Since these views are shared by the heretics of the present age, who have joined themselves with the Manichaeans, I now bring out from the Augustinian "camps" into the sunlight and the field of battle the doctrine of Saint Augustine against both new and old Manichaeans. I do this to defend the free choice of the human will against the principles that would force our will—principles from which the destruction of free choice follows. The Manichaeans believed that there are two souls in a man, one good by nature, from which...

...all good things; the other [principle] is evil by nature, from which all of man's evils follow by an inevitable necessity. From this, under a double principle of necessity, the Manichaeans <note>A religious movement founded by the prophet Mani that taught a dualistic struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness</note> once taught that no free will <term>liberum arbitrium: the capacity to make choices independent of biological or divine necessity</term> exists in man. Moreover, they claimed that these two contrary natures, powers, and actions of souls were signified by those words in Matthew 7:18: *A good tree cannot bear bad fruit; nor can a bad tree bear good fruit.* 

Against this, however, Augustine (1) said: *In order that you may understand,* he says, *that these two trees were placed by the Lord in such a way as to signify free will there—and that these two trees are not natures, but our own wills—He Himself says in the Gospel (Matthew 12:33): "Either make the tree good, or make the tree bad." Who is it that can create a nature? If, therefore, it has been commanded of us to make the tree either good or bad, it is ours to choose what we wish.* 

Likewise (2): *These two trees,* he says, *are most clearly presented as a likeness of two types of men—that is, the just and the unjust. Because unless a person changes his will, he cannot perform what is good. He teaches in another place (Matthew 12:33) that this is placed within our own power, where He says: "Either make the tree good, and its fruit good; or make the tree bad, and its fruit bad..." Therefore, a bad tree cannot produce good fruit, but from being a bad tree it is possible to become a good one, so that it may then bear good fruits.* 

Furthermore (3): *Listen,* he says, *concerning Free Will from the Lord Himself, where He commemorates the two trees of which you yourself made mention; hear Him saying (Matthew 12:33): "Either make the tree good, and its fruit good; or make the tree bad, and its fruit bad." When, therefore, He says, "Either make this, or make that," He indicates power, not nature. For no one except God can create a nature <note>original: "arbor" (tree), here used interchangeably with nature</note>; but each person has it in his will either to choose what is good, and thus be a good tree; or to choose what [is bad]...*

CXII. Against the Manichaeans <note>Followers of a dualistic religion that believed humans were trapped in a struggle between light and dark natures, leaving no room for choice.</note>, Augustine teaches that through those two trees, the **free choice of our will** <term>liberum arbitrium: the capacity to make choices independent of biological or divine necessity</term> is signified. By this free and elective power, we are able to conceive both a good will and an evil one; that is, we can wish well or wish poorly according to our own judgment. <margin>Augustine’s doctrine of Free Will against the ancient Manichaeans fundamentally overthrows the "new Manichaeans"—the Lutherans and Calvinists; but especially the Jansenist defenders of the "twin delights" that impose necessity.</margin> Yet this doctrine of Augustine fundamentally overthrows, along with the Manichaean view, the Lutheran, Calvinist, and Jansenist <note>A 17th-century Catholic movement, often criticized for views on grace and predestination that resembled Protestant theology.</note> opinions. I shall address the Jansenists alone, whose error is more dangerous because it is more cunning. 

According to the Jansenist authors, under an "indeliberate evil delight"—if it is stronger than the good—we cannot conceive a good will, but we necessarily break out into an evil will. Likewise, under an "indeliberate good delight"—if it is stronger than the evil—we cannot conceive an evil will, but we necessarily break out into a good will. However, when faced with equal and contrary "indeliberate delights," we can break out into neither a full nor a complete good or evil will. Instead, we waver, hesitant and indecisive on both sides, unable to proceed into either a deliberate good will or a deliberate evil will. 

From these points, it follows that we either escape from one inevitable necessity only to run into another of the same kind, or we fall into an inability that we cannot overcome to will anything deliberately. Therefore, in the Jansenist school of the "two delights," there is no free choice of our will by which we might be able—through free and elective power, and by our own judgment—to conceive either a good or an evil will. Yet this is entirely contrary to the arguments mentioned above against the ancient Mani- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the word "Manichaeans" on the next page.</note>

<meta>catchword: and to be</meta>

<margin>Augustine’s doctrine against the ancient Manichaeans <note>original: "veteres Manichæos"</note> concerning man’s free power to change an evil will into a good one fundamentally overthrows the "New Manichaeans," who defend the necessity imposed by the "twin delights."</margin>
[Manichaeans] <note>This continues the word from the previous page.</note> by Saint Augustine’s doctrine. Furthermore, against the ancient Manichaeans, Augustine teaches that it is placed within our power to change an evil will into a good one. But in the Jansenist <note>Followers of Cornelius Jansen, who argued that human nature is so corrupted by sin that we cannot do good without an irresistible impulse of grace.</note> school of the "twin delights," this is completely impossible for a human to do. For anyone who possesses an evil will is, according to Jansenius, weighed down by an **indeliberate evil delight**, which is greater than any indeliberate good delight. To actually change an evil will into a good one, according to that same author, it is necessary for the **indeliberate good delight** <term>indeliberata delectatio: a spontaneous feeling of pleasure or attraction that arises in the soul before the mind has a chance to consciously decide on an action</term> to be greater than the indeliberate evil delight. Yet, according to this same teacher, this is in no way within a person's power, but is in the power of God alone. Therefore, in the Jansenist school of the twin delights—contrary to and in opposition to Augustine—it is not placed within our power to change an evil will into a good one.

<margin>Augustine’s doctrine against the ancient Manichaeans regarding man's free power to choose good and evil, regarding just reward and punishment, and regarding God as a just judge and rewarder, fundamentally overthrows the "New Manichaeans" who defend the necessity of the twin delights.</margin>
Once again, against the ancient Manichaeans, Augustine teaches that it is placed within the power of each person either to choose those things which are good, and thus possess a good will; or to choose those things which are evil, and thus possess an evil will. One is to receive a reward if they choose good from a just rewarder, or undergo punishment if they choose evil from a just judge. But in the Jansenist school of the **twin delights** <term>geminæ delectationis: the theory that a person's choice is always determined by whichever is stronger: the "delight" of grace or the "delight" of worldly desire</term>, for a human to choose good and possess a good will, it is necessary to have an indeliberate good delight that is greater than the indeliberate evil delight. Conversely, to choose evil and possess an evil will, it is necessary to have an indeliberate evil delight that is greater than the indeliberate good delight. However, according to Jansenius, it is neither in a person's power to have an indeliberate good delight that is greater than the evil one, nor to have an indeliberate evil delight that is greater than the good one. Therefore, in the Jansenist school of the twin delights, it is neither in a person’s power to choose what is good and possess a good will, nor to choose what is evil and be...

…and to be of an evil will. It remains, therefore, that both a good and an evil choice are irresistibly necessary for us. Jansenius <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638), a Catholic bishop whose writings on Saint Augustine sparked a massive controversy over grace and free will.</note> admits this. But if this is the case, there is no good <term>merit: the quality of being particularly good or worthy, especially so as to deserve a reward from God</term> in a good choice, and no evil merit in an evil one. Therefore, we would receive no reward for a good choice and will, and we would undergo no punishment for an evil choice and will. Finally—something that Christian ears cannot bear—God would be neither a just rewarder nor a just punisher.

<margin>Augustine’s doctrine against the ancient Manichaeans <note>original: "veteres Manichæos"</note> regarding the **Indifference of the human will**—which acts like a hinge—and regarding the movement of the free will and the just praise or blame of man, fundamentally overthrows the New Jansenist Manichaeans, who defend the necessity of the "twin delights."</margin>

CXIII. Furthermore, against the ancient Manichaeans, Augustine teaches the following: (1) *“The movement by which the will is turned here and there—unless it were voluntary and placed within our own power—a man would neither be worthy of praise when he turns toward higher things, nor worthy of blame when he twists toward lower things, acting as a kind of hinge for the will.”* <note>original Latin: "Motus, quo huc atque illuc voluntas convertitur, nisi esset voluntarius, atque in nostra positus potestate, neque laudandus cum ad superiora, neque culpandus homo esset, cum ad inferiora detorquet quasi quemdam cardinem voluntatis."</note> Therefore, the human will, according to Augustine, is entirely indifferent <note>In this context, "indifferent" means the will is not naturally tilted toward one side but remains free to move in either direction.</note> like a hinge: the movement of this will, by which it is carried here and there, is within the free power of the person. For if this were not so, a person would neither be praised when they turn toward higher things, nor blamed when they turn their will toward lower things, like a hinge. 

But in the Jansenist school of the "two delights," the human will is not indifferent like a hinge; because under a greater good delight, it is irresistibly compelled to will what is good; while under a greater evil delight, it is irresistibly compelled to will what is evil. The movement by which the human will is carried here and there is not within the free power of the person, but is an insuperable <note>Insuperable here means "impossible to overcome" or "unavoidable."</note> necessity for them. Once this insuperable necessity of willing good or evil is established, a person is neither to be praised for willing good, nor blamed for willing evil. Regarding this same free power of man to will good or evil, there are many arguments that the Holy Doctor <note>A traditional title for Saint Augustine.</note> gathers against the ancient Manichaeans which apply equally to these "New Manichaeans."

...they provide. I bring forth a few points (1): *Nothing*, he says, *is so much in our power as the will itself.* Again (2): *Our will would not even be a will unless it were in our power. Furthermore, because it is in our power, it is free for us. For that which we do not have in our power, or which can fail to be what we have, is not free for us.* Again (3): *Whatever this cause of the will is, if it cannot be resisted, one yields to it without sin; but if it can be resisted, let one not yield to it, and one will not sin. Or perhaps it deceives the unwary? Then let him beware, lest he be deceived. Is the deception so great that it cannot be avoided at all? If so, there are no sins. For who sins in that which can in no way be avoided? But is there sin? Therefore it can be avoided.* Finally (4): *To hold anyone guilty of sin because they did not do what they could not do is the height of injustice and madness.* Wherefore, whatever those souls do, if they do it by nature and not by will—that is, if they lack a free movement of the mind toward doing or not doing; if, finally, no power of abstaining from their work is granted to them—we cannot hold them guilty of sin.

<margin>Augustine’s doctrine against the ancient Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans were a dualistic sect that believed human nature was trapped in evil and lacked true free will.</note> regarding man's will being placed in his free power, regarding his power to resist any cause of an evil will, regarding the avoiding of sin and the abstaining from sin, and regarding the injustice and madness of declaring someone guilty who did not do what they could not do, fundamentally overthrows the "New Manichaeans" or Jansenists, who defend the theory of the <term>necessitating twin delight: the Jansenist idea that the will is always compelled by either a "delight" in God or a "delight" in sin, whichever is stronger at the moment.</term></margin>

The sum of the above Augustinian doctrine against the ancient Manichaeans is this: There exists in man a freedom, which in the schools is called **freedom of contradiction** <note>The philosophical ability to choose between acting or not acting.</note>, by which he can act or not act through a free movement of the mind; and therefore he can sin and not sin. Our will is entirely within our own free power. Everyone can abstain from sin. The Soul has the free power to abstain from sin. It is the height of injustice and madness to hold anyone guilty of sin who did not do what they could not do. There is no cause for sinning that one cannot avoid. ...[they] clash <note>original: "gnant", likely continuing from "pugnant" on the previous page</note> entirely with the Jansenist theory of the **two delights**. For in the Jansenist school, under an **indeliberate good delight** <note>In this context, "delight" (delectatio) refers to an inner spiritual attraction or impulse that draws the soul toward an action before the mind has time to fully weigh it.</note> that is greater than an indeliberate evil delight, a man *cannot* sin. Conversely, under an **indeliberate evil delight** that is greater than an indeliberate good delight, a man *cannot help but* sin. Therefore, in the Jansenist view, man lacks the **liberty of contradiction** <term>liberty of contradiction: the specific freedom to choose between doing an act or not doing it</term>, by which he might sin or not sin through a free movement of the soul.

Likewise, according to Jansen, our will is not in our own power, but is in the power of whichever delight overcomes the other by its strength and weight. Furthermore, he who sins is entirely unable to abstain from sin. For he who sins, according to Jansen, is weighed down by an indeliberate evil delight which is greater or heavier than the indeliberate good delight. But under such a heavy weight, one is entirely unable to abstain from sin.

Moreover, Jansen identifies a person as guilty of sin for not resisting a greater evil delight with a lesser good delight. Yet, according to that same author, it is impossible for someone to resist a greater delight with a lesser one. Therefore, according to Jansen, a man is called guilty of sin for *not doing what he could not do*. On the contrary, according to Augustine, to say or judge such a thing is the "height of injustice and madness."

Finally, according to Jansen, an indeliberate evil delight that is greater than an indeliberate good delight is the truest cause of sinning. Since this cause of sinning is indeliberate, we cannot avoid it at all; and since it is greater than the good delight, we have no power to resist it. Such are the things Jansen affirms and preaches. Such are the things Augustine detests and curses when writing against both the new and ancient Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans believed in a cosmic struggle between Good and Evil where human souls were trapped, often arguing that evil actions were the result of a dark nature rather than free choice.</note>.

But for no one is the will as free as it was for him <note>Referring to Adam, the first man.</note>, who stood before his God, by whom he was created righteous, corrupted by no vice whatsoever. This is the summarized teaching of the Holy Doctor <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western Christian theology.</note> against both the new and ancient Manichaeans, contained in the preceding passages. The choice of things lies within the free, deciding, and sovereign will of man. No fault can be found where a necessity of sinning holds dominion. If we are good by necessity, there is no good merit in us. We ought to be good not by necessity, but by free will. Punishment would be unjust, and reward would be unjust, if man did not have a will free from every necessity that is irresistible to him. When liberty from all irresistible necessity is removed, there is no good, and no merit; no just reward, and no just punishment. This truth is known by the light of nature and universally declared by all men: That no one is worthy of blame or punishment who does not do that which he cannot do. <note>original: "Neminem esse vituperatione, suppliciove dignum, qui id non faciat, quod facere non potest." A foundational principle of moral philosophy: "Ought implies can."</note>

Augustine’s teaching against the ancient Manichaeans <note>A dualist sect that taught humanity had no free will because it was controlled by the struggle between light and dark forces.</note> concerning free choice under the deciding, sovereign, and free will of man; regarding the lack of fault under the necessity of sinning; regarding the lack of good merit under the necessity of goodness; regarding unjust judgment.

For he [Adam] could abstain from sinning with the greatest ease; we, however, can do so not without much difficulty.

Secondly, Augustine teaches that the free choice of our will—by which we live either well or poorly—must be vindicated from every bond of necessity, so that God’s judgment in decreeing rewards and punishments is not unjust. Augustine teaches, therefore, that the free choice of our will, by which we live either well or poorly, must be protected both from the Jansenist "good delight" (which, when it is greater than the evil one, irresistibly necessitates us to live well) and from the Jansenist "evil delight" (which, when it is greater than the good one, irresistibly necessitates us to live poorly). This is necessary so that God's judgment in awarding prizes and punishments is not unjust. 

Thirdly, Augustine teaches: *If souls do not have the power to resist evil, they are condemned though innocent; but if they are unwilling to resist, though they could if they wished, their crime is one of free will, not of irresistible necessity.* Yet in the Jansenist school of the two delights, souls do not have the power to resist an indeliberate evil delight if it is greater than the indeliberate good delight; therefore, in that school, the innocent are condemned. Likewise, in that same school, souls are "unwilling" to resist such a delight in such a way that they *cannot* wish to resist it; therefore, in that same school, their crime is not one of free will, but of irresistible necessity.

CXIX. <margin>Augustine’s doctrine against the ancient Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans were a dualistic sect that believed evil was a physical, irresistible force; here the author accuses Jansenists of sharing this error</note> regarding the duty of self-control, which involves ruling, restraining, and curbing all unbidden evil delights; concerning unbidden evil delight, which we always can and must conquer and overcome by the grace of God; concerning the unbidden evil delights within us, which we must bridle, punish, conquer, and fight off; concerning the consent we give to unbidden evil delights—which we are always commanded not to consent to, but to resist and fight—and which we are therefore always able to resist. **CXIX.** In his primary opinion, Augustine teaches that it belongs to the duty of self-control to rule, restrain, and curb all unbidden <note>original: "indeliberatas," referring to spontaneous impulses or "first motions" of the mind that occur before one has time to consciously think</note> evil delights that are contrary to unbidden good delights. But if it should happen—as often occurs in practice—that the unbidden evil delights are more robust and more powerful than the unbidden good delights, then, according to Jansenius, it is outside the power of self-control. Therefore, in that case, it would not at all pertain to the duty of self-control to rule, restrain, and curb those unbidden evil delights that oppose unbidden good delights. For this reason, Augustine’s doctrine regarding contrary delights is utterly repugnant to the Jansenist doctrine.

To this slander by Julian, the Holy Doctor responds that an unbidden evil delight—which is resisted by an unbidden good delight—is of such a nature that we can and must always win and overcome it by the grace of God <note>original: "Dei gratia"</note>. 

On the contrary, according to Jansenius, if the unbidden evil delight is greater than the unbidden good delight (which comes from the grace of God), then we are entirely unable to win or overcome an evil delight of this kind. But if we are unable, then we are not obligated to do so. Therefore, Augustine’s doctrine regarding these two types of delights is entirely contrary to the Jansenist doctrine. 

Again, clearing away Julian’s slander, Augustine affirms with a free voice that the unbidden evil delights dwelling deep within us must be punished, bridled, and fought off by us. Therefore, according to Augustine, we are always able to punish, bridle, fight off, and conquer them. For if we are not able, then we are not obligated. For who...

[...must he] owe that which he cannot do? On the contrary, according to Jansenius, as often as evil delights of this kind are more robust and more powerful than the contrary good delights—which frequently happens in practice—then it is entirely impossible for us to punish, bridle, storm, or conquer them. Therefore, the sound doctrine of Augustine fights against the insane doctrine of Jansenius.

**CXX.** Furthermore, Augustine admits that even though we are baptized, we are engaged in a perpetual conflict with unbidden <note>original: "indeliberatis," referring to spontaneous impulses or "first motions" of the mind that occur before one has time to consciously think</note> evil delights; and in that conflict, he greatly exhorts us to fight, to resist, and to disagree. He puts forward that precept of Ecclesiasticus: *Do not follow your lusts* <note>original: "Post concupiscentias tuas non eas" from Sirach 18:30</note>; which is the same as saying, "Do not consent to your unbidden evil delights." 

But in the Jansenist doctrine of the "two delights" <note>the theory that the human will is like a balance scale, moved necessarily by whichever is heavier: earthly pleasure or divine grace</note>, there is no place for these counsels and exhortations of Augustine. For if unbidden evil delights surpass unbidden good delights in strength—which happens not infrequently—it is then impossible for us not to be overcome, not to yield, and not to succumb; and thus we are commanded to do what is entirely impossible for us. Therefore, in explaining the conflict of the two delights, these two utterly contrary doctrines—the Augustinian and the Jansenist—clash most greatly and most sharply, with Augustine always emerging as the victor and the one who triumphs.

<margin>The doctrine of Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century monk and theologian</note> against the ancient Manichaeans concerning our free power over two contraries, and therefore concerning two contrary unbidden delights, to give the palm <note>a symbol of victory</note> and victory to either the good or the bad.</margin>
Having thus far blocked and raised the massive defenses of Augustine against these "New Manichaeans" (the Jansenists), I now place the authority of Damascene—who fought against the ancient Manichaeans—as the crowning peak. On the authority of Damascene, it is placed within our free power to give the victory to one of two contrary principles, either good or evil; and we ourselves are the cause of one overcoming the other. Therefore, by Damascene’s authority, it is placed within our free power to give the palm and the victory to either a good or an evil delight; and we are the cause of one surpassing the other.

<summary>The author argues that the Jansenist belief in "necessitating delight" makes moral effort impossible, whereas St. Augustine and John Damascene insist that humans have the free power to resist even the strongest spontaneous temptations.</summary>
<keywords>Jansenism, St. Augustine, free will, unbidden delights, John Damascene, Manichaeism, moral responsibility, spiritual conflict</keywords>

# DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENTS
<meta>catchword: INDEX</meta>

<margin>...to give the prize; and that we are the cause that one delight overcomes the other, utterly overthrows the new Jansenist Manichaeans <note>Manichaeism was an ancient dualistic religion; calling the Jansenists "Manichaeans" was a common polemical tactic to accuse them of believing that humans have no free will and are controlled by opposing forces of good and evil.</note>, defenders of the dual necessitating delight.</margin>...overcome. But in the Jansenist school of the "two delights," if both delights are equal, we can award the prize to neither; but if they are indeed unequal, is the good delight less than the evil, or the evil delight less than the good? If the good is less than the evil, then we cannot favor the good; if the evil is less than the good, then we cannot favor the evil. Furthermore, we ourselves are not the cause <note>original: "in causa," meaning the responsible agent or the deciding factor.</note> of one overcoming the other; rather, the delights themselves are the cause, so that we are overcome now by one and now by the other, whichever has prevailed in strength.

->T H E   E N D .<-

| Term | Contextual Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Jansenist** | A follower of the theological movement within Catholicism that emphasized original sin and the necessity of divine grace, often accused of fatalism. |
| **Manichaeans** | Here used as a derogatory term for those who supposedly deny human free will in the face of spiritual forces. |
| **Delight** | (Latin: *delectatio*) An internal pull or attraction toward either a virtuous or sinful action. |
| **Award the prize** | (Latin: *palmam dare*) To grant victory or to consciously choose one side over the other. |

<summary>This page concludes a theological argument against Jansenism, asserting that their "two delights" theory removes human agency and makes individuals passive victims of their strongest impulses. The author argues that for morality to exist, the human will must be the deciding factor rather than just the strength of the spiritual or worldly attraction.</summary>

The **Council of Trent** <note>original: "Tridentinum"; the 16th-century ecumenical council that defined Catholic doctrine against the Reformation</note>, session 6, canon 4, and chapter 5, does not speak of sufficient grace, but of efficacious grace <note>Sufficient grace provides the capacity to do good; efficacious grace is that which actually produces the good effect</note>. 159

The **Council of Trent** teaches that man's free will can dissent from and resist efficacious grace. 159

By the authority of the **Council of Trent**, it is demonstrated that under efficacious grace, which man's free will can resist and dissent from, the liberty of indifference <note>the power of the will to choose between opposites</note> is preserved. 160

**Jansenius** <note>Cornelius Jansen, whose writings on grace were condemned as heretical</note> vainly attempts to evade the authority of the Council of Trent. 160
